questions.prompt: How fast can a cheetah sprint at full tilt, in km/h?
questions.reveal: A cheetah hits 100 km/h in about three seconds, but the whole chase is usually over in under 30 seconds before it overheats.

questions.prompt: Fastest bird ever clocked in a dive: what speed did a peregrine falcon hit, in km/h?
questions.reveal: Peregrines have baffles in their nostrils that slow the incoming air, so their lungs don't burst at that speed.

questions.prompt: Top speed commonly credited to a sailfish, the ocean's speed demon, in km/h?
questions.reveal: Sailfish flash electric blue stripes when hunting, a mood change produced by pigment cells firing in milliseconds.

questions.prompt: Top running speed of an ostrich, the fastest two-legged animal on land, in km/h?
questions.reveal: An ostrich has just two toes per foot, and one of them carries almost all the weight, like a sprinter's spike.

questions.prompt: How fast can a black mamba slither across open ground, in km/h?
questions.reveal: That makes it the fastest snake on Earth, though it would still lose a footrace to a jogging human.

questions.prompt: A common garden snail cruises at roughly what speed, in centimeters per second?
questions.reveal: Snails glide on a ribbon of mucus they secrete as they go, which lets them cross a razor blade unharmed.

questions.prompt: A ruby-throated hummingbird beats its wings how many times per second in normal flight?
questions.reveal: Their wings trace a figure eight, which is why they are the only birds that can fly properly backwards.

questions.prompt: During a deep dive, a blue whale's heart can slow to how few beats per minute?
questions.reveal: At the surface it rockets back up to about 37 beats a minute, near the theoretical maximum for a heart that size.

questions.prompt: A bloodhound's nose packs roughly how many scent receptors?
questions.reveal: A bloodhound's trail evidence has been accepted in court, and the loose facial skin helps waft scent up toward the nose.

questions.prompt: How long was the longest blue whale ever reliably measured, in meters?
questions.reveal: No dinosaur came close: the blue whale is the largest animal known to have ever lived on Earth.

questions.prompt: The colossal squid has the animal kingdom's biggest eye. How wide is it, in cm?
questions.reveal: That is roughly a dinner plate, built to catch the faint glow of prey a kilometer down in the dark.

questions.prompt: The bee hummingbird, the world's smallest bird, tips the scales at how many grams?
questions.reveal: It weighs less than a Canadian penny, and its nest is about the size of a thimble.

questions.prompt: An ostrich egg, the largest egg laid by any living animal, weighs about how many kg?
questions.reveal: The shell is so thick it takes about 90 minutes to hard-boil, and an adult human can stand on an intact one.

questions.prompt: The heaviest insect ever recorded, a giant weta, weighed how many grams?
questions.reveal: That is heavier than a sparrow. New Zealand's wetas grew large in the absence of land mammals to eat them.

questions.prompt: A sperm whale's brain, the largest on Earth, weighs about how many kg?
questions.reveal: About five times a human brain, and it sits behind a head full of spermaceti oil used for echolocation.

questions.prompt: How long is a giraffe's tongue, in centimeters?
questions.reveal: It is a dark purple-black, likely a sunscreen for an organ that spends all day out in the African sun.

questions.prompt: A newborn giant panda cub weighs about how many grams?
questions.reveal: That is roughly 1/900th of its mother, and the cub is born pink, blind and nearly hairless.

questions.prompt: A newborn red kangaroo joey weighs roughly how many grams?
questions.reveal: Blind and jellybean-sized, it crawls unaided through its mother's fur to the pouch, a journey of about three minutes.

questions.prompt: The longest snake ever recorded, a reticulated python, measured how many meters?
questions.reveal: Reticulated pythons can unhinge their jaws via a stretchy ligament, swallowing prey wider than their own head.

questions.prompt: A saltwater crocodile's bite has been measured at roughly how many newtons of force?
questions.reveal: The muscles that open those jaws are so weak that a few loops of tape can hold a croc's mouth shut.

questions.prompt: An elephant's trunk contains roughly how many muscles?
questions.reveal: There is not a single bone in there, yet it can uproot a tree or pick up one tortilla chip without breaking it.

questions.prompt: A North American porcupine carries about how many quills?
questions.reveal: Porcupines cannot shoot their quills; the barbed tips simply detach on contact and work deeper with every muscle twitch.

questions.prompt: Deepest dive by any bird: how far down did an emperor penguin go, in meters?
questions.reveal: Emperors can stay under for more than 20 minutes, hardening their bones so they don't collapse under pressure.

questions.prompt: The record dive by a Cuvier's beaked whale reached what depth, in meters?
questions.reveal: The same species holds the mammal breath-hold record: one whale stayed under for 3 hours and 42 minutes.

questions.prompt: How deep is Challenger Deep, the lowest known point in the ocean, in meters?
questions.reveal: Drop Mount Everest in and its summit would still be more than 2 km underwater.

questions.prompt: How tall is Mount Everest above sea level, per the 2020 China-Nepal survey, in meters?
questions.reveal: The summit rock is marine limestone: it was once seafloor, shoved skyward by India crashing into Asia.

questions.prompt: Hyperion, the world's tallest known tree, stands how many meters tall?
questions.reveal: Its exact location in Redwood National Park is a secret, and visiting it now carries a fine.

questions.prompt: Methuselah, a Great Basin bristlecone pine, is roughly how many years old?
questions.reveal: It was already a sapling when the Great Pyramid was being built, and it still produces viable seeds.

questions.prompt: The fastest-growing bamboo can shoot up how many centimeters in a single day?
questions.reveal: That is roughly 4 cm an hour, fast enough that a patient observer can actually watch it happen. Individual stalks have been clocked past 120 cm.

questions.prompt: The Arctic tern's yearly round-trip migration covers roughly how many km?
questions.reveal: Chasing two summers a year, an Arctic tern sees more daylight in its life than any other animal.

questions.prompt: A monarch butterfly's one-way migration to central Mexico can span how many km?
questions.reveal: No single butterfly makes the round trip; it takes three or four generations to complete the circuit.

questions.prompt: A bar-tailed godwit flew nonstop from Alaska to Tasmania in 2022. How many km was it?
questions.reveal: It flew for 11 days without landing, eating or drinking, having shrunk its own digestive organs to save weight.

questions.prompt: How many months does an African elephant stay pregnant?
questions.reveal: The longest gestation of any land mammal, and the calf arrives already weighing around 120 kg.

questions.prompt: The Virginia opossum has one of the shortest mammal pregnancies: how many days?
questions.reveal: The bee-sized newborns finish developing in the pouch, where a whole litter can fit in a tablespoon.

questions.prompt: The longest-cycle periodical cicada broods stay underground for how many years?
questions.reveal: Prime-numbered cycles of 13 and 17 years make it nearly impossible for predators to sync their own boom years.

questions.prompt: The shortest-lived adult mayfly, female Dolania americana, survives about how many minutes?
questions.reveal: She emerges, mates, drops her eggs and dies before breakfast, having spent nearly two years as a larva.

questions.prompt: At peak season, a queen honeybee can lay how many eggs in a single day?
questions.reveal: That is more than her own body weight in eggs daily, laid one per cell at roughly one every 20 seconds.

questions.prompt: How many years can a Greenland shark, the longest-lived vertebrate, live?
questions.reveal: They don't reach sexual maturity until about age 150, and many carry a parasite dangling from each eye.

questions.prompt: 'Ming' the ocean quahog clam was how many years old when scientists finally aged it?
questions.reveal: Researchers accidentally killed it while prying it open, then had to recount the rings to correct an earlier estimate.

questions.prompt: Creme Puff, the oldest cat ever verified, lived how many years?
questions.reveal: Her Texas owner reportedly fed her bacon, eggs, broccoli and a splash of coffee with cream.

questions.prompt: A koala spends how many hours of each day asleep?
questions.reveal: Eucalyptus leaves are so low in energy and so full of toxins that sleeping is basically a digestion strategy.

questions.prompt: How many vertebrae are in a giraffe's very long neck?
questions.reveal: The same number as a human, a mouse and a whale: each giraffe vertebra is just up to 25 cm long.

questions.prompt: How many hearts does an octopus have?
questions.reveal: Two pump blood through the gills and one serves the body, and that one stops beating when the octopus swims.

questions.prompt: How many eyes does a honeybee have, counting the simple ones on top of its head?
questions.reveal: Two big compound eyes plus three tiny ocelli that track sunlight and keep the bee level in flight.

questions.prompt: How many chambers does a cow's stomach have?
questions.reveal: The rumen alone can hold around 150 liters, a fermentation vat run entirely by microbes.

questions.prompt: The leggiest animal ever found, the millipede Eumillipes persephone, had how many legs?
questions.reveal: It was discovered 60 meters down a mining borehole in Western Australia, blind and thread-thin.

questions.prompt: How many teeth does an adult dog have?
questions.reveal: Puppies get 28 baby teeth and swap the lot out by about six months, usually swallowing them unnoticed.

questions.prompt: A garden snail's rasping tongue carries roughly how many microscopic teeth?
questions.reveal: The radula works like a chainsaw belt, and limpet versions of it are made of the strongest known biological material.

questions.prompt: How many chromosomes does a domestic dog have?
questions.reveal: That is 39 pairs against a human's 23, which is one reason dog genetics gets messy fast.

questions.prompt: Roughly how many beetle species have scientists formally described?
questions.reveal: About one in four known animal species is a beetle, which prompted a famous quip about the Creator's fondness for them.

questions.prompt: Roughly how many living bird species do ornithologists currently recognize?
questions.reveal: The count keeps creeping up, not from new discoveries but from DNA splitting old species into several.

questions.prompt: A 2022 study estimated how many individual ants are alive on Earth?
questions.reveal: Their combined dry weight outweighs all wild birds and mammals put together.

questions.prompt: The longest beaver dam on record, spotted from space in Canada, stretches how many meters?
questions.source: Wood Buffalo National Park, Parks Canada
questions.reveal: It is visible in satellite imagery and was probably started in the 1970s by generations of the same family.

questions.prompt: The heaviest bird nest ever recorded, built by bald eagles, weighed about how many kg?
questions.reveal: Eagles reuse and enlarge nests for decades; this Florida one was nearly 3 m wide and 6 m deep.

questions.prompt: An ocean sunfish can carry how many eggs at once, the most of any known vertebrate?
questions.reveal: A sunfish larva is about 2.5 mm long and grows up to 60 million times heavier, the biggest size jump in vertebrates.

questions.prompt: Light in a vacuum covers how many kilometres in a single second?
questions.reveal: Since 1983 the metre has been defined by this speed, so light's speed can never be measured wrong again.

questions.prompt: How far is the Moon from Earth on average, centre to centre, in km?
questions.reveal: Every other planet in the solar system could be lined up side by side in the gap between Earth and the Moon.

questions.prompt: How many km from Earth to the Sun on average, i.e. one astronomical unit?
questions.reveal: The AU is now fixed by definition at exactly 149,597,870,700 metres, so nobody has to remeasure it.

questions.prompt: How wide is the Sun across its equator, in km?
questions.reveal: Line up 109 Earths edge to edge and you would just about span the face of the Sun.

questions.prompt: Jupiter is the solar system's giant. How wide is it at the equator, in km?
questions.reveal: Jupiter spins once in under 10 hours, which bulges it out about 9,000 km wider at the equator than pole to pole.

questions.prompt: How many km across is Earth, measured at the equator?
questions.reveal: Earth is 43 km fatter through the equator than through the poles, so it is a very slightly squashed ball.

questions.prompt: How many km across is the Moon?
questions.reveal: That is just over a quarter of Earth's width, the largest moon-to-planet ratio anywhere in the solar system.

questions.prompt: A year on Mercury: how many Earth days does one orbit of the Sun take?
questions.reveal: One Mercury day-night cycle lasts 176 Earth days, which is two full Mercury years of sunlight and dark.

questions.prompt: How many Earth years does Neptune need to orbit the Sun once?
questions.reveal: Discovered in 1846, Neptune only completed its first full orbit since discovery in 2011.

questions.prompt: Venus spins painfully slowly. How many Earth days does one Venus rotation take?
questions.reveal: Venus takes longer to spin once than to orbit the Sun in 225 days, and it spins backwards while doing it.

questions.prompt: A Martian sol runs longer than an Earth day. By how many minutes?
questions.reveal: Rover teams live on Mars time, sliding their whole working day about 40 minutes later every single day.

questions.prompt: How many light-years away is Proxima Centauri, the nearest star to our Sun?
questions.reveal: Voyager 1, our fastest departing probe, would need roughly 70,000 years to cover that distance.

questions.prompt: One light-year equals how many trillion km?
questions.reveal: Despite the name, a light-year measures distance, not time, which trips up screenwriters constantly.

questions.prompt: Roughly how many light-years across is the disc of the Milky Way?
questions.reveal: Light leaving one rim of the galaxy today will still be crossing it when human civilisation is ancient history.

questions.prompt: How old is the universe, in billions of years?
questions.reveal: The figure comes from the cosmic microwave background, the faint afterglow of light released 380,000 years in.

questions.prompt: How old is planet Earth, in billions of years?
questions.reveal: The age comes from lead isotopes in meteorites, because Earth's own original crust was long ago recycled away.

questions.prompt: How many minutes does sunlight take to travel from the Sun to Earth?
questions.source: derived from the speed of light and 1 AU
questions.reveal: If the Sun switched off, we would carry on sunbathing for over eight minutes before anyone noticed.

questions.prompt: How many Earths would fit inside the Sun, by volume?
questions.reveal: By mass the Sun is even more dominant: it holds 99.86% of everything in the solar system.

questions.prompt: How fast does the International Space Station orbit Earth, in km/h?
questions.reveal: At that pace the crew laps the planet every 90 minutes and sees 16 sunrises a day.

questions.prompt: How fast must a rocket travel to escape Earth's gravity, in km/s?
questions.reveal: That is about 40,300 km/h. On the Moon a gentle 2.4 km/s would be enough to leave for good.

questions.prompt: How hot is the visible surface of the Sun, the photosphere, in kelvin?
questions.reveal: Sunspots look black only by contrast. At around 3,800 K they would still outshine any furnace on Earth.

questions.prompt: How hot is the Sun's core, in millions of kelvin?
questions.reveal: At that heat and pressure the core fuses roughly 600 million tonnes of hydrogen every second.

questions.prompt: Venus is the hottest planet. What is its average surface temperature in Celsius?
questions.reveal: Hot enough to melt lead, and barely changing between day and night thanks to a runaway CO2 greenhouse.

questions.prompt: Standing on Jupiter's cloud tops, what would surface gravity be in m/s squared?
questions.reveal: You would weigh about two and a half times more. Jupiter's sheer size softens what its huge mass would otherwise do.

questions.prompt: How many years does Halley's Comet take to swing back past Earth?
questions.reveal: Last seen in 1986 and due back in 2061, most people get at most one viewing in a lifetime.

questions.prompt: How many kg of Moon rock and soil did the six Apollo landings bring home in total?
questions.reveal: Some samples are still sealed and deliberately unopened, waiting for instruments nobody has invented yet.

questions.prompt: As of 2024, how many people have walked on the surface of the Moon?
questions.reveal: All twelve walked between 1969 and 1972, and every one of them flew on an Apollo mission.

questions.prompt: Olympus Mons on Mars is the tallest volcano known. How many km does it rise?
questions.reveal: It is roughly 600 km wide, so standing on it the slope would vanish over the horizon before the summit appeared.

questions.prompt: At what temperature in Celsius does liquid nitrogen boil at sea level?
questions.source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics
questions.reveal: Splash it on the floor and it skitters, because each droplet rides on a cushion of its own vapour.

questions.prompt: Helium boils at the lowest temperature of any element. What is it, in kelvin?
questions.source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics
questions.reveal: Chill it below 2.17 K and it becomes a superfluid that climbs the walls of its container and escapes.

questions.prompt: Absolute zero sits at what temperature in Celsius?
questions.reveal: It is unreachable in principle. Labs have hit billionths of a degree above it, but never zero itself.

questions.prompt: Tungsten has the highest melting point of any metal. What is it, in Celsius?
questions.source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics
questions.reveal: That stubbornness is why tungsten filaments glowed white-hot inside light bulbs for a century without melting.

questions.prompt: At what temperature in Celsius does iron melt?
questions.source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics
questions.reveal: Earth's inner core is far hotter than this and still solid, because crushing pressure beats heat.

questions.prompt: At what temperature in Celsius does pure gold melt?
questions.source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics
questions.reveal: Gold is so unreactive that almost every gram ever melted down still exists somewhere on Earth today.

questions.prompt: Mercury is liquid at room temperature. At what Celsius does it finally freeze?
questions.source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics
questions.reveal: Frozen mercury turns into a soft, dull metal you could dent with a fingernail.

questions.prompt: Dry ice skips being liquid. At what Celsius does solid CO2 turn straight to gas?
questions.source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics
questions.reveal: That solid-to-gas leap is called sublimation, and it is exactly why dry ice never leaves a puddle.

questions.prompt: Osmium is the densest natural element. What is its density in kg per cubic metre?
questions.source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics
questions.reveal: A one-litre bottle of osmium weighs about 22.6 kg, roughly a full airline carry-on bag.

questions.prompt: How many protons are packed into a single atom of gold?
questions.reveal: Take one proton away and you get platinum. The alchemists were only ever one particle out.

questions.prompt: As of 2024, how many chemical elements appear on the periodic table?
questions.reveal: Everything past uranium is synthetic, and element 118, oganesson, survives for less than a millisecond.

questions.prompt: How many chemical elements are named after the tiny Swedish village of Ytterby?
questions.reveal: Yttrium, ytterbium, terbium and erbium all came out of one small quarry. No other place on Earth comes close.

questions.prompt: How fast does sound travel through dry air at 20 Celsius, in m/s?
questions.reveal: Every extra degree of warmth adds about 0.6 m/s, so sound genuinely travels quicker on a hot afternoon.

questions.prompt: Sound moving through fresh water at 20 Celsius travels how many m/s?
questions.reveal: Water carries sound over four times faster than air, which is how whale song crosses entire ocean basins.

questions.prompt: How many times could a light beam lap Earth's equator in one second?
questions.source: derived from speed of light and Earth's circumference
questions.reveal: Even at that pace, a call bounced off a distant satellite still lands with a delay you can hear.

questions.prompt: What percentage of Earth's dry atmosphere is nitrogen, by volume?
questions.reveal: Oxygen is only 21%, so the gas we actually depend on is very much the sidekick in every breath.

questions.prompt: How many bones are there in a typical adult human skeleton?
questions.reveal: More than half of them are in your hands and feet: 106 bones sit below the wrists and ankles.

questions.prompt: How many chromosomes are in a typical human body cell?
questions.reveal: That is 23 pairs. A potato has 48, so chromosome count says nothing at all about sophistication.

questions.prompt: What percentage of the human body's mass is made up of oxygen atoms?
questions.reveal: Almost all of it is locked inside water. Carbon comes a distant second at around 18%.

questions.prompt: Roughly how many times does an average adult human heart beat in a single day?
questions.reveal: That works out to roughly 2.5 billion beats across a lifetime, with no maintenance breaks allowed.

questions.prompt: How many litres of blood does a resting adult heart pump every minute?
questions.reveal: Your whole blood supply is about 5 litres, so the entire lot completes a lap roughly every minute.

questions.prompt: Laid end to end, how many km of blood vessels are in an adult human body?
questions.reveal: That is two and a half times around the equator, and most of it is capillaries thinner than a hair.

questions.prompt: How many days does a human red blood cell survive before it is recycled?
questions.reveal: Your spleen retires about two million of them every second while your marrow builds replacements just as fast.

questions.prompt: Unwound and stretched out, the DNA in one human cell measures how many metres?
questions.reveal: Add up every cell in your body and that thread would reach the Sun and back hundreds of times over.

questions.prompt: How many billion base pairs make up one set of the human genome?
questions.reveal: Written out in tiny type it would fill about a million pages, and 99.9% of it matches the person next to you.

questions.prompt: How many billion neurons are in the average adult human brain?
questions.source: Azevedo et al. neuron counting study
questions.reveal: The old textbook figure of 100 billion was a guess. Researchers finally counted by dissolving brains into a soup.

questions.prompt: What is the top speed of a nerve signal in the human body, in m/s?
questions.reveal: That is about 430 km/h on fat myelinated motor nerves, while dull pain signals crawl at under 1 m/s.

questions.prompt: One small step: in what year did Apollo 11 first land humans on the Moon?
questions.reveal: Neil Armstrong's boot prints are still up there — the Moon has no wind to blow them away.

questions.prompt: The 'unsinkable' Titanic struck an iceberg and sank in what year?
questions.reveal: The band famously kept playing as the ship went down; the wreck itself wasn't found until 1985.

questions.prompt: In what year was the US Declaration of Independence adopted in Philadelphia?
questions.reveal: Most delegates actually signed on August 2 — weeks after the famous July 4 adoption.

questions.prompt: In what year did the Berlin Wall fall?
questions.reveal: A botched press-conference answer — 'immediately, without delay' — opened the border that very night.

questions.prompt: In what year did Columbus first reach the Americas?
questions.reveal: Columbus made four voyages and went to his grave insisting he had reached Asia.

questions.prompt: In what year did World War I begin?
questions.reveal: Sparked by an assassination in Sarajevo, the war ultimately toppled four empires.

questions.prompt: The very first iPhone went on sale in what year?
questions.reveal: Steve Jobs pitched it as three devices in one: an iPod, a phone, and an 'internet communicator'.

questions.prompt: The Wright brothers made the first powered airplane flight at Kitty Hawk in what year?
questions.reveal: That first flight lasted 12 seconds — shorter than a modern airliner's wingspan is long.

questions.prompt: Japan attacked Pearl Harbor in what year?
questions.reveal: The attack lasted about 90 minutes and pulled the United States into World War II the next day.

questions.prompt: President John F. Kennedy was assassinated in Dallas in what year?
questions.reveal: The Zapruder home movie of the motorcade became one of the most scrutinized films in history.

questions.prompt: The original Star Wars film first hit theaters in what year?
questions.reveal: It opened in just 32 US theaters — studio executives were bracing for a flop.

questions.prompt: Larry Page and Sergey Brin founded Google in what year?
questions.reveal: The pair once tried to sell their search engine for under a million dollars — and were turned down.

questions.prompt: Wikipedia went live in what year?
questions.reveal: It now spans tens of millions of articles in over 300 languages — all volunteer-written.

questions.prompt: Disneyland opened its gates in Anaheim, California in what year?
questions.reveal: Opening day was nicknamed 'Black Sunday' — a heat wave melted the freshly laid asphalt.

questions.prompt: The first Harry Potter book was published in the UK in what year?
questions.reveal: The first print run was just 500 copies — and about 300 of those went to libraries.

questions.prompt: The Chernobyl nuclear disaster happened in what year?
questions.reveal: The city of Pripyat was evacuated in a single afternoon — 36 hours after the explosion.

questions.prompt: The Eiffel Tower was completed in Paris in what year?
questions.reveal: It was meant to be torn down after 20 years — its usefulness as a radio antenna saved it.

questions.prompt: Parisians stormed the Bastille, igniting the French Revolution, in what year?
questions.reveal: For all the drama, the fortress held just seven prisoners that day.

questions.prompt: Nintendo was founded — as a playing-card company — in what year?
questions.reveal: Nintendo made hanafuda playing cards for nearly a century before touching video games.

questions.prompt: Pharmacist John Pemberton first served Coca-Cola in Atlanta in what year?
questions.reveal: In its first year, Coca-Cola sold about nine glasses a day.

questions.prompt: New Zealand became the first country to give women the national vote in what year?
questions.reveal: Suffragist Kate Sheppard now appears on New Zealand's ten-dollar note.

questions.prompt: The Montgolfier brothers' balloon carried the first humans into the sky in what year?
questions.reveal: A sheep, a duck, and a rooster flew first as test pilots two months earlier.

questions.prompt: Karl von Drais rode the very first bicycle — no pedals yet — in what year?
questions.reveal: Riders pushed it along with their feet, earning it the nickname 'dandy horse'.

questions.prompt: Harvard, the oldest university in the United States, was founded in what year?
questions.reveal: That's a full 140 years before the United States itself existed.

questions.prompt: Ray Tomlinson sent the first ever email between computers in what year?
questions.reveal: Tomlinson chose the @ symbol — and admitted the first message was probably just 'QWERTYUIOP'.

questions.prompt: The Mona Lisa was stolen from the Louvre in what year?
questions.reveal: It vanished for two years — and Picasso was briefly questioned as a suspect.

questions.prompt: The WHO officially declared smallpox eradicated worldwide in what year?
questions.reveal: Smallpox remains the only human disease ever deliberately wiped off the planet.

questions.prompt: Chinese farmers digging a well discovered the Terracotta Army in what year?
questions.reveal: Emperor Qin Shi Huang's clay army numbers around 8,000 soldiers — no two faces alike.

questions.prompt: Concorde carried its first paying supersonic passengers in what year?
questions.reveal: Crossing the Atlantic in under 3.5 hours, you could land in New York 'before' you left London.

questions.prompt: John Logie Baird first demonstrated true television to a live audience in what year?
questions.reveal: Baird's ventriloquist-dummy test subject was nicknamed 'Stooky Bill'.

questions.prompt: Euro banknotes and coins first jingled in European pockets in what year?
questions.reveal: Twelve countries swapped their francs, marks, and lire essentially overnight.

questions.prompt: The oldest surviving photograph was taken by Nicéphore Niépce in what year?
questions.reveal: The exposure took at least eight hours of sunlight — possibly several days.

questions.prompt: The volcano Krakatoa blew itself apart in a colossal eruption in what year?
questions.reveal: The blast was heard nearly 5,000 km away and turned sunsets blood-red worldwide for months.

questions.prompt: James Naismith invented basketball in a Massachusetts gym in what year?
questions.reveal: The first hoops were peach baskets — someone had to fetch the ball after every score.

questions.prompt: The Beatles made their famous US debut on The Ed Sullivan Show in what year?
questions.reveal: About 73 million Americans tuned in — more than a third of the country.

questions.prompt: Bitcoin's very first block — the genesis block — was mined in what year?
questions.reveal: Its creator, known only as Satoshi Nakamoto, has never been identified.

questions.prompt: King John sealed the Magna Carta at Runnymede in what year?
questions.reveal: Only four original copies of the 1215 charter survive today.

questions.prompt: William the Conqueror won the Battle of Hastings in what year?
questions.reveal: The Bayeux Tapestry, embroidered soon after, tells the whole story in 70 meters of cloth.

questions.prompt: Charlemagne was crowned emperor by the Pope on Christmas Day of what year?
questions.reveal: The coronation revived the idea of a Western Roman Empire after more than 300 years.

questions.prompt: Emperor Hadrian began building his famous wall across Britain in what year AD?
questions.reveal: The wall ran about 117 km coast to coast and took roughly six years to build.

questions.prompt: Mount Vesuvius erupted and buried Pompeii in what year AD?
questions.reveal: The ash preserved loaves of bread still sitting in Pompeii's ovens.

questions.prompt: Constantinople fell to the Ottoman Empire in what year?
questions.reveal: The Ottomans hauled warships overland on greased logs to bypass the harbor's defensive chain.

questions.prompt: Gutenberg finished printing his famous Bible — Europe's first major printed book — in what year?
questions.reveal: About 180 copies were printed; roughly 49 survive, each worth tens of millions.

questions.prompt: Plague ships brought the Black Death to Sicily — its arrival in Europe — in what year?
questions.reveal: Within five years the plague had killed perhaps a third of Europe's population.

questions.prompt: Temujin was proclaimed Genghis Khan, ruler of all Mongols, in what year?
questions.reveal: His empire grew into the largest contiguous land empire in history.

questions.prompt: England's navy — with help from storms — defeated the Spanish Armada in what year?
questions.reveal: Atlantic storms actually wrecked more Spanish ships than English cannons did.

questions.prompt: The Mayflower carried the Pilgrims across the Atlantic in what year?
questions.reveal: Its 102 passengers shared a living space about the size of a tennis court for 66 days.

questions.prompt: William Shakespeare died in Stratford-upon-Avon in what year?
questions.reveal: He died on April 23 — traditionally believed to be his own birthday.

questions.prompt: Galileo first pointed a telescope at the night sky in what year?
questions.reveal: Within months he had spotted Jupiter's moons and the craters of our own.

questions.prompt: Isaac Newton published the Principia, laying out his laws of motion, in what year?
questions.reveal: Edmond Halley — of comet fame — personally paid for its printing.

questions.prompt: The Great Fire of London torched the city in what year?
questions.reveal: It destroyed some 13,000 houses, yet the official death toll was only a handful.

questions.prompt: French soldiers in Egypt unearthed the Rosetta Stone in what year?
questions.reveal: Its one decree in three scripts let Champollion finally crack hieroglyphs in 1822.

questions.prompt: Edward Jenner performed the first smallpox vaccination in what year?
questions.reveal: Jenner tested it on his gardener's 8-year-old son, using material from a milkmaid's cowpox blister.

questions.prompt: Ether was first publicly demonstrated as surgical anesthesia in Boston in what year?
questions.reveal: The operating theater is preserved today as the 'Ether Dome' at Massachusetts General Hospital.

questions.prompt: Samuel Morse telegraphed 'What hath God wrought' from Washington to Baltimore in what year?
questions.reveal: The famous message was a Bible quote, chosen by the daughter of a friend.

questions.prompt: Height of Mount Everest above sea level, in metres?
questions.reveal: The 2020 joint China-Nepal survey settled it at 8,848.86 m — and tectonics nudge it a few millimetres higher every year.

questions.prompt: Commonly cited length of the Nile, the classic answer to 'world's longest river', in km?
questions.reveal: Nile vs Amazon is a genuine scientific spat — the Nile's usual figure edges out the Amazon's by a couple hundred km.

questions.prompt: Total area of Russia, the world's biggest country, in millions of km²?
questions.reveal: Russia spans 11 time zones and is nearly twice the size of runner-up Canada.

questions.prompt: How many billion humans were on Earth in 2024 (rounded)?
questions.reveal: Humanity crossed the 8 billion mark in November 2022, per the UN.

questions.prompt: Height of the Burj Khalifa, the world's tallest building, in metres?
questions.reveal: At 828 m it snatched the world record from Taipei 101 by a jaw-dropping 320 m.

questions.prompt: Great-circle (straight-line) distance from New York City to London, in km?
questions.reveal: Concorde once dashed it in under 3 hours; today's jets take about 7.

questions.prompt: How many UN member states are on the continent of Africa?
questions.reveal: That's more than a quarter of the entire UN roster from a single continent.

questions.prompt: Height of Mount Kilimanjaro, Africa's tallest peak, in metres above sea level?
questions.reveal: Kilimanjaro is a free-standing volcano, so trekkers walk from savannah heat to summit ice in under a week.

questions.prompt: Commonly cited length of the Amazon, the world's biggest river by flow, in km?
questions.reveal: Depending on where you say it starts, some expeditions claim the Amazon actually beats the Nile for length.

questions.prompt: Total area of Australia in millions of km²?
questions.reveal: Australia is the only country that covers an entire continent all by itself.

questions.prompt: Population of India, the world's most populous country, in billions (2024)?
questions.reveal: India overtook China as the world's most populous country in 2023.

questions.prompt: Height of the Eiffel Tower to its antenna tip, in metres (as of 2024)?
questions.reveal: A new antenna in 2022 nudged it from 324 m up to 330 m — it grew at age 133.

questions.prompt: Great-circle distance from Sydney to London, in km?
questions.reveal: That's nearly halfway around the planet — the maximum possible for any city pair is about 20,000 km.

questions.prompt: How many member states does the United Nations have (2024)?
questions.reveal: The newest member is South Sudan, which joined in 2011.

questions.prompt: Height of Mont Blanc, Western Europe's highest peak, in metres (2023 survey)?
questions.reveal: Its icy snowcap breathes, so the official height wobbles a metre or two every time surveyors re-measure.

questions.prompt: Length of the Mississippi River alone (without the Missouri), source to sea, in km?
questions.reveal: Add the Missouri and you get a roughly 6,275 km system, one of the longest on Earth.

questions.prompt: Area of Vatican City, the world's smallest country, in hectares?
questions.reveal: That's roughly 60 football pitches — you can stroll border to border in about 20 minutes.

questions.prompt: Population of Iceland, rounded (2024)?
questions.reveal: Fewer people than many single city districts, sharing an island bigger than Portugal.

questions.prompt: Height of the Empire State Building to the very tip of its spire, in metres?
questions.reveal: It reigned as the world's tallest building for about 40 years, until the World Trade Center rose in the 1970s.

questions.prompt: Distance all the way around Earth's equator, in km?
questions.reveal: The metre was originally defined so pole-to-equator measures 10,000 km — hence the suspiciously neat 40,000-ish total.

questions.prompt: How many independent countries are in South America?
questions.reveal: French Guiana looks like number 13 on the map, but it's legally a slice of France.

questions.prompt: Height of Aconcagua, the tallest mountain outside Asia, in metres?
questions.reveal: Aconcagua's summit sits in Argentina, and the normal route needs no ropes — just very good lungs.

questions.prompt: Length of the Danube from Germany's Black Forest to the Black Sea, in km?
questions.reveal: The Danube touches 10 countries — more than any other river on Earth.

questions.prompt: Area of Monaco in km² — the world's second-smallest country?
questions.reveal: Monaco packs about 38,000 residents into that sliver, making it the world's most densely populated country.

questions.prompt: Population of the Greater Tokyo area, the world's largest metro, in millions (2023)?
questions.reveal: Roughly one in three residents of Japan lives somewhere in the Greater Tokyo sprawl.

questions.prompt: Original height of the Great Pyramid of Giza when completed, in metres?
questions.reveal: Erosion and lost casing stones have trimmed it to about 139 m — after roughly 3,800 years as the world's tallest structure.

questions.prompt: At its narrowest point, how many km of sea separate England from France?
questions.reveal: On a clear day you can see France from the white cliffs of Dover with the naked eye.

questions.prompt: How many member countries does the European Union have (2024)?
questions.reveal: Croatia was the most recent to join, in 2013 — and the UK remains the only country ever to leave.

questions.prompt: Height of Ben Nevis, the UK's highest mountain, in metres?
questions.reveal: Modest by Alpine standards, but its summit hosts the ruins of a Victorian weather observatory.

questions.prompt: Total length of the River Thames from source to sea, in km?
questions.reveal: The Thames Barrier has swung shut over 200 times to shield London from surge tides.

questions.prompt: Total area of Brazil in millions of km²?
questions.reveal: Brazil borders every South American country except Chile and Ecuador.

questions.prompt: Population of Australia in millions, rounded (2024)?
questions.reveal: That's roughly the population of Shanghai, spread across an entire continent.

questions.prompt: Height of the Statue of Liberty from ground level to torch tip, in metres?
questions.reveal: Lady Liberty's copper skin is only about as thick as two pennies.

questions.prompt: Great-circle distance from Los Angeles to New York City, in km?
questions.reveal: Flying east often beats flying west by 30-plus minutes, thanks to the jet stream.

questions.prompt: Counting land and territorial waters, how many countries does the equator pass through?
questions.reveal: Of the 13, only Ecuador is literally named after the line.

questions.prompt: Height of Japan's Mount Fuji in metres above sea level?
questions.reveal: Fuji is an active volcano that last erupted in 1707, dusting Tokyo — then called Edo — with ash.

questions.prompt: Length of the Yangtze, Asia's longest river, in km?
questions.reveal: The Yangtze runs entirely within one country — no other river that long can say the same.

questions.prompt: Total area of India in millions of km²?
questions.reveal: India is only about a third the size of the USA yet holds more than four times the people.

questions.prompt: Population of Nigeria, Africa's most populous country, in millions (2023)?
questions.reveal: Nigeria is projected to blow past 400 million people by around 2050.

questions.prompt: Height of the Shanghai Tower, China's tallest building, in metres?
questions.reveal: Its spiral form twists 120 degrees on the way up to shrug off typhoon winds.

questions.prompt: End to end, how many km long is the Panama Canal, deep water to deep water?
questions.reveal: Ships climb 26 m above sea level through locks to sneak between the oceans.

questions.prompt: Elevation of the Dead Sea's surface in metres — Earth's lowest land, so go negative (as of 2015)!
questions.reveal: The lake's surface keeps dropping about a metre a year as its inflow is diverted upstream.

questions.prompt: Length of the Volga, Europe's longest river, in km?
questions.reveal: The Volga empties into the landlocked Caspian Sea, so its water never reaches an ocean.

questions.prompt: Area of metropolitan France — the mainland 'Hexagon' plus Corsica — in km²?
questions.reveal: The nickname 'l'Hexagone' comes from the mainland's roughly six-sided shape.

questions.prompt: Canada's population hit a big round number of millions in 2023 — what was it?
questions.reveal: About 90% of Canadians live within roughly 250 km of the US border.

questions.prompt: Height of Elizabeth Tower (Big Ben's tower) in London, in metres?
questions.reveal: The famous name actually belongs to the 13.7-tonne bell inside, not the tower.

questions.prompt: Length of Egypt's Suez Canal from Port Said to Suez, in km?
questions.reveal: It has no locks at all — the Mediterranean and Red Sea sit close enough to the same level.

questions.prompt: Measured from its ocean-floor base to its summit, how many metres tall is Hawaii's Mauna Kea?
questions.reveal: Base-to-summit, Mauna Kea out-talls Everest — most of the mountain hides under the Pacific.

questions.prompt: Length of the Seine from Burgundy through Paris to the English Channel, in km?
questions.reveal: It's navigable enough that freight barges still glide right through central Paris.

questions.prompt: Surface area of the Caspian Sea, the world's largest inland water body, in km²?
questions.reveal: That's about the area of Japan — legally a lake to some countries, a sea to others.

questions.prompt: Roughly how many people live inside Vatican City (2023)?
questions.reveal: Its residents are mostly clergy and Swiss Guards — citizenship comes with the job, not by birth.

questions.prompt: Height of Toronto's CN Tower in metres?
questions.reveal: It reigned as the world's tallest free-standing structure for 32 years until Dubai stole the crown in 2007.

questions.prompt: Combined length of all Great Wall of China sections, per China's official 2012 survey, in km?
questions.source: China State Administration of Cultural Heritage (2012)
questions.reveal: Counting every branch, trench and ruined stretch, that's over half the circumference of the Earth.

questions.prompt: Height of Rio's Christ the Redeemer statue itself, not counting the pedestal, in metres?
questions.reveal: Its outstretched arms span 28 m from fingertip to fingertip.

questions.prompt: Rail distance of the Trans-Siberian Railway from Moscow to Vladivostok, in km?
questions.reveal: The full run takes about a week, and your watch shifts seven hours along the way.

questions.prompt: A medium banana packs about how many calories?
questions.reveal: Bananas are botanical berries, and each one also delivers about 3 grams of fiber.

questions.prompt: How many calories in a regular 52-gram Snickers bar?
questions.reveal: The bar was named after the Mars family's beloved horse, Snickers.

questions.prompt: On Everest's summit, water boils at what temperature in Celsius?
questions.reveal: Air pressure up there is about a third of sea level, so climbers' tea brews weak and lukewarm.

questions.prompt: One large chicken egg, shell and all — how many grams?
questions.reveal: US egg sizes are set by the dozen: a carton of 'large' must weigh at least 24 ounces.

questions.prompt: USDA's safe internal temperature for cooked chicken, in Celsius?
questions.reveal: That's 165°F — the point where salmonella is destroyed almost instantly.

questions.prompt: A true Neapolitan pizza oven blazes at about how many degrees Celsius?
questions.reveal: At that heat, a pizza is done in just 60 to 90 seconds.

questions.prompt: Calories in one level teaspoon of white sugar?
questions.reveal: A can of cola holds nearly ten of these teaspoons.

questions.prompt: Calories in a single tablespoon of olive oil?
questions.reveal: Pure fat is the calorie king at 9 per gram — more than double sugar's 4.

questions.prompt: How wide is a standard credit card, in millimeters?
questions.reveal: Every card follows the ISO ID-1 format — the same size as driver's licenses around the world.

questions.prompt: How tall is a standard poker-size playing card, in millimeters?
questions.reveal: Bridge cards are an eighth of an inch narrower — easier to fan when you're holding thirteen.

questions.prompt: Grams of sugar dissolved in a 355 mL can of Coca-Cola Classic?
questions.reveal: That's roughly ten sugar cubes swimming in one can.

questions.prompt: Milligrams of caffeine in a typical 240 mL cup of brewed coffee?
questions.reveal: The FDA pegs 400 mg a day as safe for adults — about four of these cups.

questions.prompt: Calories in 100 grams of raw avocado flesh?
questions.reveal: The avocado is technically a single-seeded berry, cousin to the bay laurel.

questions.prompt: Calories in 100 grams of dry spaghetti, straight from the box?
questions.reveal: Once boiled, water plumps it down to about 160 calories per 100 grams.

questions.prompt: A full US gallon of milk weighs about how many kilograms?
questions.reveal: That's 8.6 pounds — why a two-gallon grocery run feels like a dumbbell workout.

questions.prompt: How wide is a standard US queen-size mattress, in centimeters?
questions.reveal: A king is the same length but adds another 40 centimeters of width.

questions.prompt: The WHO says adults should cap daily salt at how many grams?
questions.reveal: Most people worldwide eat roughly double that every single day.

questions.prompt: Calories in 100 grams of butter?
questions.reveal: In the US, anything labeled 'butter' must be at least 80% milkfat by law.

questions.prompt: Calories in 100 grams of iceberg lettuce?
questions.reveal: It earned its name in the 1920s, shipped cross-country under mountains of crushed ice.

questions.prompt: One medium apple: about how many calories?
questions.reveal: Apples float in water because they're about 25% air.

questions.prompt: About how many seeds stud the outside of an average strawberry?
questions.reveal: Each 'seed' is an achene — technically its own individual fruit.

questions.prompt: About how many kernels grow on an average ear of corn?
questions.reveal: Ears almost always grow an even number of rows — usually 16.

questions.prompt: How many keys on a full-size US computer keyboard?
questions.reveal: The 104-key layout exists because Windows keys were bolted onto the old 101-key standard.

questions.prompt: Add up every pip on a single six-sided die — what's the total?
questions.reveal: Opposite faces of a die always add up to exactly 7.

questions.prompt: How many holes are punched into a classic saltine cracker?
questions.reveal: The holes vent steam during baking so the cracker stays flat instead of pillowing.

questions.prompt: How many ridges line the edge of a US quarter?
questions.reveal: Reeded edges originally foiled crooks who shaved slivers of silver off coins — a dime has 118.

questions.prompt: Standard height of a US kitchen countertop, in centimeters?
questions.reveal: The 36-inch standard was settled in the mid-1900s to suit average elbow height.

questions.prompt: How much pressure hides inside a corked champagne bottle, in psi?
questions.reveal: That's about three times your car tire — which is why corks can rocket out at highway speed.

questions.prompt: The recommended home freezer setting, in Celsius?
questions.reveal: At -18°C microbes stop multiplying, though your ice cream still slowly turns gummy.

questions.prompt: Household microwave ovens cook at what frequency, in megahertz?
questions.reveal: It shares the 2.4 GHz neighborhood with Wi-Fi — old microwaves could stutter your internet.

questions.prompt: What percentage of a watermelon's weight is water?
questions.reveal: Cucumbers are even juicier, clocking in around 96% water.

questions.prompt: Roughly how many flowers must honeybees visit to make one pound of honey?
questions.reveal: A single worker bee makes about one-twelfth of a teaspoon of honey in her entire life.

questions.prompt: Heinz ketchup oozes from its glass bottle at about how many meters per hour?
questions.reveal: Heinz rejects bottles that pour too fast — and pros tap the embossed '57' to get it moving.

questions.prompt: A popcorn kernel finally pops at about what temperature, in Celsius?
questions.reveal: Steam pressure inside the hull builds to about 135 psi before the kernel explodes inside-out.

questions.prompt: US federal limit for water per toilet flush, in liters?
questions.reveal: Toilets from before the 1990s guzzled 13 liters or more per flush.

questions.prompt: How many 2×4 LEGO bricks can stack before the bottom one buckles? (lab-tested)
questions.reveal: Stacked up, that tower would stand about 3.5 kilometers tall.

questions.prompt: Water expands by what percent when it freezes?
questions.reveal: That 9% swell is why ice floats — and why forgotten sodas burst in the freezer.

questions.prompt: A modern US penny weighs how many grams?
questions.reveal: Since 1982, pennies are 97.5% zinc wearing a thin copper coat.

questions.prompt: One sheet of standard 80 gsm A4 printer paper weighs how many grams?
questions.reveal: The A-series is clever math: A0 is exactly one square meter, so the gsm arithmetic stays tidy.

questions.prompt: A UK imperial pint holds how many milliliters?
questions.reveal: It's 20% roomier than a US pint — mind the gap when swapping beer stories.

questions.prompt: A whole wheel of Parmigiano-Reggiano weighs about how many kilograms?
questions.reveal: Italian banks have long accepted aging Parmesan wheels as loan collateral.

questions.prompt: The heaviest watermelon ever grown (Guinness) weighed how many kilograms?
questions.reveal: Chris Kent of Tennessee grew the monster — about the weight of two adults.

questions.prompt: The heaviest pumpkin ever weighed (Guinness) hit how many kilograms?

questions.prompt: An ostrich's eye, the biggest of any land animal, measures how many cm across?
questions.reveal: Each eye is bigger than the ostrich's brain, and the retina is packed so densely that a larger eye would actually start to blur the image.
questions.reasoningPath: A human eyeball is about 2.4 cm across. An ostrich's head is small but the eye visibly dominates it, so clearly bigger than a human's — roughly double. That lands near 5 cm.

questions.prompt: A giraffe's heart weighs about how many kg?
questions.source: widely documented (National Geographic; Giraffe Conservation Foundation)
questions.reveal: The left ventricle wall is about three times thicker than the right, and valves in the jugular veins stop blood surging back into the brain when the animal lifts its head from a drink.
questions.reasoningPath: A human heart is ~0.3 kg in a 70 kg body, about 0.4% of mass. A giraffe weighs roughly 1,000 kg, so a proportionate heart would be ~4 kg — and it must be oversized to push blood two metres uphill, so 8-15 kg.

questions.prompt: A narwhal's tusk, really a spiral tooth, can grow to how many metres?
questions.reveal: The tusk carries up to ten million nerve endings and appears to taste the water for salinity, and it spirals anticlockwise on every narwhal ever examined.
questions.reasoningPath: A narwhal's body is 4-5 m long. In every photograph the tusk looks a little over half the body length, which puts it at 2.5-3.5 m.

questions.prompt: Largest wingspan ever measured on a living bird: a wandering albatross at how many metres?
questions.reveal: A sheet of tendon locks the wings open so gliding costs almost no muscle effort — tracked albatrosses have circled Antarctica in about 46 days.
questions.reasoningPath: An albatross photographed beside a person is plainly wider than a tall human is high, but not double it — so somewhere between 3 and 4 m.

questions.prompt: A single camel hump can store how many kg of fat?
questions.reveal: The hump holds fat, not water. The camel's real trick is blood that keeps flowing after it has lost a quarter of its body water — a loss that would kill most mammals.
questions.reasoningPath: A full hump is roughly the volume of a large suitcase, maybe 40 litres, and fat weighs about 0.9 kg per litre — so a few tens of kg.

questions.prompt: At its thickest, a sea otter's fur packs how many hairs into one square centimetre?
questions.reveal: Sea otters have no blubber at all, so the fur is their only insulation — which is why they spend hours a day grooming air bubbles down into it.
questions.reasoningPath: A human head has ~100,000 hairs over ~600 cm², about 150 per cm². Otter fur is the densest known and feels like solid velvet, so think roughly a thousand times denser.

questions.prompt: Counting every row, roughly how many teeth line a great white shark's jaws?
questions.reveal: The rows run like a conveyor belt: a lost tooth is pushed forward and replaced within about a day, and one shark can get through tens of thousands in a lifetime.
questions.reasoningPath: About 50 teeth stand in the working front row, with five to seven back-up rows queued behind them. 50 × 6 is roughly 300.

questions.prompt: A honeybee's brain, about a cubic millimetre of it, holds roughly how many neurons?
questions.source: widely documented (honey bee brain atlas literature)
questions.reveal: With that much, a bee learns to count to about four, recognises human faces in photographs, and can be trained on the abstract idea of 'same' versus 'different'.
questions.reasoningPath: A human brain holds ~86 billion neurons in ~1,200 cm³. A bee's brain is ~1 mm³, over a million times smaller, which suggests tens of thousands — but insect neurons pack far tighter, so round up towards a million.

questions.prompt: The goliath frog, the world's largest, weighs up to how many kg?
questions.reveal: Goliath frogs build their own nursery ponds, heaving stones of up to 2 kg into place — the only frog known to do construction work.
questions.reasoningPath: It is described as the size of a house cat or a large loaf of bread. A cat is 4-5 kg and a big loaf under 1 kg, so the answer sits at a few kg.

questions.prompt: An elephant grows how many sets of molars in a lifetime before the last one wears out?
questions.reveal: Each new set slides forward from the back of the jaw instead of pushing up from below. When the last set wears flat, usually past 60, the elephant can no longer grind its food — and starvation is the commonest death in old wild elephants.
questions.reasoningPath: Elephants live 60-70 years, and a set of grinding teeth chewing coarse vegetation lasts roughly a decade, so about six sets in a life.

questions.prompt: How many degrees can an owl swivel its head to one side?
questions.reveal: Owls have 14 neck vertebrae to our seven, and the arteries feeding the brain run through bony holes about ten times wider than the vessel itself, so nothing pinches shut mid-twist.
questions.reasoningPath: An owl can plainly look straight back over either shoulder — that alone is 180° — and clearly some way past it, but nowhere near a full circle. So about three-quarters of a turn.

questions.prompt: How many fleshy tentacles ring the snout of a star-nosed mole?
questions.reveal: The star is the most sensitive touch organ known in any mammal — roughly five times the nerve fibres of an entire human hand — and it lets the mole find, identify and swallow prey in about a fifth of a second.
questions.reasoningPath: Photographs show a symmetrical pink starburst of short rays, about a dozen on each side of the snout, so somewhere around twenty.

questions.prompt: Roughly how many separate lenses make up one compound eye of a dragonfly?
questions.reveal: The two eyes wrap almost the entire head for nearly 360-degree vision, and a hunting dragonfly catches around 95% of the prey it commits to.
questions.reasoningPath: Each facet is roughly 50 micrometres wide, so about 400 fit in a square millimetre. One eye covers maybe 50-70 mm² of the head, giving tens of thousands.

questions.prompt: How many decibels does a blue whale's call reach underwater?
questions.reveal: The calls sit near 20 hertz, right at the bottom edge of human hearing, and deep-sea sound channels can carry them for hundreds of kilometres.
questions.reasoningPath: A jet engine at takeoff is about 140 dB and a rifle shot about 160. The loudest animal sounds beat both, but decibels are logarithmic so the number cannot run away — the high 180s.

questions.prompt: How many whiskers does a typical cat carry on its muzzle?
questions.reveal: They sit in follicles three times deeper than ordinary hairs and span roughly the cat's own body width — a built-in gauge for whether a gap is worth attempting.
questions.reasoningPath: Look at a cat's face: four rows of three or four whiskers on each side of the nose, so about a dozen per side and two dozen in total.

questions.prompt: Top sprinting speed of an ordinary house cat, in km/h?
questions.reveal: That is quicker than any human has ever run. The cat's sprinting muscles work without oxygen, though, so it gives out after a few seconds and 30 or 40 metres.
questions.reasoningPath: A fit human sprints at about 35 km/h. A cat visibly outruns a running person over a short dash but is nowhere near a cheetah's 120 km/h — so mid-to-high 40s.

questions.prompt: Deer antlers are the fastest-growing tissue in any mammal. How many cm per day at the peak?
questions.reveal: Antlers are grown, hardened and thrown away every single year — the only mammalian organ that fully regenerates — and a bull moose can carry more than 20 kg of brand-new bone by autumn.
questions.reasoningPath: A big rack reaches over a metre in one summer: 120 cm in about 120 days is roughly 1 cm a day averaged, and peak growth runs two or three times the average.

questions.prompt: A common swift can stay airborne without landing for how many months at a stretch?
questions.reveal: A young swift may not touch anything solid for its first two or three years, and adults climb a couple of kilometres up at dusk to sleep in a slow descending glide.
questions.reasoningPath: Swifts come down only to breed. Breeding takes roughly two months of the year, and they famously feed and sleep on the wing the rest of the time, leaving about ten.

questions.prompt: Jonathan the tortoise, the oldest living land animal, hatched in roughly what year?
questions.reveal: He arrived on St Helena in 1882 already fully grown. He is now blind from cataracts and has lost his sense of smell, but his hearing is still excellent.
questions.reasoningPath: Giant tortoises live 150-250 years and Jonathan is the record holder at just under two centuries. Counting back about 190 years from today lands in the 1830s.

questions.prompt: A nursing blue whale calf puts on how many kg of weight per day?
questions.reveal: Blue whale milk is about 40% fat, roughly ten times as rich as human milk, and the calf drinks close to 200 litres of it a day.
questions.reasoningPath: A calf is born at about 2,700 kg and is weaned six or seven months later at over 20 tonnes. That is ~18,000 kg gained in ~200 days, near 90 kg a day.

questions.prompt: How many billion chickens are alive on Earth at any one moment?
questions.reveal: Poultry now outweighs every wild bird species on Earth combined, and a modern broiler reaches slaughter weight in about six weeks.
questions.reasoningPath: There are 8 billion people and chicken is the world's most eaten meat, with birds replaced every couple of months. A standing flock of about three per person gives the mid-20s of billions.

questions.prompt: Of the combined biomass of all mammals on Earth, what percentage is wild mammals?
questions.reveal: Livestock account for roughly 60% of the total and humans about 36% — the world's cattle alone outweigh every wild mammal on the planet several times over.
questions.reasoningPath: Cattle number ~1.5 billion at ~500 kg each; humans are 8 billion at ~60 kg. Wild mammals are mostly small and thinly spread, so their share of the total must be a few percent.

questions.prompt: A landmark 2011 study put the number of species on Earth at how many million?
questions.reveal: Only about 1.7 million species have ever been formally described, so the great majority of species alive today will go extinct before anyone gives them a name.
questions.reasoningPath: Roughly 1.7 million species have been named, and most insects, fungi and deep-sea life remain undescribed. Multiplying the catalogue by about five gives high single-digit millions.

questions.prompt: A 2021 global census estimated how many individual wild birds are alive?
questions.reveal: Only four species pass a billion birds each — house sparrow, European starling, ring-billed gull and barn swallow — while roughly one bird species in eight numbers fewer than 5,000.
questions.reasoningPath: There are about 11,000 bird species. A typical species might number in the low millions, with a handful in the billions: 11,000 × ~5 million is around 50 billion, or a few birds per person.

questions.prompt: China's last full wild census counted how many giant pandas?
questions.source: China's Fourth National Giant Panda Survey (2014)
questions.reveal: The count had climbed enough since the previous survey that the IUCN moved the giant panda from endangered down to vulnerable in 2016.
questions.reasoningPath: Pandas are the emblem of endangerment but nowhere near the brink of the northern white rhino, and they occupy several mountain ranges — so thousands, not hundreds or tens of thousands.

verdicts.note: Answer checks out: Wikipedia (Common ostrich) gives eyes '50 mm (2.0 in) in diameter', 'the largest of any land vertebrate' — 5 cm confirmed. Track position 0.31, fine. Dropping on the reveal. Sentence 1 ('eye bigger than the brain') is a well-repeated and plausible claim (ostrich brain is ~26-42 g vs a ~50 mm globe), but sentence 2 — 'the retina is packed so densely that a larger eye would actually start to blur the image' — is optically backwards and I could find no source for it. A larger eye means a longer focal length, which spreads the image over MORE receptors and improves angular resolution; denser packing sharpens rather than blurs. I could not locate this claim in any source; it reads as invented. Secondary concern: verified.json nature already has #10 'The colossal squid has the animal kingdom's biggest eye. How wide is it, in cm?' — near-identical framing ('biggest eye', 'cm across') — plus #3 (ostrich speed) and #12 (ostrich egg), so this would be the third ostrich question. The 5 cm answer is sound and could be resubmitted with an honest reveal and a non-ostrich framing.

Two independent problems. (1) The reveal reverses the physiology. Wikipedia's Giraffe article states the jugular valves 'prevent blood flowing back into the head from the inferior vena cava and right atrium WHILE THE HEAD IS LOWERED.' The reveal says they stop blood surging back into the brain 'when the animal LIFTS its head from a drink' — the wrong phase of the movement. The hazard is head-down (blood pooling in the head), not head-up. (2) The 11 kg figure is contested. Wikipedia repeats '11 kg (25 lb) and 60 cm heart' unqualified, but Mitchell & Skinner's allometric analysis of the giraffe cardiovascular system (Comp Biochem Physiol A, 2009) reports giraffe heart mass at roughly 0.5% of body mass — unremarkable for a mammal that size, i.e. ~6 kg for a 1,200 kg bull — and argues the high blood pressure comes from a thick-walled, small-radius left ventricle rather than an oversized heart. I could not open the paper directly (ScienceDirect 403, PubMed cookie wall), so I am flagging this as an unresolved dispute rather than a confirmed error, but 6 vs 11 kg is a ~45% spread across sources. Wikipedia does confirm the 7.5 cm wall thickness and 'most commonly seven' jugular valves. Drop on the reveal error alone; the mass dispute compounds it.

Tried to break it and could not. Wikipedia (Narwhal) gives tusk lengths of '1.5 to 3 m', so 3 m as the upper end is right; position 0.26 on a 0.5-10 linear track. Reveal checks out point by point: Wikipedia confirms the tusk is a sensory organ with 'millions of nerve endings' detecting temperature and possibly particle concentration and water pressure (the ~10 million figure and the salinity-tasting result are Nweeia et al.'s work, consistent with this), and confirms the spiral direction — 'the tusk... maintain[s] its characteristic outer large-scale LEFT-HANDED spiral,' i.e. anticlockwise, on every specimen. No duplicate in verified.json nature.

The reveal misattributes a record. I checked Wikipedia's Grey-headed albatross article: 'the fastest recorded circumnavigation took 46 days' — that is the GREY-HEADED albatross (Croxall et al. tracking of 22 non-breeding birds), not the wandering albatross this question is about. Placing it in a wandering-albatross reveal will read to every player as a wandering-albatross fact. Wikipedia's own wandering/snowy albatross article instead says some individuals 'circumnavigate the Southern Ocean three times in one year, covering more than 120,000 km' — no 46-day figure. Separately, the answer number is shakier than claimed: Wikipedia says 'the longest-winged specimens have been about 3.7 m,' and does not mention 3.63 m at all; the Guinness page for largest wingspan is now a 404, so I could not verify the claimed source. 3.63 vs 3.7 is only 2%, so the number is survivable — the reveal is not. The wing shoulder-lock tendon detail is genuine.

Verified: Wikipedia (Dromedary) states the hump stores 'up to 80 lb (36 kg) of fat', in the Adaptations section. Reveal verified too: Wikipedia (Camel) says 'Camels can withstand losing 25% of their body weight in water, whereas most other mammals can withstand only about 12-14% dehydration before cardiac failure results from circulatory disturbance' — which is exactly the reveal's 'blood that keeps flowing after it has lost a quarter of its body water.' The hump-holds-fat-not-water correction is standard. Noted but not disqualifying: 36 kg is a conversion of a round 80 lb, so the underlying measurement is imperial in origin — but the question asks and answers in kg and needs no imperial units to make sense, so it does not trip the imperial rule. Position 0.45. No duplicate.

Verified verbatim: Wikipedia (Sea otter) — 'With up to 150,000 strands of hair per square centimetre (970,000/in2), its fur is the densest of any animal.' Reveal also verified: sea otters have no blubber and rely entirely on fur, and groom air into it. Tried to disprove via the alternative popular figure of '1 million hairs per square inch' — that converts to ~155,000/cm², i.e. the same number, not a contradiction. Position 0.73 on the log track. No duplicate in verified.json.

Verified: Wikipedia (Great white shark) — 'A total of around 300 teeth are arranged in rows like a conveyor belt, with teeth at the back moving to replace those at the front.' The reveal's two claims also check out against Wikipedia's Shark tooth article: 'lost teeth can be replaced within a day' and some Carcharhiniformes 'shed approximately 35,000 teeth in a lifetime' (the reveal's 'tens of thousands'). Caveat I could not close: neither figure is specifically measured for great whites — the day-replacement and 35,000 numbers are cross-species — but the reveal is worded generally enough ('the rows run like a conveyor belt', 'one shark') that it does not assert something false. Distinct from verified.json #46 (dog teeth) and #47 (snail radula teeth).

Verified: Wikipedia's List of animals by number of neurons gives Apis mellifera at 960,000 neurons and ~1x10^9 synapses. One imprecision I checked and am flagging rather than failing it on: that table labels 960,000 as the WHOLE NERVOUS SYSTEM count, while the question says 'brain'. The 960,000 figure originates with Menzel & Giurfa, who state it for the bee brain, and the great majority of bee neurons are in the brain, so the two usages are not ~10% apart in practice. All three reveal claims trace to real experiments: counting to about four (Dacke & Srinivasan), face recognition in photographs (Dyer et al. 2005), and the abstract same/different concept (Giurfa et al. 2001, Nature). Position 0.40. Distinct from verified.json #43 (bee eyes) and #36 (queen egg-laying).

I specifically went hunting for source disagreement here and found the consensus holds. Animal Diversity Web: max mass 3,250 g. San Diego Zoo: '6 to 7.2 pounds (2.7 to 3.3 kilograms)'. Britannica is blocked to fetch (403) but is widely quoted at 3.3 kg. Three independent references cluster at 3.25-3.3 kg. Wikipedia is the outlier at '4.5 kilograms (9.9 lb)' — a single dissenting figure against three, so I am treating 3.3 as correct rather than dropping for source spread; note also that on this 0.1-15 log track the 3.3-vs-4.5 gap is only ~0.06 of the bar, well inside scoring noise. Reveal verified: Wikipedia confirms goliath frogs build nests and move 'quite large stones', with nests exceeding 1 m in diameter (the 2 kg stone figure is from Schäfer et al. 2019). Position 0.70.

Verified in detail: Wikipedia (Elephant) confirms six sets of molars, and confirms the reveal's mechanism explicitly — 'Unlike most mammals, teeth are not replaced by new ones emerging from the jaws vertically. Instead, new teeth start at the back of the mouth and push out the old ones' — with the replacement schedule (2-3, 4-6, 9-15, 18-28, early 40s) and 'The final (usually sixth) set must last the elephant the rest of its life.' The reveal's 'usually past 60' and starvation-as-commonest-death are consistent with the article's account of the last set wearing out. Position 0.26 on 1-20 linear. Distinct from verified.json #20 (trunk muscles) and #32 (elephant gestation).

Every element verified against Wikipedia (Owl), which supports the reveal almost verbatim: 270-degree rotation; 14 cervical vertebrae versus 7 in humans; and 'the foramina in their vertebrae through which the vertebral arteries pass are about ten times the diameter of the artery' (vs roughly equal in humans). Wikipedia adds two supporting details the reveal omits (arteries entering higher in the spine for slack, and the largest carotid anastomosis of any bird). I considered dropping this as too-famous/pure recall, but with a 0-360 linear track a player still has to judge between 180, 270 and 360, so it remains estimable. Position 0.75. No duplicate.

Verified: Wikipedia (Star-nosed mole) — '22 fleshy finger-like appendages, or tendrils, that ring their nostrils.' Reveal checks out with one number worth watching: Wikipedia gives 106,000-117,000 myelinated nerve fibres and calls the star 'about 6 times more sensitive than the human hand, which contains about 17,000 receptors' — the reveal says 'roughly five times', which is Catania's own habitual phrasing and is on the conservative side of the Wikipedia figure, so it understates rather than overstates. Feeding speed also checks out: prey consumed in 'as little as 120 milliseconds (average: 227 ms)', i.e. the reveal's 'about a fifth of a second'. The claimed source (Guinness) is not what I verified against — the count comes from the mammalogy literature — but the number itself is solid. Position 0.42.

The number is inflated. Wikipedia (Dragonfly) states 'An adult dragonfly's compound eyes have nearly 24,000 ommatidia each', citing two actual species counts: 22,650 and 23,890. The candidate's 30,000 is the popular-media figure, ~25% above the measured values — past the 10% tolerance — so I am correcting to 24,000 rather than dropping, since the underlying question is sound and the measured range (22,650-23,890) is tight. I could not find independent support for 30,000 in a source that reports a measurement; Wikipedia's Compound eye article gives no dragonfly figure at all. Both reveal claims verified: 'A dragonfly can see in 360 degrees, and nearly 80 percent of the insect's brain is dedicated to its sight', and 'dragonflies are efficient hunters, catching up to 95% of the prey they pursue.' Corrected position on the 100-300,000 log track is 0.685, in band.

Verified: Wikipedia (Blue whale) gives call loudness of 188 decibels with fundamental frequencies 'ranging from 8 to 25 Hz' — which supports the reveal's 'near 20 hertz, right at the bottom edge of human hearing' (human hearing bottoms out around 20 Hz). Long-range propagation via the SOFAR/deep sound channel is standard acoustics. The one thing I probed: 188 dB is referenced to 1 microPascal at 1 m underwater, a different reference than airborne dB, so a naive comparison to a jet engine would be wrong — but the question says 'underwater', which correctly scopes it. Position 0.71 on 60-240 linear. Note for the set as a whole: with verified.json #7 (blue whale dive heart rate) and #9 (blue whale length) already in, plus candidate [19], the blue whale would appear four times in this category.

I could not verify the count from any authoritative source, and the reveal contains a claim Wikipedia itself flags as unsupported. I checked Wikipedia's Whiskers/Vibrissa article, the Cat article, and Cat anatomy: none gives a muzzle whisker count for cats. Whiskers gives 'approximately 30 macrovibrissae on each side of the face' for rats and mice but nothing for cats; Cat says only that cats have 'dozens of movable whiskers (vibrissae) over their body'. The 24 figure (12 per side in 4 rows) is standard in the cat-vibrissae literature but I could not close it in-session, and it varies between individuals — 'a typical cat' is doing a lot of work for a question scored to the unit. Worse, on the reveal: Wikipedia states cats' whiskers 'extend out to about the same width as the cat's body' but explicitly notes this claim LACKS STRONG CITATION, and the whisker-as-gap-gauge story is described as anecdotal. The reveal asserts as fact what the source flags as uncited.

48 km/h is exactly 30 mph — a round imperial folk-figure with no measurement behind it that I could find. Wikipedia's Fastest animals list, which is the natural place for it, has NO entry for the domestic cat at all; neither Cat nor Cat anatomy gives a running speed. So the figure traces to popular-source repetition, not to any clocked trial, and competing popular figures run from ~30 to ~48 km/h. That matters because the reveal is built on the margin: Wikipedia gives Usain Bolt's peak instantaneous speed as 44.35 km/h, so 'quicker than any human has ever run' holds only if the cat figure really is 48 and collapses if the true value is 45 or lower — the reveal is load-bearing on an unsourced number. Compounding it, verified.json nature already carries four animal-top-speed questions (#0 cheetah, #2 sailfish, #3 ostrich, #4 black mamba), so this is the fifth speed question in the category.

Tried to disprove the rate and it held: Wikipedia (Elk) states antlers grow 'at a rate of 2.5 centimetres (0.98 in) per day.' Two corrections that do not change the verdict. First, the claimed source is wrong — this is not a Guinness record; the general Antler article says only that antlers 'grow faster than any other mammal bone', and the Moose article calls them 'one of the fastest growing animal organs', so the prompt's 'fastest-growing tissue in any mammal' is a slight overstatement of what sources actually assert (fastest-growing BONE is the defensible claim). Second, the reveal's moose figure is conservative and safe: Wikipedia records an Alaskan moose antler set at 36 kg, so 'more than 20 kg' is comfortably true. The 'only mammalian organ that fully regenerates' claim is the standard framing in the regeneration literature. Position 0.78.

Verified down to the citation: Wikipedia (Common swift) cites the exact paper claimed — Hedenström et al., 'Annual 10-Month Aerial Life Phase in the Common Swift Apus apus', Current Biology (2016) — for 10 months airborne without landing. So the claimed source is real and correctly attributed, which was not true of several others in this batch. Wikipedia confirms swifts 'drink, feed, and often mate and sleep on the wing'; the reveal's dusk ascent to a couple of kilometres to sleep in a descending glide matches the radar work on high-altitude roosting flights, and the two-to-three-year first-landing figure follows from swifts remaining aloft until first breeding. Position 0.67. No duplicate.

Verified line by line against Wikipedia (Jonathan the tortoise): 'hatched c. 1832'; arrived on Saint Helena in 1882 'at about 50 years of age', i.e. already fully grown; and a 2015 veterinary assessment finding he is 'blind from cataracts, has lost his sense of smell, and so cannot detect food ... but he has retained excellent hearing' — the reveal is essentially a paraphrase of the source. Guinness recognition as 'oldest known living land animal' is confirmed, and he is recorded as alive as of 2026 (193-194 years old), so the premise is current. I checked the staleness angle: the hatch year is fixed and does not drift, and it is genuinely estimable — a player who knows he is the oldest living land animal at ~190 years can back into the 1830s. Position 0.66.

Verified: Wikipedia (Blue whale) states a calf gains 'approximately 90 kg (200 lb) per day.' Reveal is supported but with one number worth noting: Wikipedia gives maternal milk production at ~220 kg/day (range 110-320), while the reveal says the calf drinks 'close to 200 litres a day' — same order and inside the cited range, so not a conflict. The ~40% milk fat is consistent with the published 35-50% range for blue whale milk (roughly ten times human milk's ~4%, so the comparison holds). Position 0.76 on the 2-300 log track. Same category-crowding note as [13]: this would be the fourth blue whale question alongside verified.json #7 and #9.

Verified: Wikipedia (Chicken) — 'As of 2023, the global chicken population exceeded 26.5 billion, with more than 50 billion birds produced annually for consumption.'
