Note the article does NOT attribute this to the FAO, so the claimed source is unconfirmed even though the number is right. I weighed dropping this under the 'changes year to year' rule, since FAO chicken stocks do drift upward by roughly 2% a year: 26 billion (2023) will read as ~27-28 billion by the late 2020s. I am keeping it because the drift is far inside scoring tolerance on a 0.5-100 log track (a full billion moves the bar by under 0.01) and the prompt says 'at any one moment' rather than pinning a year. Reveal verified against Bar-On et al.: poultry biomass (~0.005 Gt C) exceeds all wild birds (~0.002 Gt C), and six-week broiler grow-out is standard. Distinct from verified.json #50 (bird species count).

I recomputed the reveal's arithmetic from the primary figures rather than trusting it. Bar-On, Phillips & Milo (2018 PNAS) give wild mammals ~0.007 Gt C, humans ~0.06, livestock ~0.1, total ~0.167 — which yields wild 4.2%, humans 35.9%, livestock 59.9%. That matches the answer (4%) and the reveal ('livestock roughly 60%, humans about 36%') exactly. Wikipedia's Biomass (ecology) article confirms the headline: 'Humans and their livestock represent 96% of all mammals on earth in terms of biomass, whereas all wild mammals represent only 4%.' Caution flag: that same Wikipedia passage renders the components as 3 / 80 / 90 million tonnes C, which would give wild ~1.7%, not 4% — the Wikipedia component breakdown is internally inconsistent with its own 4% headline, whereas the original Bar-On numbers are consistent. I am going with the paper. The cattle-outweigh-all-wild-mammals claim checks out at roughly 9x. Position 0.13 — inside the band but near the low edge, so most players will overshoot, which is the point of the question.

Verified: Wikipedia (Global biodiversity) attributes to Mora et al. (2011) an estimate of '8.7 million +/- 1.3 million eukaryotic species on Earth', and confirms the reveal's second half — approximately 1.74 million species formally described, with over 80% remaining undescribed. One precision point I checked and judged non-fatal: Mora's estimate is specifically for EUKARYOTIC species, while the prompt says 'species on Earth'; the study is universally reported under the shorter phrasing and the reveal's 1.7 million described figure is the matching comparison, so no player is misled about magnitude. The +/- 1.3 million uncertainty (15%) is real but the question says 'a landmark 2011 study put the number at', which correctly asks for the study's point estimate rather than ground truth. Position 0.35. Distinct from verified.json #49 (beetle species) and #50 (bird species).

Partially verified — I could not reach the paper itself (PNAS 403, Science 403, phys.org and the UNSW release both 404), so I triangulated. Wikipedia's List of birds by population gives a global total of 50-100 billion mature individuals citing Bar-On et al. 2018 and Gaston et al., which brackets the candidate's 50 billion at the low end and is consistent with it. The reveal's specifics match Callaghan et al.'s published findings as I know them: four species above a billion (house sparrow, European starling, ring-billed gull, barn swallow) and ~1,180 species (about 12%, i.e. one in eight) under 5,000 individuals. Two honest caveats. The estimate carries a very wide confidence interval (roughly 40-118 billion), so 50 billion is a point estimate on a fuzzy distribution — mitigated by the extremely wide 5e9-1e12 log track. And Wikipedia's species-by-species list, which uses BirdLife rather than Callaghan's model, puts barn swallow at 290-487 million, far below Callaghan's ~1.1 billion; that is a methodology difference, not an error in the reveal, but it means the four-species claim is one study's result, not a cross-source consensus. Position 0.44. Distinct from verified.json #50.

The number is confirmed but the prompt wording is a staleness trap. Wikipedia (Giant panda) verifies the count exactly: the Fourth National Survey (2011-2014, published 2015) found 'the wild giant panda population aged over 1.5 years, excluding dependent young, had increased to 1,864 individuals', and confirms the reveal's IUCN downgrade to Vulnerable in 2016. My problem is with 'China's LAST full wild census': China has had a Fifth National Giant Panda Survey in progress, and I could not establish whether results have been published (no Wikipedia article exists for it; the WWF species page is 403). The moment a fifth survey reports, this prompt silently starts asking for a different number while the answer stays 1,864 — exactly the kind of drift that gets a player scored wrong. Fixing by pinning the prompt to the named survey, which also matches the claimed source and makes the question permanently checkable. Answer and 0-5000 linear range unchanged (position 0.37).
verdicts.correctedPrompt: China's Fourth National Giant Panda Survey, completed in 2014, counted how many wild giant pandas?

questions.prompt: A lightning bolt heats the air in its channel to roughly what temperature, in kelvin?
questions.reveal: The channel is only a few centimetres wide, and the air around it expands so violently that the shock wave reaches us as thunder.
questions.reasoningPath: The Sun's surface is about 6,000 K, and lightning is famously hotter than that — but it is superheated air, not fusion, so not millions. A few times the Sun's surface lands you in the tens of thousands.

questions.prompt: Lowest air temperature ever recorded at ground level, at Vostok Station in Antarctica, in Celsius?
questions.reveal: Satellites have since read the ice surface on the Antarctic plateau even colder, but only a thermometer standing on the ground counts for the official record.
questions.reasoningPath: A brutal Siberian winter reaches about -50 °C. Vostok sits 3 km up on an ice plateau with months of no sunlight, so push well past that — but nowhere near liquid nitrogen's -196 °C.

questions.prompt: Mawsynram in India, the wettest inhabited place on Earth, averages how many mm of rain a year?
questions.source: Guinness World Records / India Meteorological Department
questions.reveal: Two Colombian towns, Lloró and López de Micay, report even higher averages. In Meghalaya the rain rots timber, so villagers train fig roots into living bridges instead.
questions.reasoningPath: A rainy temperate city gets around 1,000 mm a year and a wet tropical monsoon site a few thousand. The record holder should be roughly ten times a rainy European city — so about ten metres of rain.

questions.prompt: Strongest surface wind gust ever measured, on Barrow Island in a 1996 cyclone, in km/h?
questions.reveal: The reading sat unverified for 14 years. Before it was confirmed, the record belonged to a mountain observatory gust of 372 km/h measured back in 1934.
questions.reasoningPath: A severe tropical cyclone sustains roughly 250 km/h, and gusts run well above the sustained wind. The all-time record should beat that but stay far short of the 1,235 km/h speed of sound.

questions.prompt: A typical fair-weather cumulus cloud carries how many tonnes of water?
questions.reveal: The droplets are spread so thinly — about half a gram of water per cubic metre — that the cloud is still lighter than the dry air it displaces, which is why it floats.
questions.reasoningPath: A modest cumulus is about a kilometre on each side, so a billion cubic metres. Cloud water is famously sparse, roughly half a gram per cubic metre: a billion times half a gram is 500 tonnes.

questions.prompt: A rainbow's arc always sits at what angle from the point directly opposite the Sun, in degrees?
questions.reveal: This is why you can never reach a rainbow — it is an angle, not a place. From an aircraft you can see the whole circle, and the person beside you sees a different one, built from different raindrops.
questions.reasoningPath: Rainbows arch high when the Sun is near the horizon and vanish once the Sun climbs high, so the radius is a large slice of the 90° from horizon to overhead — but clearly under half of it.

questions.prompt: The Kola Superdeep Borehole, the deepest hole ever drilled, reached what depth in metres?
questions.reveal: Drilling stopped because the rock at the bottom was 180 °C rather than the predicted 100 °C and flowed like plastic. It took about 20 years to get that far.
questions.reasoningPath: The deepest mines bottom out near 4 km, and the continental crust runs 30-40 km thick. A record-breaking drill should beat the mines several times over without approaching the mantle: low tens of kilometres.

questions.prompt: The Atlantic widens at the Mid-Atlantic Ridge by how many millimetres each year?
questions.reveal: That is about the speed your fingernails grow. Iceland straddles the ridge, so the island is quietly being pulled in half.
questions.reasoningPath: The Atlantic is roughly 5,000 km wide and opened over about 200 million years. Five billion millimetres divided by 200 million years gives around 25 mm a year.

questions.prompt: The 1883 Krakatoa eruption was heard by people how many km away?
questions.reveal: The pressure wave circled the planet several times and kept registering on barographs for days. Sailors 65 km away had their eardrums ruptured.
questions.reasoningPath: Thunder carries about 15 km and a large explosion tens of km. For the loudest event in recorded history think continental scale — thousands of km, but not the 20,000 km to the far side of the world.

questions.prompt: How far below its entrance does the deepest cave yet explored descend, in metres?
questions.reveal: The two deepest known caves, Veryovkina and Krubera, sit in the same Caucasus massif and are within metres of each other. A flash flood trapped a team near the bottom in 2018.
questions.reasoningPath: Caves are carved downward by water, so their depth is capped by the height of the limestone massif above. A big karst mountain block is about 2 km thick, and mines reach 4 km — so a couple of thousand metres.

questions.prompt: Averaged over its whole floor, how deep is the ocean, in metres?
questions.reveal: The average height of dry land above sea level is only about 840 m, so Earth's solid surface is far more low-lying basin than mountain.
questions.reasoningPath: The trenches reach 11 km but are narrow slivers, and the continental shelves are only about 150 m deep. Most of the sea floor is abyssal plain a few kilometres down, so the average is around 3-4 km.

questions.prompt: How many grams of salt are dissolved in one litre of average seawater?
questions.reveal: Extract all of it and spread it over the land and you would have a salt layer roughly 150 m thick.
questions.reasoningPath: Seawater tastes strongly salty but is nowhere near saturated brine, which holds about 360 g per litre. A mouthful is maybe a couple of tablespoons of salt per litre, and a tablespoon is roughly 15 g.

questions.prompt: What percentage of a floating iceberg's volume sits below the waterline?
questions.reveal: The ratio falls straight out of the densities: ice at about 917 kg per cubic metre against seawater at 1,025. As melting shifts the balance, icebergs sometimes roll over without warning.
questions.reasoningPath: Ice only just floats — it is a few percent less dense than water, not half as dense. So only a thin sliver can ride above the surface and the great majority must be submerged.

questions.prompt: Crossing deep open ocean, a tsunami travels at roughly what speed, in km/h?
questions.reveal: Out at sea the wave can be under a metre high and slide beneath a ship unnoticed. It only slows and piles up when it reaches shallow water.
questions.reasoningPath: Tsunamis are known to cross the whole Pacific in about a day. Roughly 15,000 km in around 20 hours works out near 750 km/h — the speed of an airliner.

questions.prompt: Greatest tidal range ever recorded, in Canada's Bay of Fundy, in metres?
questions.reveal: The bay narrows from 80 km wide to about 5 km, and the water sloshing in and out takes almost exactly one tidal cycle — so every tide reinforces the last.
questions.reasoningPath: An ordinary coastal tide runs 1-2 m and a big funnelled estuary 5-10 m. The world record should be several times a normal tide: a wall of water about five storeys tall.

questions.prompt: The Great Barrier Reef stretches along the Australian coast for how many km?
questions.source: Great Barrier Reef Marine Park Authority
questions.reveal: It is not one reef but roughly 2,900 of them, plus 900 islands — the largest structure on Earth built by living creatures.
questions.reasoningPath: Australia is about 4,000 km across, and the reef shadows the Queensland coast from Cape York down past Cairns — over half that coastline, so a couple of thousand kilometres.

questions.prompt: The Amazon pours how many cubic metres of water into the Atlantic every second?
questions.source: widely documented (mean discharge at the mouth)
questions.reveal: That is about a fifth of all the river water reaching the world's oceans, and the plume keeps the Atlantic noticeably fresh more than 100 km offshore.
questions.reasoningPath: The basin covers roughly 6 million km² and catches about 2 m of rain a year; suppose a third runs off. That is 4 trillion cubic metres a year, divided by 31 million seconds — a couple of hundred thousand per second.

questions.prompt: What percentage of the world's fresh water is locked up in glaciers, ice caps and snow?
questions.reveal: Nearly all the rest is groundwater. Lakes and rivers together hold about 1%, and Antarctica alone accounts for roughly 60% of all the fresh water on Earth.
questions.reasoningPath: Fresh water is essentially ice, groundwater, and a sliver of lakes and rivers. Two continent-sized ice sheets kilometres thick must beat all the world's aquifers, so ice takes a clear majority — two-thirds or so.

questions.prompt: Roughly how many trillion trees are alive on Earth?
questions.reveal: The same study found humans fell about 15 billion trees a year, and that Earth carried roughly twice as many before farming began.
questions.reasoningPath: Forests cover something like 40 million km². A forest holds on the order of 50,000 trees per km² once saplings are counted, and 40 million times 50,000 is about 2 trillion.

questions.prompt: The largest single flower ever measured, a Rafflesia in Sumatra, spanned how many cm?
questions.reveal: The plant has no leaves, stems or roots — it lives as threads inside a jungle vine and surfaces only to bloom, smelling of rotting meat to draw carrion flies.
questions.reasoningPath: Every photograph shows it filling an adult's lap, comparable to a car tyre or a bicycle wheel. That puts it around a metre across, not a few centimetres and not several metres.

questions.prompt: Pando, a single aspen that grew into a whole forest, covers roughly how many hectares?
questions.reveal: All 47,000 trunks share one root system and one genome — a single male tree weighing some 6,000 tonnes. Deer eating the young shoots are now stopping it from replacing itself.
questions.reasoningPath: Photographs show a grove you could walk across in under an hour, not a whole mountainside. A football pitch is about 0.7 ha, so a few dozen hectares — a large city park.

questions.prompt: The honey fungus in Oregon, the largest known organism, spreads across how many km²?
questions.reveal: Almost all of it is invisible: shoelace-like cords threading through soil and roots, thought to be thousands of years old, quietly killing the conifers it grows through.
questions.reasoningPath: It is described as covering a patch of forest a few kilometres across, and a 3 km by 3 km block is 9 km². Big enough to walk around in a day, far smaller than a national park.

questions.prompt: How many milliseconds does a Venus flytrap take to snap shut?
questions.reveal: The trap counts. Two touches on its trigger hairs within about 20 seconds close it, and five touches start the digestive glands — so rain and falling debris do not waste a meal.
questions.reasoningPath: It has to beat an insect that reacts in tens of milliseconds, but it is a plant flexing water pressure rather than a muscle. So a fraction of a second — around a tenth.

questions.prompt: The oldest plant tissue ever regrown into a living, flowering plant was how many years old?
questions.reveal: It came from an Ice Age ground squirrel's burrow in Siberian permafrost. The oldest actual seed ever sprouted is far younger: a 2,000-year-old date palm from Masada.
questions.reasoningPath: Permafrost preservation points to the last ice age — tens of thousands of years, not millions, since DNA would not survive that long, and far more than the ancient seeds famously grown from archaeological digs.

questions.prompt: How many million km² does the Sahara, the largest hot desert, cover?
questions.reveal: Sand dunes make up only about a quarter of it; most of the Sahara is bare rock and gravel plain. Six thousand years ago it held lakes, grassland and hippos.
questions.reasoningPath: Africa is about 30 million km², and the Sahara runs across the entire northern third of it from the Atlantic to the Red Sea. Roughly a third of Africa gives around 9-10 million km².

verdicts.note: Checked NWS lightning-science page and Wikipedia Lightning/Thunder. NWS states 50,000 F = 27,760 C = 28,033 K ('5x hotter than the sun's surface'). Wikipedia Lightning: core 'may exceed 27,800 C'. Wikipedia Thunder gives the channel rising to ~30,000 K peak, average ~20,400 K over its 50-microsecond life. So 30,000 K is the standard PEAK figure and sits 7% above NWS's number - inside the 10% band. Reveal verified: Thunder article confirms the rapid expansion forms a shock wave 'similar in principle to an explosion' which we hear as thunder; the 1-2 cm channel core is the standard figure. Track: log ln(30)/ln(60)=0.831, inside band. Caveat for the reveal writer: 30,000 K is peak, not average.

Verified against Wikipedia 'Lowest temperature recorded on Earth': -89.2 C (-128.6 F; 184.0 K) at Vostok Station, 21 July 1983, still certified by WMO as the official ground-level air-temperature record. Date, station and value in the source string all match exactly. Reveal verified: the satellite figure (-92 C along the Dome Argus/Dome Fuji ridge, 10 Aug 2010, reported Dec 2013) is explicitly described as provisional and NOT the record because it measures ice-surface rather than air temperature - exactly what the reveal says. Track: linear (-89.2+120)/120 = 0.257, inside band.

Checked Wikipedia Mawsynram. 11,872 mm (467.4 in) is confirmed as the headline average. BUT the same article gives IMD's own means as 12,393 mm (1950-2000) and 12,120 mm (2000-2020) - so the answer is 2-4% BELOW the IMD figures it claims as a source, and Guinness is separately cited there only for a 26,000 mm single-year (1985) figure, not the 11,872 average. Spread stays inside 10% and the log range spans 50x, so scoring impact is nil. Reveal verified exactly: Lloro 12,717 mm (1952-1989) and Lopez de Micay 12,892 mm (1960-2012) both reported higher. Note both Colombian rivals are inhabited municipalities, so 'the wettest inhabited place on Earth' is a Guinness title, not an undisputed fact - suggest rewording to 'credited as the wettest inhabited place'. Track: log 0.455.

Verified against Wikipedia 'Wind speed': 113.3 m/s = 408 km/h = 253 mph, Barrow Island, Cyclone Olivia, 10 April 1996, certified by WMO in 2010. That is exactly 14 years unverified, matching the reveal. Previous record confirmed: Mount Washington, 12 April 1934, 103.266 m/s = 371.76 km/h, i.e. the reveal's 372 km/h and 1934 - both correct, and it is a mountain observatory. One real caveat I tried to break it on: Doppler radar has measured far higher speeds in tornadoes (up to 150 m/s in the 2013 El Reno tornado), but those are explicitly 'not considered official records'. Since the prompt anchors to Barrow Island and a 1996 cyclone the target is unambiguous, but 'ever measured' would be safer as 'ever recorded by a surface weather station'. Track: linear 408/500 = 0.816, inside band.

Could not reach the USGS Water Science School page (404s and a TLS cert failure), and neither Wikipedia Cloud nor Cumulus cloud carries a cloud-mass figure, so I verified by reconstructing the calculation instead: 1 km^3 of cloud at 0.5 g/m^3 = 5x10^8 g = 500 tonnes, which matches the widely reproduced 1.1 million pounds (499 t). Internally consistent, and the reveal's 0.5 g/m^3 is consistent with Wikipedia Cumulus cloud's stated max of 1.25 g/kg of air. Flag honestly: this is one back-of-envelope (LeMone/USGS) with an arbitrary assumed 1 km^3 volume, not a measurement - double the cloud's linear size and you get 8x the mass. The 100,000x log range makes that harmless. Weakest part is the reveal's 'lighter than the dry air it displaces': true because moist air is less dense than dry air (virtual temperature effect), but the condensed droplets actually add density, and the textbook reason clouds persist is the ~1 cm/s droplet terminal velocity plus updrafts. Track: log 0.600.

Verified against Wikipedia Rainbow: primary bow at 40-42 deg from the antisolar point, red at 42.5 deg, blue at 40.6 deg. 42 deg is the standard single figure and sits within the stated band. Every reveal claim checked out verbatim in the source: 'observers at different positions, and each observer's two eyes, never see exactly the same rainbow' (different raindrops, person beside you sees a different bow), and 'from a high viewpoint, such as a high building or an aircraft... the full-circle rainbow can be seen' - at ground level 50%+ of the circle is below the horizon. The 'angle, not a place' framing is a genuine explanation, not a restatement of 42. Track: linear (42-10)/80 = 0.400.

Verified against Wikipedia Kola Superdeep Borehole: 12,262 m reached in 1989, and it 'has been the world's deepest borehole since 1979'. I specifically tried to break the superlative with the extended-reach wells: Al Shaheen BD-04A (Qatar, 2008) has a total LENGTH of 12,289 m but a true vertical depth of only 1,387 m, so Kola still holds the depth (true vertical) record while losing the length record - the prompt's 'deepest hole ever drilled... reached what depth' is the vertical measure, so it stands. Reveal verified: bottom temperature 180 C against a predicted 100 C is confirmed as the reason drilling halted; drilling ran 1970-1989, so 'about 20 years' is right. Track: linear 12262/20000 = 0.613.

Verified against Wikipedia Mid-Atlantic Ridge: 'an average spreading rate of about 2.5 centimetres per year' = 25 mm/yr exactly. Iceland straddling the ridge is confirmed in the same article (the ridge runs through Iceland as the Neovolcanic Zone, exposed at Thingvellir), so the reveal's 'Iceland is quietly being pulled in half' is sound. Fingernail analogy checks out arithmetically: nails grow ~3 mm/month = ~36 mm/yr, same order as 25 mm/yr, and it is the standard USGS comparison. Track: log ln(25)/ln(1000) = 0.466. Only cosmetic issue: the 1-1000 mm/yr range extends well past any real spreading rate (fastest, East Pacific Rise, is ~150 mm/yr), but the position is fine.

Verified against Wikipedia '1883 eruption of Krakatoa'. Every number matches: heard at Rodrigues Island near Mauritius, 4,800 km (3,000 mi) away - the exact answer; and Perth at 3,110 km. Reveal verified: barographs worldwide 'recorded the wave seven times over five days' (four outbound to the antipode, three returning), matching 'circled the planet several times and kept registering on barographs for days'. Sailors on the Norham Castle 64 km (40 mi) away had eardrums ruptured - the reveal's 65 km is right. Track: log ln(48)/ln(200) = 0.731.

This one is stale and the reveal is now wrong. Checked Wikipedia Veryovkina Cave, Krubera Cave and List of deepest caves: after an August 2024 full resurvey plus a dive in the terminal sump, KRUBERA-VORONJA is again the deepest known cave at 2,224 m, and Veryovkina was re-measured DOWN to 2,209 m and is now second. Veryovkina's 2,212 m held the title only from 2017 to 2024. So the answer must become 2224. The reveal must also be rewritten: as written it names Veryovkina first as if it were the record holder, and 'within metres of each other' reads as physical proximity when the two entrances are kilometres apart in the Arabika Massif (they are within ~15 m in DEPTH, which is the real point and worth saying explicitly). The Sept 2018 flood detail is genuine but belongs to Veryovkina, not the record cave - keep it only if the reveal names the cave. Also relabel the source: this is the Arabika Massif survey record, not Guinness. Flagging that the record has flipped twice in eight years, so re-check before publishing. Track with 2224: linear (2224-200)/3300 = 0.613, inside band, so lo/hi are fine.

Verified directly against the claimed source: NOAA Ocean Service oceandepth.html states verbatim 'The average depth of the ocean is about 3,682 meters (12,080 feet).' Exact match to the answer and the source attribution is genuine. Reveal's 840 m mean land elevation is the standard cited figure and the contrast it draws (Earth's solid surface is mostly low basin) is a real insight, not a restatement. Checked for duplication against verified.json: the nature set already has 'How deep is Challenger Deep' (10,935 m) - that is the ocean's deepest POINT, a different quantity from mean depth, and NOAA's page states both side by side, so this is not a duplicate. Track: linear (3682-500)/5500 = 0.579.

Verified against NOAA whysalty.html ('about 3.5 percent of the weight of seawater comes from the dissolved salts') and Wikipedia Seawater ('every kilogram, roughly one liter by volume, of seawater has approximately 35 grams of dissolved salts'; vast majority 31-38 g/kg; surface density 1.025 kg/L). 35 g/L confirmed. I then tried to break the reveal's 150 m salt layer, because NOAA elsewhere quotes 'more than 500 feet (166 m)'. Ran the calculation myself: ocean volume 1.335e18 m^3 x 35 kg/m^3 = 4.67e19 kg salt; at halite density ~2,170 kg/m^3 that is 2.15e16 m^3; over 1.49e14 m^2 of land = ~144 m. So the reveal's 'roughly 150 m' is the physically correct number and NOAA's 166 m uses different assumptions - the reveal survives. Track: linear 35/100 = 0.350.

Verified against Wikipedia Iceberg: 'typically about one-tenth of the volume of an iceberg is above water, which follows from Archimedes's Principle', i.e. 90% below. Densities cited there are ice ~920 kg/m^3 and seawater ~1,025 kg/m^3; the reveal's 917 is the pure-ice figure. Checked the arithmetic the reveal claims falls out of the densities: 917/1025 = 0.895, and 920/1025 = 0.898 - both round to 90%, so the reveal's derivation is genuine and not circular. Capsizing verified: 'an iceberg may flip, or capsize, as it melts and breaks apart, changing the center of gravity' and icebergs 'can capsize anytime and without warning'. Track: linear (90-50)/50 = 0.800, inside band but near the top - a player who knows the fact lands high on the track, which is acceptable.

Verified against Wikipedia Tsunami, which gives 806 km/h (501 mph) in the deep ocean - the answer of 800 is within 1%. I also checked the physics rather than taking the number: v = sqrt(g x depth), so sqrt(5000 m x 10 m/s^2) = 224 m/s = 806 km/h, which reproduces it. Reveal verified: deep-water amplitude is only about 1 metre ('under a metre high' and passing a ship unnoticed), and the article confirms the wave slows and grows as it reaches shallow water. Track: log ln(16)/ln(100) = 0.602.

Broke this one. 'Greatest tidal range ever recorded' has no single defensible value - the sources I checked span 11.7 to 21.6 m, far beyond 10%. Wikipedia Tidal range gives Burntcoat Head a MEAN range of 11.7 m (Ungava Bay second at 9.75 m). Wikipedia Burntcoat Head gives an AVERAGE range of 17.0 m (55.8 ft) and a HIGHEST RECORDED range of 21.6 m (70.9 ft) in the 1869 Saxby Gale. The 16.3 m in the question is Guinness's 'extreme range' from a 1975 edition, quoted there alongside a 14.5 m 'greatest mean spring range'. So a player answering 17 or 21 - both sourced, and 21.6 is literally the greatest range ever recorded - would be scored wrong. The definitional ambiguity (mean / mean spring / extreme / storm-augmented) cannot be fixed without jargon that ruins it as an estimation question. Separately the reveal is wrong: it says the bay 'narrows from 80 km wide to about 5 km', but Wikipedia gives the Bay of Fundy a max width of 52 km. Two independent failures; drop rather than patch.

Verified against Wikipedia Great Barrier Reef: stretches 'over 2,300 kilometres (1,400 mi)', consists of 'over 2,900 individual reefs and 900 islands', and is 'the world's biggest single structure made by living organisms'. Every element of the answer and the reveal matches the source, including the 2,900 and 900 figures. Checked verified.json for duplicates: no GBR question exists in nature or geography. Track: log ln(23)/ln(100) = 0.681. One thematic flag only: coral polyps are animals, and the brief excludes animals - the reef itself is an oceanic/geological feature so I would allow it, but the reveal's 'built by living creatures' leans into the animal side if you want to keep the sub-theme clean.

Tried hardest to break this one. Wikipedia Amazon River now gives mean discharge at the delta as 223,700 m^3/s, not the 209,000 in the question - a 7% gap, inside the 10% bar but worth knowing. 209,000 is the long-standing widely cited mean-at-mouth figure; the much lower ~176,000 numbers you will find are gauged at Obidos, which is upstream and so not 'at the mouth', and I excluded them for that reason rather than counting them as disagreement. On a log track spanning 200x, 209,000 vs 223,700 is visually indistinguishable, so scoring is unaffected. Reveal checks out: global river discharge to the oceans is ~1.2-1.3 million m^3/s, so the Amazon is ~17-18%, fairly described as 'about a fifth'; the freshwater plume extends hundreds of km, so 'more than 100 km' is safely true. Not a duplicate of geography's 'length of the Amazon' - different quantity. Track: log 0.574.

The USGS page itself failed on a TLS cert error, so I cross-checked two other ways. Wikipedia Fresh water gives 1.75-2% of ALL water frozen in glaciers/ice/snow out of 2.5-2.75% total fresh, which implies 70-73% of fresh water is ice - bracketing the USGS/Shiklomanov 68.7% the answer rounds from. Wikipedia Ice sheet independently confirms the reveal's Antarctica claim: the Antarctic ice sheet holds 26.5 million km^3 of ice, 'equivalent to 61% of all fresh water on Earth' - the reveal says roughly 60%, correct, and it is arithmetically consistent with the 69% headline (Antarctica being ~90% of the world's ice). Groundwater as nearly all the remainder and lakes+rivers at ~1% match the standard USGS breakdown. Track: linear 0.690.

Verified against Wikipedia Tree, which cites the Crowther et al. 2015 estimate as 3.04 trillion - matching both the answer and the claimed source. Both reveal claims confirmed in the same source: ~15 billion trees cut down each year (against ~5 billion planted), and 'in the 12,000 years since the start of human agriculture, the number of trees worldwide has decreased by 46%'. I checked that the reveal's 'roughly twice as many before farming' follows: 3.04 / (1-0.46) = 5.6 trillion, i.e. 1.85x, which 'roughly twice' fairly describes. Track: log ln(60)/ln(1000) = 0.593.

The number holds but the source attribution does not. Wikipedia Rafflesia confirms a bloom in West Sumatra in January 2020 measuring 111 cm (44 in) in diameter, 'the largest flower ever recorded', 4 cm wider than the 2017 record - so the answer, the place and the framing are all verified. However I could not confirm Guinness as the source: Guinness's standing 'largest flower' entry is Rafflesia arnoldii at ~91 cm, and the 111 cm measurement traces to the Indonesian conservation agency (BKSDA West Sumatra) via news reports, a single field measurement. Relabel the source accordingly rather than citing Guinness. Reveal verified against the same article and Rafflesia biology: holoparasite with no leaves, stems or roots, living as threads inside a Tetrastigma vine, emitting a carrion smell to attract flies. Track: log ln(22.2)/ln(100) = 0.673.

Verified against Wikipedia Pando: 42.89 hectares (106 acres), so 43 is exact. Every reveal detail confirmed in the same source: an estimated 47,000 stems on one root system, ~6,000 metric tons, and specifically described as a single MALE clone (confirmed by pollen production, leaves and root structure) - the reveal's 'single male tree' is right, which is the kind of detail that is usually wrong. Overbrowsing by mule deer and elk preventing regeneration is confirmed as the central conservation threat. Checked one cross-question risk: Wikipedia calls Pando 'the world's single largest organism by weight' while Q21 calls the honey fungus 'the largest known organism' - as worded the two do not contradict (heaviest vs largest by area), but do not let a future edit make Pando claim the outright 'largest' title. Track: linear (43-5)/115 = 0.330.

Verified against Wikipedia Armillaria ostoyae for the Malheur National Forest specimen, which gives 3.5 sq mi = 9.1 km^2 (2,200 acres). The question's 9.6 km^2 comes from the original Forest Service/Ferguson survey figure of 2,385 acres (3.7 sq mi) - a 5% spread between the two, inside the bar. Confirmed it is described as 'the world's largest single living organism' and 'possibly the largest living organism on Earth by mass, area, and volume', so the prompt's superlative holds. Reveal verified: age estimated at ~8,000 years ('thousands of years old'), and the black rhizomorphs are explicitly described as 'mycelial cords - the shoestrings' that spread nutrients through soil and roots and are the main factor in its pathogenicity toward conifers. Track: linear 9.6/30 = 0.320.

Verified against Wikipedia Venus flytrap: the trap closes in 'approximately 1/10 of a second' = 100 ms exactly. This is the best-sourced reveal in the batch - every count in it is confirmed verbatim: 'two trigger hairs must be touched in succession within 20 seconds of each other or one hair touched twice in rapid succession' to close, and after closing the plant 'counts additional stimulations of the trigger hairs, to five total, to start the production of digesting enzymes'. The rain-and-debris rationale is the stated energy-conservation purpose. Track: log ln(10)/ln(1000) = 0.333.

Verified against Wikipedia Silene stenophylla: tissue radiocarbon-dated to 31,800 +/- 300 years, regenerated into a living flowering plant, published by Yashina et al. in PNAS on 25 January 2012 - the answer of 32,000 is within 0.6% and the claimed source is exactly right. Reveal verified: the material was placental tissue from frozen fruit in Arctic ground squirrel hibernation burrows in permafrost (loess-ice deposits at Duvanny Yar, Sakha Republic, Siberia), and the previous record holder was the ~2,000-year-old Judean date palm - so the reveal's Masada date palm as oldest actual germinated SEED is correct and correctly distinguished from regenerated tissue. Worth knowing: the result has drawn contamination criticism in the literature, though it stands as published and widely cited. Track: linear 32000/40000 = 0.800, inside band.

Verified against Wikipedia Sahara: 9,200,000 km^2 (3,600,000 sq mi), exactly matching the answer; the article notes the figure rises to ~11 million km^2 if you include everywhere under 250 mm annual rainfall, which is a stated alternative definition rather than a disagreement. Britannica's 8,600,000 km^2 is 7% lower - inside the bar, and 9.2 is the more commonly cited number. Reveal: the African Humid Period is confirmed in detail (wetter from ~8000 to ~6000 BCE, monsoon retreating ~4200 BCE, savanna grassland and 'green Sahara' fauna), so 'six thousand years ago it held lakes, grassland and hippos' is sound. The '~quarter sand dunes' claim I could NOT pin to a figure - Wikipedia Sahara and Erg (landform) both list hamada, erg and reg without percentages - but 20-25% erg is the standard textbook figure and is not the graded answer. Track: linear 9.2/25 = 0.368. Style note only: geography already runs several 'area of X in millions of km^2' questions, so this reads as geography-flavoured within nature.

questions.prompt: Mercury hugs the Sun. What is its average distance from it, in million km?
questions.reveal: Mercury's orbit is the most lopsided of the eight planets, swinging from 46 to 70 million km, and it is locked into spinning exactly three times for every two trips around the Sun.
questions.reasoningPath: Earth sits 150 million km out. Mercury is the innermost planet and never strays far from the Sun in our sky, so its orbit must be a large fraction smaller than Earth's but not a tiny sliver: roughly a third to a half of 150 million, i.e. 50-70 million km.

questions.prompt: Neptune orbits how many times farther from the Sun than Earth does?
questions.reveal: Neptune was found by arithmetic before it was found by telescope: predicted from wobbles in Uranus's orbit, then spotted within a degree of the prediction on the first night of searching.
questions.reasoningPath: The planets spread out roughly geometrically: Jupiter is about 5 times Earth's distance, Saturn about 10, and Neptune is two more steps out beyond that. Roughly doubling each step from Saturn lands near 20-40.

questions.prompt: Earth's orbit isn't a circle: how many million km separate its nearest and farthest points from the Sun?
questions.reveal: Earth is closest to the Sun in early January, in the depth of northern winter. Seasons come from the 23.4-degree tilt of the axis, not from distance.
questions.reasoningPath: Earth's orbit is famously near-circular, and the seasons are not caused by it, so the variation can only be a few percent of the 150 million km average. A few percent of 150 million is a few million km.

questions.prompt: Ganymede, the largest moon in the solar system, measures how many km across?
questions.reveal: Ganymede is wider than the planet Mercury, and it is the only moon known to generate its own magnetic field, produced by a churning iron core beneath a buried salty ocean.
questions.reasoningPath: Our Moon is about 3,500 km across and Mercury about 4,900 km. The largest moon is known to edge past Mercury but not dramatically, so it must land a little above 5,000 km.

questions.prompt: Pluto, demoted from planet in 2006, is how many km wide?
questions.reveal: Pluto's moon Charon is more than half its width, so the two swing around a balance point that sits outside Pluto's surface, making them the closest thing to a true double world nearby.
questions.reasoningPath: Pluto is smaller than our Moon (3,475 km) but is still a substantial round world with an atmosphere and moons, so it should be a large fraction of the Moon, roughly two-thirds: about 2,000-2,500 km.

questions.prompt: How many Earths would it take to match Jupiter's mass?
questions.reveal: Jupiter outweighs every other planet combined two and a half times over, enough to tug the Sun around a balance point that lies just above the solar surface.
questions.reasoningPath: Jupiter is about 11 times Earth's diameter, so roughly 11 cubed, about 1,300 times the volume. But it is mostly hydrogen and helium, roughly a quarter of Earth's density, so 1,300 divided by 4 gives around 300 Earth masses.

questions.prompt: The Moon's mass is what percentage of Earth's?
questions.reveal: The Moon is still freakishly large for its planet: most moons are a few thousandths of their planet's width, while ours is more than a quarter of Earth's.
questions.reasoningPath: The Moon is about a quarter of Earth's diameter, so about 1/64 of the volume. It is also less dense, having almost no iron core, so knock that down further: about 1/80, a bit over 1 percent.

questions.prompt: Saturn's average density, in kg per cubic metre? Water is 1,000.
questions.reveal: Saturn's rings are nearly pure water ice, and all of them together weigh less than half of Mimas, one of its small inner moons.
questions.reasoningPath: Saturn is the planet famous for being able to float in water, so it must be under 1,000 kg per cubic metre. It is not a wisp either, being mostly compressed hydrogen, so somewhere in the 500-900 band.

questions.prompt: Drop a hammer on Mars: how many m/s squared does it accelerate downward?
questions.reveal: Mercury is less than half Mars's size yet pulls almost exactly as hard, because it is a ball of iron: its metallic core reaches about 85% of the way to the surface.
questions.reasoningPath: Mars has roughly a tenth of Earth's mass and about half its radius. Surface gravity scales as mass over radius squared: 0.1 divided by 0.25 is about 0.4 of Earth's 9.8, so near 4.

questions.prompt: At the Sun's visible surface, gravity pulls at how many m/s squared? Earth's is 9.8.
questions.reveal: Escape velocity from that surface is 618 km/s, which is why the solar wind has to be flung out along magnetic field lines rather than simply thrown.
questions.reasoningPath: The Sun holds about 333,000 Earth masses in a ball 109 times Earth's radius. Gravity goes as mass over radius squared: 333,000 divided by 109 squared (about 11,900) is roughly 28 times Earth's 9.8, so near 270.

questions.prompt: How many Celsius degrees separate Mercury's hottest day from its coldest night?
questions.reveal: Despite the daytime furnace, Mercury hoards water ice in craters near its poles, on floors that have not seen sunlight for billions of years.
questions.reasoningPath: With no atmosphere to move heat around and sunlight far stronger than Earth's, noon runs hot enough to melt lead (327 °C), so around 400 °C. Night has nothing to hold heat and falls toward deep-space cooling, near -180 °C. The gap is about 600.

questions.prompt: Surface temperature on Titan, Saturn's largest moon, in Celsius?
questions.reveal: Titan is the only other world with standing liquid on its surface: lakes and rivers of methane and ethane, fed by rain that falls in slow, fat drops through air thicker than Earth's.
questions.reasoningPath: Titan orbits Saturn, about 10 times Earth's distance from the Sun, so sunlight there is about 1% as strong. Temperatures that far out sit near 90-100 kelvin, which is roughly -180 °C.

questions.prompt: Jupiter spins faster than any other planet. How many hours is one rotation?
questions.reveal: That spin flings the planet's middle outward: Jupiter is about 7% wider through the equator than pole to pole, an oval you can see in a backyard telescope.
questions.reasoningPath: Earth turns in 24 hours and Jupiter is famously faster, with cloud belts visibly moving across the disc in a single evening at the eyepiece. Faster than Earth but not by an enormous factor puts it near 10 hours.

questions.prompt: One rotation of the Sun at its equator takes how many Earth days?
questions.reveal: Being gas, the Sun does not turn as one body: its poles take about ten days longer than its equator, and that shearing is what winds the magnetic field up into sunspots.
questions.reasoningPath: Sunspots take roughly two weeks to cross the visible face of the Sun, which is half a rotation, so a full turn is somewhere near a month, slightly under.

questions.prompt: How fast does Earth travel along its orbit around the Sun, in km/s?
questions.reveal: On top of that, the whole solar system carries you around the centre of the galaxy at about 230 km/s, completing one lap roughly every 230 million years.
questions.reasoningPath: The orbit's circumference is about 2 x pi x 150 million km, roughly 940 million km. A year holds about 31.5 million seconds. Divide and you get about 30 km per second.

questions.prompt: Surface pressure on Venus equals how many Earth atmospheres?
questions.reveal: The Soviet Venera 7 lander survived 23 minutes down there in 1970, the first data ever returned from the surface of another planet.
questions.reasoningPath: Venus's air is thick carbon dioxide, and landers are described as being built like deep-sea submersibles, crushed rather than melted. Ocean pressure rises about 1 atmosphere per 10 m, and 'like a kilometre down' means around 100 atmospheres.

questions.prompt: Above the atmosphere, sunlight delivers how many watts per square metre?
questions.reveal: Only about 1,000 of those watts reach sea level on a clear day; Mars, half again as far from the Sun, receives less than half what Earth does.
questions.reasoningPath: A square metre of solar panel in full sun produces a couple of hundred watts at roughly 20% efficiency, implying about 1,000 watts arriving. Above the air, before scattering and absorption, it must be somewhat more, so a bit over 1,300.

questions.prompt: To hover over one spot on the equator, a satellite must orbit at what altitude in km?
questions.reveal: That ring is such valuable real estate that dead satellites are pushed a few hundred km higher into a 'graveyard orbit' to free their slot for a replacement.
questions.reasoningPath: The space station orbits 400 km up in 90 minutes. To stretch the period to 24 hours, 16 times longer, the orbital radius grows by 16 to the two-thirds power, about 6.3 times: 6,800 km becomes roughly 42,000 km from Earth's centre. Subtract Earth's 6,400 km radius.

questions.prompt: How many days pass from one full moon to the next?
questions.reveal: The Moon actually finishes its orbit in 27.3 days. The extra two days are Earth moving along its own orbit, so the Moon has to catch up before it lines up with the Sun again.
questions.reasoningPath: Calendar months were built around this cycle, and they average about 30.4 days while lunar calendars run a bit short of solar ones. So the lunar cycle must be a little under 30 days.

questions.prompt: At most, how many minutes can totality last during a total solar eclipse?
questions.reveal: In 1973 a prototype Concorde chased the Moon's shadow across Africa at twice the speed of sound and held totality for 74 minutes.
questions.reasoningPath: Every eclipse report describes totality as lasting a couple of minutes, with the famous long ones singled out as exceptional. The ceiling is therefore a small multiple of the typical two to four minutes, not an hour.

questions.prompt: How many degrees wide does the full Moon appear in the sky?
questions.reveal: The Sun happens to span almost exactly the same width from Earth, which is the coincidence that makes total solar eclipses possible at all.
questions.reasoningPath: A thumbnail held at arm's length covers roughly 1.5 to 2 degrees, and the Moon is comfortably smaller than a thumbnail. That puts it below one degree, around a half.

questions.prompt: Sunspot activity rises and falls on a cycle of how many years?
questions.reveal: The Sun's magnetic north and south swap places at every peak, so the true magnetic cycle is twice as long as the sunspot one.
questions.reasoningPath: Solar maximum makes the news, with aurorae and satellite worries, roughly once a decade rather than once a year or once a century. So the cycle is around ten years.

questions.prompt: Average surface temperature on Mars, in Celsius?
questions.reveal: Noon at the Martian equator in summer can climb above 20 °C, yet the air is so thin that the ground and the air a metre above it can differ by tens of degrees.
questions.reasoningPath: Mars gets about 43% of Earth's sunlight and has almost no atmospheric blanket. Earth averages 15 °C and interior Antarctica averages about -50 °C, so Mars should sit around or below the Antarctic figure.

questions.prompt: The Moon drifts away from Earth by how many cm each year?
questions.reveal: The same tidal braking stretches Earth's day by about 1.7 milliseconds per century. Coral growth bands from 400 million years ago record a year of roughly 400 days.
questions.reasoningPath: The drift is measured by bouncing lasers off Apollo reflectors, which implies a rate too small to notice by eye over a lifetime but big enough to accumulate over geological time: centimetres per year, not millimetres or metres.

questions.prompt: Uranus is tipped on its side: how many degrees is its axis tilted from its orbit?
questions.reveal: Each pole gets 42 years of unbroken sunlight followed by 42 years of night, and the planet's rings and moons are tipped over with it, circling like a target facing the Sun.
questions.reasoningPath: Uranus is described as rolling on its side rather than spinning upright, which means about 90 degrees. It is usually said to be tipped slightly past the horizontal, so a little under 100.

verdicts.note: Pulled the NASA planetary fact sheet (NSSDC now 307-redirects to nasa.gov/nssdc; used the Wayback snapshot). Mercury: Distance from Sun 57.9 x10^6 km, perihelion 46.0, aphelion 69.8, eccentricity 0.206 - the highest of the eight, confirmed independently on the Mercury article ('most eccentric orbit of all the planets'). Reveal's '46 to 70' matches exactly; 3:2 spin-orbit resonance confirmed (sidereal year 88.0 d vs sidereal day 58.65 d, ratio 3:2). Track position 0.382. Tried to break it on the eccentricity-ranking claim (Pluto is more eccentric at 0.244) but the reveal says 'of the eight planets', which excludes Pluto. No disproof found.

NASA fact sheet: Neptune 4515.0 x10^6 km, Earth 149.6 -> 30.18 AU, so 30x is right (semi-major axis basis). Checked the reveal against the Discovery of Neptune record: Le Verrier predicted from Uranus's perturbations, Galle found it the night of 23-24 Sept 1846 'after less than an hour of searching and less than 1 degree from the position Le Verrier had predicted' - both the 'first night' and 'within a degree' claims hold. Position 0.588.

NASA fact sheet Earth: perihelion 147.1, aphelion 152.1 x10^6 km. Difference = 5.0 exactly. Reveal: perihelion falls in early January (Jan 2-5) and NASA lists Earth's obliquity to orbit as 23.4 degrees - both correct, and the seasons-are-tilt-not-distance point is right. Position 0.575. Nothing to disprove.

NASA's Ganymede page confirms 'largest moon in our solar system, even bigger than the planet Mercury' and 'the only moon known to have its own magnetic field' but gives no km figure. Cross-checked the measured value: mean radius 2,634.1 +/- 0.3 km -> diameter 5,268 km. Mercury is 4,879 km (NASA fact sheet), so 'wider than Mercury' is correct. Iron-sulfide/iron core and subsurface saltwater ocean both confirmed (Hubble/Juno). Sources agree to within 0.15% (5,262-5,270 km). Position 0.638.

science.nasa.gov Pluto facts states verbatim 'an equatorial diameter of about 1,477 miles (2,377 kilometers)' - exact match. NASA fact sheet table lists 2,376, i.e. 0.03% apart. Stress-tested the reveal's 'more than half its width': Charon's diameter is 1,212 km, 1212/2377 = 51.0%, so 'more than half' survives but only just (NASA's prose says 'about half'). Barycentre sits ~2,110 km from Pluto's centre vs a 1,188 km radius, so it is genuinely outside Pluto - correct. 2006 IAU demotion correct. Position 0.630.

NASA fact sheet: Jupiter 1898 x10^24 kg, Earth 5.97 -> 317.9, so 318 is right. Checked the reveal's '2.5 times all other planets combined' by summing the fact sheet masses: Saturn 568 + Neptune 102 + Uranus 86.8 + Earth 5.97 + Venus 4.87 + Mars 0.642 + Mercury 0.330 = 768.6, and 1898/768.6 = 2.47. Confirmed. Sun-Jupiter barycentre at 1.068 solar radii from the Sun's centre, i.e. just above the surface - correct. Position 0.653.

NASA Moon fact sheet gives the Moon/Earth mass ratio directly as 0.0123 = 1.23%, so 1.2% is right. Radius ratio listed as 0.2727, so 'more than a quarter of Earth's' is exact. Probed the loosest claim, 'most moons are a few thousandths of their planet's width': the big ones are percent-level (Ganymede/Jupiter 3.7%, Titan/Saturn 4.3%, Triton/Neptune 5.5%), but the great majority of the ~300 known moons are small irregulars far below 0.5% (Phobos/Mars is 0.33%), so 'most' holds numerically. Position 0.338.

NASA fact sheet gives Saturn density 687 kg/m3 exactly. Both reveal claims verified rather than assumed: ring composition is 99.9% water ice with trace tholins/silicates, and Cassini's gravity measurement puts the ring mass at 1.54 (+/-0.49) x10^19 kg = 0.41 +/- 0.13 Mimas masses, so 'less than half of Mimas' is correct and is a real Cassini result, not folklore. Position 0.418.

The answer is fine - NASA fact sheet gives Mars gravity 3.7 m/s2, position 0.308 - but the reveal is wrong. 'Mercury is less than half Mars's size' fails on the two readings a player would use: diameter 4,879 vs 6,792 km = 72%, and mass 0.330 vs 0.642 x10^24 kg = 51%, i.e. MORE than half. It is only true by volume (6.083 vs 16.318 x10^10 km3 = 37%). The rest of the reveal checks out (Mercury's gravity is also 3.70, and its core does reach ~83-85% of the radius), so the question is salvageable with a rewritten reveal - but as written it invites exactly the correction email. Secondary reason to cut: this is the third 'surface gravity in m/s2' question in the pool, after verified.json space #23 (Jupiter) and candidate [9] (Sun).

NASA Sun fact sheet: 'Surface gravity (eq.) 274.0 m/s2' and 'Escape velocity 617.6 km/s' - the answer and the reveal's 618 both match the claimed source exactly. Position 0.685. Checked for duplication against verified.json space #23 (Jupiter's surface gravity, 24.8): same template but a different body and an order-of-magnitude different answer, so not a duplicate - though note this is now the second gravity question, which is why I cut [8] rather than this one. The solar-wind sentence is a simplification of coronal acceleration but not a false statement.

science.nasa.gov Mercury facts states '800 degrees Fahrenheit (430 degrees Celsius)' by day and 'minus 290 degrees Fahrenheit (minus 180 degrees Celsius)' at night: 430 - (-180) = 610, an exact match. Checked the competing figure - the NSSDC fact sheet implies 700 K to 100 K = 600 - so the spread is 1.6%, far inside tolerance. No unit trap: a Celsius *difference* equals a kelvin difference. NASA's page also confirms water ice in permanently shadowed polar craters (MESSENGER), so the reveal holds. Position 0.762.

NASA's Titan facts page gives the surface temperature as -290 F / -179 C / ~94 K - exact match to the answer. Same page confirms surface pressure 'about 60 percent greater than on Earth' (so 'air thicker than Earth's' is right) and 'clouds, rain, rivers, lakes and seas of liquid hydrocarbons like methane and ethane'. NASA's own wording is 'the only place besides Earth known to have liquids on its surface', which backs the reveal's standing-liquid claim. Position 0.355.

NASA fact sheet lists Jupiter rotation period 9.9 hours (9.9250 h = 9h 55m 30s), and it is the fastest of the eight (Saturn is next at 10.7). Verified the reveal's oblateness figure rather than taking it: equatorial 142,984 km vs polar 133,684 km, and the source states outright that 'the equatorial radius is 7% longer than the polar radius' (flattening 0.06499). Position 0.330.

Went to the claimed source's actual data. The NASA Sun fact sheet's adopted 609.12 h (25.38 d) is footnoted as the value at 16 deg latitude, but the sheet publishes the differential-rotation law (14.37 - 2.33 sin^2 L - 1.56 sin^4 L deg/day): at L=0 that gives 360/14.37 = 25.05 days, and at the pole 360/10.48 = 34.3 days. So 25 is NASA's own equatorial value, and 'poles take about ten days longer' is 9.3 days - both correct. Caveat I checked and accepted: other references give 25.6 d equatorial sidereal and ~27-28 d synodic (as seen from Earth), a spread of up to ~12%; on the 0..60 linear track that whole spread is under 5% of the track, so it cannot meaningfully hurt a player. Position 0.417.

NASA fact sheet gives Earth orbital velocity 29.8 km/s exactly. Checked both reveal numbers separately: the Solar System's speed around the galactic centre is ~230 km/s, and a galactic year is ~225 million years - the reveal says 'roughly every 230 million years', about 2% off a hedged figure, which I let stand. Position 0.595.

NASA fact sheet gives Venus surface pressure 92 bars; 92 bar = 90.8 atm, so quoting '92 atmospheres' is a 1.3% unit slip that every popular source makes - not worth a fix. Chased the reveal's '23 minutes', which is the disputed part: the record shows Venera 7 landed 15 Dec 1970, transmitted ~53 minutes total, and Oleg Rzhiga later recovered '23 minutes of very weak signals' from the tapes - the origin of the widely-cited 23. One source phrases it as 'about 20 minutes from the surface'. The 23 figure is legitimate and sourced, and 'first data ever returned from the surface of another planet' is confirmed. Position 0.616.

Two independent confirmations of 1361 W/m2: the NASA Moon fact sheet lists 'Solar irradiance 1361.0' for Earth, and the solar-irradiance literature gives 'about 1361 W/m2' at the top of the atmosphere. Reveal's ~1000 W/m2 at sea level on a clear day confirmed verbatim. Computed the Mars claim myself since no source stated it: Mars is at 228.0/149.6 = 1.524 AU ('half again as far' - correct), so irradiance is 1361/1.524^2 = 586 W/m2 = 43% of Earth's, i.e. 'less than half' - correct. Position 0.680.

Geostationary altitude confirmed as 35,786 km (22,236 mi) above the equator, and it is derivable from Kepler's third law rather than pure recall, so it is genuinely estimable. Reveal's graveyard orbit: the disposal requirement is a 90% chance of reaching more than 200 km above the GEO belt, with practice around 200-300 km - so 'a few hundred km higher' is accurate. Position 0.675. No brand or US dependence.

NASA Moon fact sheet gives synodic period 29.53 days (answer 29.5) and sidereal rotation 655.720 h = 27.32 days (reveal's 27.3). The reveal's explanation of the ~2.2-day gap - Earth's own orbital motion means the Moon must catch up to re-align with the Sun - is the correct mechanism, not a restatement of the answer. Position 0.322.

Theoretical maximum totality is 7 min 32 s, so 7.5 minutes is right for the 'at most... can' phrasing. Deliberately looked for the trap: the longest *observed* totality was 7 min 3 s (30 June 1973), so a pedant answering 7.0 differs by only 2.5% of the 0..20 track - harmless. The Concorde detail checks out: on that same 1973 eclipse, observers aboard Concorde 001 flew along the umbra and held totality for ~74 minutes, at Mach ~2. Position 0.375.

Verified the Moon's apparent size spans 29'20" to 34'6" (0.49-0.57 deg), mean ~31' = 0.517 deg, so 0.5 is right. Reveal's coincidence claim confirmed from two sources: the Sun spans 31'27" to 32'32" (0.52-0.54 deg), and NASA's Sun fact sheet independently lists 1919 arcsec at 1 AU = 0.533 deg. Position 0.167 - low on the track but comfortably inside the 0.08 floor, so no range fix needed.

Solar cycle averages about 11 years, with observed cycles ranging 9-14 years - the average is the right target and it is stable, not a year-to-year figure. Reveal checked: the Sun's magnetic field flips near each solar maximum and the full Hale cycle spans two solar cycles (22 years) before polarity returns to its original state. That is a genuine added fact, not a restatement. Position 0.275.

NASA fact sheet lists Mars mean temperature -65 C exactly, matching the claimed source (NASA's Mars page quotes -85 F / -65 C, consistent). Reveal's '20 C at noon at the equator in summer' matches NASA's stated 70 F high, and the large ground-vs-air gradient in the thin atmosphere is real. Checked against verified.json space #22 (Venus mean surface temperature, 465 C): same template, different planet and a 530-degree different answer, so not a duplicate. Position 0.417.

Best-sourced item in the batch. NASA's Moon fact sheet has a dedicated line: 'Recession rate from Earth (cm/yr) 3.8'. Independently, lunar laser ranging 1970-2015 gives 38.30 +/- 0.08 mm/yr. Both reveal claims verified separately: the day lengthens by 1.72 +/- 0.03 ms per century from the historical eclipse record (reveal says 'about 1.7'), and the ~400-days-per-year Devonian figure is Wells's 1963 coral growth-band result. Position 0.253.

NASA fact sheet lists Uranus obliquity to orbit as 97.8 degrees, matching the claimed source and the answer. Flag I checked and cleared: some references list 82.23 degrees, which is the same physical tilt expressed under the opposite (right-hand-rule) pole convention, 180 - 97.77 - not a genuine measurement disagreement, and 97.8 is the canonical NASA/IAU figure. A player answering 82 loses only ~11% of the 0..140 track. Reveal confirmed: 42 years of continuous sunlight then 42 of darkness per pole on the 84-year orbit, with the ring and moon system tipped over with the planet. Position 0.700.

questions.prompt: What percentage of the Sun's mass is hydrogen?
questions.reveal: Helium was identified in the Sun 27 years before anyone found it on Earth, spotted as an unexplained yellow line in eclipse sunlight in 1868.
questions.reasoningPath: The universe began as roughly three-quarters hydrogen and a quarter helium, and the Sun formed from that gas. It has only fused a few percent of its hydrogen so far, so its composition is still close to primordial: a bit over 70%, with almost all the rest helium and a sliver of heavier elements.

questions.prompt: How many stars in the whole sky are bright enough to see with the naked eye?
questions.reveal: You can only see half the sky at once, and a well-lit city sky cuts what actually reaches your eye to a few dozen.
questions.reasoningPath: On a genuinely dark night people report seeing a few thousand stars at once. Only half the celestial sphere is above the horizon at any moment, and haze near the horizon hides more, so double that count for the whole sky: a few thousand becomes roughly ten thousand.

questions.prompt: How many million tonnes of hydrogen does the Sun fuse every second?
questions.reveal: About four of those million tonnes disappear as pure energy every second, so the Sun is measurably lighter by the time you finish reading this.
questions.reasoningPath: The Sun radiates roughly 4x10^26 watts. Fusion converts about 0.7% of the hydrogen's mass to energy, so E=mc^2 gives a mass loss of about 4 million tonnes per second, and the hydrogen consumed is that divided by 0.007 — around 600 million tonnes.

questions.prompt: Roughly how many billion more years will the Sun shine before swelling into a red giant?
questions.reveal: Trouble arrives long before that: in about a billion years the Sun's slowly rising output should be enough to boil Earth's oceans away.
questions.reasoningPath: A Sun-like star spends about 10 billion years burning hydrogen, and the Sun is about 4.6 billion years old — roughly halfway through. So a little under half of its main-sequence life is left.

questions.prompt: A neutron star packs more than the Sun's mass into a sphere how many km across?
questions.reveal: Its surface gravity is roughly 100 billion times Earth's, so an object dropped from one metre would arrive at about seven million km/h.
questions.reasoningPath: A white dwarf squeezes a Sun's mass into something Earth-sized, about 13,000 km. A neutron star is denser still — matter crushed to nuclear density, thousands of times more compact than a white dwarf — which shrinks that to the size of a city, tens of km rather than thousands.

questions.prompt: The fastest known pulsar spins how many times per second?
questions.reveal: Pulsars are so metronomic that the first one found was labelled LGM-1, for 'little green men', before a natural explanation was accepted.
questions.reasoningPath: A neutron star is about 20 km across, so its equator traces a circle of roughly 60 km. Spinning 1,000 times a second would move that surface at 60,000 km/s, a fifth of light speed — near the limit before it flies apart. So the record must be high hundreds, not tens and not tens of thousands.

questions.prompt: How many million light-years away is the Andromeda Galaxy, our nearest large neighbour?
questions.reveal: It is falling towards us at about 110 km/s, and the two galaxies are expected to merge into a single one in roughly four billion years.
questions.reasoningPath: The Milky Way's disc is about 100,000 light-years wide. Galaxies in a small group sit a few tens of galaxy-diameters apart, so the nearest big one should be a couple of million light-years away — and Andromeda is famously the most distant thing visible to the unaided eye.

questions.prompt: How many billion light-years across is the observable universe?
questions.reveal: That is far more than 13.8 billion light-years because space itself kept stretching while the light was still in transit.
questions.reasoningPath: Light has had 13.8 billion years to reach us, so a naive answer is 27.6 billion light-years across. But expansion has carried the sources much further away since they emitted, roughly tripling the figure — so a few times 27, not a few times 1 or 1,000.

questions.prompt: The cosmic microwave background fills all of space. What is its temperature in kelvin?
questions.reveal: It was found by accident in 1964 by two engineers who spent months blaming the hiss in their antenna on pigeon droppings.
questions.reasoningPath: It is famously described as only a few degrees above absolute zero, and it is detected as microwaves rather than infrared, so it must be colder than the roughly 30 K where infrared takes over — a small single-digit number in kelvin.

questions.prompt: How many thousand years after the Big Bang did the universe turn transparent to light?
questions.reveal: Until then the cosmos glowed orange-hot like the inside of a star; expansion has since stretched that same light all the way into microwaves.
questions.reasoningPath: Gas stops scattering light once it cools enough for electrons to bind to nuclei, at a few thousand kelvin. The universe has cooled by a factor of about a thousand since then, and cooling goes roughly as the square root of time in that era — which puts the moment at a few hundred thousand years, not millions.

questions.prompt: How many million years does the Sun take to orbit the centre of the Milky Way once?
questions.reveal: The Sun has completed only about 20 laps since it formed, so the last time it was in this spot the first dinosaurs were appearing.
questions.reasoningPath: The Sun sits about 26,000 light-years out, so its orbit is roughly 160,000 light-years around. Stars in the disc move at a couple of hundred km/s, which is about 0.07% of light speed — so the lap takes around 160,000 divided by 0.0007, a couple of hundred million years.

questions.prompt: The black hole at the Milky Way's centre has the mass of how many million Suns?
questions.reveal: It was weighed by tracking individual stars whipping around an apparently empty point for nearly 30 years, work that won the 2020 Nobel Prize in Physics.
questions.reasoningPath: The galaxy holds well over 100 billion stars, and a central black hole is a tiny fraction of that — thousandths of a percent. Stars orbiting a few light-weeks from the centre complete a lap in decades, which demands millions of solar masses rather than thousands or billions.

questions.prompt: How many centimetres does light travel in one nanosecond?
questions.reveal: Grace Hopper handed out 30 cm lengths of wire as 'nanoseconds' to explain to admirals why a satellite link can never feel instant.
questions.reasoningPath: Light covers 300,000 km in a second. A nanosecond is a billionth of that, so 300,000 km divided by a billion is 0.0003 km — three ten-thousandths of a kilometre, which is 30 cm.

questions.prompt: Light slows down in water. How many km/s does it manage there?
questions.reveal: Particles from a reactor can outrun light in water, and the eerie blue Cherenkov glow is the optical equivalent of a sonic boom.
questions.reasoningPath: Speed in a medium is light speed divided by its refractive index. Water bends light noticeably but not dramatically — a straw looks kinked, not shattered — so the index is around 1.3. Dividing 300,000 km/s by 1.3 gives roughly three-quarters of vacuum speed.

questions.prompt: How many watts of sunlight fall on each square metre above Earth's atmosphere?
questions.reveal: About a quarter is lost getting through the air, which is why even a flawless panel on the ground has under 1,000 watts to work with.
questions.reasoningPath: A square metre of ground in strong midday sun feels comparable to a small electric heater, and solar panels are quoted at roughly 1 kW per square metre at the surface. Space is somewhat brighter because nothing is absorbed on the way, so a bit above 1,000.

questions.prompt: Convert one gram of matter entirely into energy: how many trillion joules?
questions.reveal: That is roughly the yield of the Hiroshima bomb, which turned well under a gram of its material into energy.
questions.reasoningPath: E=mc^2 with m = 0.001 kg and c = 3x10^8 m/s. Squaring c gives 9x10^16, and multiplying by 0.001 kg gives 9x10^13 joules — 90 trillion.

questions.prompt: One parsec is how many light-years?
questions.reveal: The name is short for 'parallax second' — the distance at which Earth's orbit would swing a star one arcsecond across the sky.
questions.reasoningPath: Both units measure the same kind of stellar distance and astronomers switch between them casually, so they must be within a small factor of each other. The nearest star is quoted as 4.2 light-years or 1.3 parsecs, which fixes the ratio at a bit over three.

questions.prompt: Yuri Gagarin's single orbit in 1961: how many minutes did the whole flight last?
questions.reveal: He ejected at about seven km and parachuted down separately, a detail the Soviets hid for years because the record required landing inside the craft.
questions.reasoningPath: One lap of low Earth orbit takes about 90 minutes, which is why the Space Station rises and sets so often. Gagarin flew a single orbit, plus the climb to orbit and the descent — so 90 minutes with a bit added at each end.

questions.prompt: The Karman line marks the edge of space at what altitude in km?
questions.reveal: Above it a wing would have to move faster than orbital speed to generate lift, so flying and orbiting stop being different things.
questions.reasoningPath: Airliners cruise near 11 km and weather balloons top out around 40 km, while the Space Station orbits at about 400 km. The boundary sits well above the highest aircraft but far below any stable orbit, and it is a round number — so around 100 km.

questions.prompt: How many km above the equator must a satellite orbit to hover over one spot?
questions.reveal: Arthur C. Clarke set out the idea in a 1945 magazine article and never patented it, later calling it the most valuable thing he ever gave away.
questions.reasoningPath: A 400 km orbit takes 90 minutes and the Moon at 384,000 km takes 27 days. A 24-hour orbit must sit between them, and orbital period grows as distance to the power 1.5 — so about a tenth of the way to the Moon, tens of thousands of km up.

questions.prompt: How many metres tall was the Saturn V rocket that carried Apollo to the Moon?
questions.reveal: Its first stage drank around 13 tonnes of propellant every second and ran itself dry in under three minutes.
questions.reasoningPath: Photographs show it dwarfing the launch tower and standing comparable to a 30-storey building. That puts it around 100 m — taller than the Statue of Liberty with its pedestal, shorter than the Great Pyramid at 139 m.

questions.prompt: Sputnik 1, the first artificial satellite, weighed how many kg?
questions.reveal: It was a polished sphere the size of a beach ball, and its batteries died after just three weeks of beeping.
questions.reasoningPath: It was a hollow metal sphere under a metre across carrying batteries and a radio transmitter. A sphere that size in thin aluminium is a few tens of kg, with the heavy batteries adding most of the rest — so a bit under 100 kg, not a tonne.

questions.prompt: Longest single spaceflight by one person: how many days did it last?
questions.reveal: Valeri Polyakov took the mission to prove a human could survive a round trip to Mars, and insisted on walking away from the capsule unaided.
questions.reasoningPath: Standard Space Station tours run about six months, and the headline record is always described as more than a year in orbit. That brackets it between 365 and roughly 500 days.

questions.prompt: How many metres across is the James Webb Space Telescope's main mirror?
questions.reveal: It is 18 gold-plated hexagons that had to unfold in space, because no rocket fairing was wide enough to carry the mirror open.
questions.reasoningPath: Hubble's mirror is 2.4 m, and Webb is repeatedly described as collecting several times more light. Area scales as diameter squared, so about six times the light means roughly 2.5 times the diameter — around 6 m, which is also why it had to fold to fit a rocket.

questions.prompt: How fast is Voyager 1 heading out of the solar system, in km/h?
questions.reveal: Even at that pace it would need around 70,000 years to cover the distance to the nearest star, which is not where it is pointed anyway.
questions.reasoningPath: Escaping the Sun from Earth's orbit needs about 42 km/s, and Earth already supplies 30 km/s of that. Voyager left with a modest surplus after gravity assists, so it coasts at roughly 17 km/s — multiply by 3,600 for about 60,000 km/h.

verdicts.note: Checked Wikipedia/Sun against the NASA solar composition figures: photosphere is 73.46% hydrogen, 24.85% helium BY MASS - answer 73 is right on. Caveat I probed: the BULK Sun is ~71% H (core helium-enriched by 4.6 Gyr of fusion), so there is a 71-73.5 spread depending on whether you mean photosphere or whole body; that is ~3.5% apart, well inside tolerance on a 0-100 linear track (position 0.73). Reveal checked independently and it is exactly right: helium was spotted as the unexplained D3 yellow line in the 1868 eclipse (Janssen/Lockyer) and not isolated on Earth until Ramsay in 1895 - 27 years, not a rounded 'nearly 30'.

This one fails the source-agreement test badly. Yale BSC5 actually contains 9,110 objects of which 9,095 are stars (11 novae/supernovae, 4 clusters) - so the claimed 9096 is off by one against the catalogue itself. Far worse: the answer depends entirely on the assumed limiting magnitude, which the prompt never fixes. Wikipedia's own Naked eye article gives ~5,600 stars brighter than mag +6 for a typical dark-adapted eye and ~45,000 brighter than mag +8 under perfect conditions; BSC's 9,095 uses mag 6.5. That is a 5,600-to-45,000 spread, an 8x disagreement, not 10%. A player who answers 5,600 from a legitimate published source gets scored wrong. The premise 'bright enough to see with the naked eye' is not a well-defined quantity.

Verified against Wikipedia/Sun: the core fuses ~600 billion kg = 600 million tonnes of hydrogen per second, converting ~4 billion kg = 4 million tonnes to energy per second at 3.846e26 W. Both the answer and the reveal's 'about four of those million tonnes disappear as pure energy' are confirmed numerically, and the two are consistent with each other (600 Mt in, ~596 Mt He out, 4 Mt mass deficit). Track position 0.69 on log 1..10000.

Checked science.nasa.gov/sun/facts directly - NASA states the Sun 'will last another 5 billion years or so' before it swells and ends as a white dwarf, matching the claimed source and the answer exactly. Wikipedia gives 4-7 billion for core-hydrogen exhaustion, so 5 sits inside the accepted band. The reveal's separate claim is the standard result and is not a restatement of the answer: rising luminosity makes Earth uninhabitable/boils the oceans in roughly 1 billion years, long before the red-giant phase. Position 0.25 on 0..20 linear.

The ANSWER survives: Wikipedia/Neutron star gives radius ~10 km at ~1.4 solar masses, i.e. ~20 km across, and the 'more than the Sun's mass' premise holds. THE REVEAL IS WRONG AND MUST BE EDITED (I have no schema field for it, so flagging here - if the reveal cannot be edited, drop this question). It says surface gravity is 'roughly 100 billion times Earth's'; the cited value is 2x10^11 = 200 BILLION times Earth's (2.0x10^12 m/s^2). The reveal's own second number proves the inconsistency: 7 million km/h from a 1 m drop requires g = 2x10^12 m/s^2 (v = sqrt(2gh) = 2,000 km/s = 7.2 million km/h, the NASA Imagine-the-Universe figure). At the stated 100 billion g you get only ~1,400 km/s = 5 million km/h, which is the number Wikipedia quotes. Change '100 billion' to '200 billion' and the two halves agree. No numeric change to answer or range (log 2..2000, position 0.33 - fine).
verdicts.correctedReveal: A teaspoon of that material would weigh over five billion tonnes, and the surface gravity is so fierce that escaping it means travelling at more than half the speed of light. The fastest known one spins over 700 times a second.

verdicts.note: Tried to break this by hunting for a faster record-holder. PSR J1748-2446ad (Terzan 5ad, found 2004) spins at 716.35 Hz and Wikipedia still labels it 'the fastest-spinning pulsar known'; the runner-up PSR J0952-0607 is at 707 Hz, so nothing has overtaken it as of now. Answer 716 confirmed. Reveal checked separately: the first pulsar (CP 1919, Bell Burnell/Hewish 1967) was indeed jokingly catalogued LGM-1 for 'little green men' before the neutron-star explanation was accepted. Position 0.71 on log 1..10000.

Answer is fine - Andromeda at 2.5 million light-years and the 110 km/s blueshifted approach are both confirmed. THE REVEAL IS NOW FACTUALLY WRONG AND MUST BE REPLACED (no schema field, so flagging here; if it cannot be edited, drop). It asserts the two galaxies 'are expected to merge into a single one in roughly four billion years.' That was the 2012 Hubble-era conclusion. The 2025 Sawala et al. analysis (Gaia + Hubble, 100,000 simulations over 22 variables) puts the merger probability at only ~50% within the next 10 billion years, and once the LMC and Triangulum are included the chance of a head-on collision in the 4-5 Gyr window drops to about 2%. Shipping this reveal is exactly the kind of confident-but-outdated claim that draws complaint mail. Suggested replacement keeping the same hook: 'It is one of the few galaxies blueshifted rather than redshifted - falling towards us at about 110 km/s instead of receding with the rest of the universe.' Range log 0.2..200, position 0.37 - fine.
verdicts.correctedReveal: Despite that distance it spans about three degrees of sky, some six times the width of the full Moon; only its bright core registers to the naked eye, the faint outer disc being far too dim to see.

verdicts.note: Confirmed against Wikipedia/Observable universe: diameter ~28.5 gigaparsecs = 93 billion light-years, comoving radius 46.5 billion ly, with age 13.787 Gyr. The reveal is not a restatement - it explains the genuine paradox (93 >> 2 x 13.8) correctly via comoving expansion during light transit. Checked for overlap with verified.json space entries #13 (Milky Way disc diameter) and #14 (age of universe); distinct fact, not a duplicate. Position 0.66 on log 1..1000.

Verified: CMB blackbody temperature is 2.72548 +/- 0.00057 K, so 2.7 is correct to the precision asked. Discovery date 1964 by Penzias and Wilson at Bell Labs Crawford Hill confirmed (Nobel 1978); the pigeon-droppings episode - they repeatedly cleaned the horn antenna of nesting pigeons and their droppings while chasing the residual hiss - is well documented, though Wikipedia's CMB article itself does not carry it.
