questions.prompt: Alexander Fleming spotted the mould that became penicillin in what year?
questions.reveal: Fleming left a dish of bacteria out while on holiday and returned to find mould killing them. He couldn't purify the drug — that took an Oxford team a decade, plus a production strain found on a mouldy melon in a market.
questions.reasoningPath: Soldiers in WWI still died routinely of infected wounds, but by WWII antibiotics were saving them. So the discovery falls between the wars, and mass production lagged it by roughly a decade — late 1920s.

questions.prompt: Watson and Crick published the double-helix structure of DNA in what year?
questions.reveal: The paper was barely a page long. The X-ray image that gave away the helix, 'Photo 51', was made in Rosalind Franklin's lab and shown to them without her knowledge.
questions.reasoningPath: Genes were known by 1900 but the structure needed X-ray crystallography, a post-war technique. The genetic code was cracked in the 1960s and the helix came first — so early 1950s.

questions.prompt: The first human heart transplant was performed in Cape Town in what year?
questions.reveal: The patient lived 18 days before pneumonia killed him, his immune system flattened by anti-rejection drugs. The donor was a young woman struck by a car near a bakery.
questions.reasoningPath: It needs heart-lung machines (1950s) and immunosuppression, and it was a global sensation in the same era as the space race — after Gagarin, just before the Moon landing.

questions.prompt: Louise Brown, the first baby conceived by IVF, was born in what year?
questions.reveal: Robert Edwards received the Nobel for the work 32 years later; his collaborator Patrick Steptoe had died, and Nobels are not awarded posthumously. More than 10 million people have since been born this way.
questions.reasoningPath: The 'test-tube baby' panic belongs to the same cultural moment as early home computers, and the first IVF child is now around fifty — so the late 1970s.

questions.prompt: Wilhelm Röntgen discovered X-rays after noticing a strange glow in his lab, in what year?
questions.reveal: He refused to patent it, wanting the technique free to all, and gave away his Nobel money. His first published image was his wife's hand with her ring; she is said to have replied, 'I have seen my death.'
questions.reasoningPath: X-rays triggered the discovery of radioactivity months later and won the very first Nobel Prize in Physics in 1901, so the discovery sits just a few years before that — mid-1890s.

questions.prompt: Dmitri Mendeleev published his periodic table of the elements in what year?
questions.reveal: He left gaps for elements nobody had found and predicted their weights and properties in advance; gallium and germanium turned up within twenty years and matched almost exactly.
questions.reasoningPath: The table was built from atomic weights alone — the electron wasn't found until 1897 — but it needed decent chemistry of dozens of elements. That puts it in the middle-to-late 1800s.

questions.prompt: Bell Labs built the first working transistor in what year?
questions.reveal: The first one was a lump of germanium with gold foil pressed onto it by a plastic wedge. Staff voted on the name, beating out 'iotatron' and 'crystal triode'.
questions.reasoningPath: It grew out of wartime radar semiconductor work, and pocket transistor radios were on sale by the mid-1950s with roughly a decade of development in between — so just after WWII.

questions.prompt: The first working laser fired its beam in what year?
questions.reveal: It used a ruby rod inside a coiled photographic flash lamp, and for years afterwards the laser was described as 'a solution looking for a problem'. The journal Physical Review Letters rejected the paper announcing it.
questions.reasoningPath: It requires quantum theory and follows the maser of the 1950s, and lasers were mature enough by 1969 to bounce off mirrors left on the Moon — so right around 1960.

questions.prompt: Alessandro Volta stacked metal discs to make the first true battery in what year?
questions.reveal: He built it to prove Galvani wrong: the twitching in frogs' legs came from the metals touching, not from 'animal electricity'. Napoleon had a medal struck for him after a demonstration in Paris.
questions.reasoningPath: It comes after Galvani's 1780s frog experiments but before Faraday's motors and generators of the 1820s-30s, and steady current was the thing those needed first — so right at the century's turn.

questions.prompt: CERN announced the discovery of the Higgs boson in what year?
questions.reveal: The particle was predicted in 1964, and one of the original papers was rejected as being of no obvious relevance to physics. Confirming it took a 27 km ring and roughly 6,000 physicists.
questions.reasoningPath: The Large Hadron Collider started colliding beams around 2010 after a famous breakdown, and the Higgs was the headline physics story a couple of years later — early 2010s.

questions.prompt: Roald Amundsen's team became the first people to stand at the South Pole in what year?
questions.reveal: His team planned from the start to eat their sled dogs, which let them carry far less food. Scott's party arrived 34 days later, found the Norwegian flag already there, and died on the way back.
questions.reasoningPath: Polar exploration by ship and dog sled peaked after the aeroplane existed but before WWI swallowed Europe, and Scott's doomed return is famously 1912 — so the year before.

questions.prompt: Howard Carter found the steps down to Tutankhamun's tomb in what year?
questions.reveal: The tomb held about 5,400 objects and took ten years to empty. It survived robbers only because rubble from a later tomb happened to bury its entrance.
questions.reasoningPath: The find set off the Egyptomania of Art Deco fashion and jazz-age design, so it must precede that wave slightly: after WWI, before the Depression — early 1920s.

questions.prompt: The wreck of the Titanic was finally located on the seabed in what year?
questions.reveal: The expedition was cover for a secret US Navy job surveying two sunken nuclear submarines. Titanic was found in the leftover days, by following a trail of scattered debris.
questions.reasoningPath: It needed deep-diving submersibles and towed sonar, and it was worldwide news within living memory — roughly seventy years after the sinking, a decade or so before the 1997 film.

questions.prompt: A living coelacanth — a fish known only from fossils — was hauled up off South Africa in what year?
questions.reveal: The museum curator who rescued it from the catch had no way to preserve the organs and had it stuffed, so the insides were lost to science. Finding a second one took 14 years.
questions.reasoningPath: The story belongs to the age of steam trawlers and small colonial museums, and is always told as happening just before the Second World War interrupted the follow-up hunt.

questions.prompt: Magellan's expedition completed the first circumnavigation of the globe in what year?
questions.reveal: Five ships and about 270 men set out; one ship and 18 men came back. Magellan was not among them — he was killed in a battle in the Philippines partway round.
questions.reasoningPath: Columbus crossed in 1492, and it took Spain a generation to push past the Americas into the Pacific. The voyage itself lasted about three years, so the return lands in the early 1520s.

questions.prompt: The Treaty of Versailles was signed in the Hall of Mirrors in what year?
questions.reveal: The room was chosen deliberately: the German Empire had been proclaimed in it after France's defeat in 1871. Keynes quit the British delegation in disgust and wrote a bestseller predicting the treaty would wreck Europe.
questions.reasoningPath: The fighting stopped in November 1918, and peace conferences take months of haggling — so the signature comes the following year.

questions.prompt: The UN adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights in what year?
questions.reveal: It passed with 48 votes in favour, none against and eight abstentions. It is now the most translated document on Earth, available in over 500 languages.
questions.reasoningPath: It was the young UN's direct answer to the war's atrocities, drafted while the evidence was fresh — a few years after the UN's founding in 1945, not decades.

questions.prompt: The Antarctic Treaty, setting the whole continent aside for science, was signed in what year?
questions.reveal: Twelve countries — including the US and USSR at the height of the Cold War — froze every territorial claim and banned weapons there, making it one of the era's first arms-control agreements.
questions.reasoningPath: It grew straight out of the International Geophysical Year of 1957-58, when rival nations built bases side by side, and predates the first human spaceflight — so the end of the 1950s.

questions.prompt: Spain and Portugal divided the unexplored world between them at Tordesillas in what year?
questions.reveal: The line was drawn 370 leagues west of the Cape Verde islands, handing Portugal a wedge of a continent nobody had yet seen — which is why Brazil speaks Portuguese.
questions.reasoningPath: The argument only became urgent once Columbus came back claiming new lands in 1493, and papal arbitration moved fast — so within a year or two of that.

questions.prompt: The Montreal Protocol, the treaty that rescued the ozone layer, was signed in what year?
questions.reveal: It is the only UN treaty every country on Earth has ratified. The Antarctic ozone hole is now projected to close around 2066.
questions.reasoningPath: The ozone hole was reported in 1985 and the treaty is famous for how fast governments moved — a couple of years, and comfortably before the 1992 Rio summit.

questions.prompt: London opened the world's first underground railway in what year?
questions.reveal: The first trains were steam locomotives hauling carriages through shallow brick tunnels, and about 38,000 people crammed aboard on the opening day.
questions.reasoningPath: Electric traction and the deep tube lines are 1890s, so the first line had to be steam in a cut-and-cover tunnel — mid-Victorian, a couple of decades after mainline railways arrived.

questions.prompt: Karl Benz patented his three-wheeled motor car, the first true automobile, in what year?
questions.reveal: Two years later his wife Bertha drove it 106 km without telling him, buying fuel at a pharmacy along the way — the first long-distance drive, and the publicity that sold the machine.
questions.reasoningPath: Cars were rich men's toys through the 1890s and mass-produced by 1908, so the original patent sits a couple of decades before that, once petrol engines had matured.

questions.prompt: Sputnik 1, the first artificial satellite, began beeping overhead in what year?
questions.reveal: It was an 84 kg polished metal sphere that did nothing but beep, and any amateur with a shortwave radio could hear it. It burned up in the atmosphere after about three months.
questions.reasoningPath: It opened the space race that ended with Apollo in 1969, and Gagarin flew in 1961; the whole race is usually described as about a dozen years — so the late 1950s.

questions.prompt: The first modern Olympic Games opened in Athens in what year?
questions.reveal: Winners received a silver medal and an olive branch — no gold was awarded — and the marathon was won by a Greek water carrier, to the vast relief of the home crowd.
questions.reasoningPath: The revival was a late-Victorian internationalist project, contemporary with the Eiffel Tower and the first cinema screenings, and the Paris games of 1900 were only the second — so mid-1890s.

questions.prompt: The first FIFA World Cup kicked off in Uruguay in what year?
questions.reveal: Only four European teams made the two-week boat crossing. Romania's squad was picked by the king himself, who talked their employers into granting them leave.
questions.reasoningPath: Football's world body formed in 1904, but a genuinely global tournament needed steamship travel and peacetime — so between the wars, and before television.

verdicts.note: Checked Wikipedia History of penicillin: Fleming returned to St Mary's on 3 September 1928 after summer leave at Barton Mills and found the mould — 1928 confirmed. Cantaloupe-from-a-Peoria-market strain (NRRL 1951) confirmed, 1943. Track position 0.829, in band. BUT the reveal is wrong on duration: the Oxford team (Florey/Chain) began in 1939 and had a highly purified compound by 1940-42 — roughly three years, not a decade. The decade is the gap between Fleming's 1928 observation and Oxford picking it up. Fix the reveal wording to e.g. 'that took an Oxford team, a decade later, to solve' rather than implying Oxford spent ten years. Answer, lo/hi and prompt all stand.
verdicts.correctedReveal: His mould then sat largely ignored for a decade. The first patient, an Oxford policeman treated in 1941, rallied within a day, then died when supplies ran out — and his infection probably came from bomb-blast wounds, not the rose thorn of legend.

questions.prompt: The Great Pyramid of Giza is built from roughly how many limestone blocks?
questions.reveal: Spread over the roughly 20 years of Khufu's reign, that works out at a block hauled and set in place every two or three minutes of daylight, for two decades.
questions.reasoningPath: The base is 230 m square and it stands 147 m, so volume = 1/3 x base x height, about 2.6 million cubic metres. The typical block is close to a cubic metre (2.5 tonnes of limestone), so the count is a couple of million, not thousands and not billions.

questions.prompt: The Terracotta Army: how many life-size clay soldiers are thought to guard China's first emperor?
questions.reveal: No two faces are the same, and every figure was once painted in bright colours; the lacquer beneath the paint curls off within minutes of meeting dry air, so most emerge grey.
questions.reasoningPath: It is described as an army in battle formation, not a shrine group: the main pit alone is the size of an aircraft hangar with eleven corridors of soldiers standing four abreast. That puts the total in the thousands rather than the hundreds, and the figure usually quoted alongside 130 chariots and 670 horses is about eight thousand.

questions.prompt: A Roman legion at full strength fielded roughly how many soldiers?
questions.reveal: Its smallest unit was the contubernium: eight men who shared a tent, a mule and a hand mill, and who were punished together when one of them failed.
questions.reasoningPath: Rome held an empire of tens of millions with somewhere around 25-30 legions and a total army in the low hundreds of thousands. Divide a few hundred thousand men by roughly thirty legions and each one comes out at a few thousand strong.

questions.prompt: How many oarsmen rowed a Greek trireme, the warship that won the battle of Salamis?
questions.reveal: Athens could put some 200 triremes to sea, needing about 40,000 rowers - poor citizens whose wages made the fleet a political force as much as a military one.
questions.reasoningPath: The hull is about 37 m long with three banks of oars on each side. Fit an oarsman roughly every metre and you get about 28-30 per bank per side, so 3 banks x 2 sides x ~28 is a bit under 200.

questions.prompt: How many ships sailed in the Spanish Armada of 1588?
questions.reveal: About 60 of them never got home, and most were lost to autumn gales off the Irish and Scottish coasts rather than to English guns.
questions.reasoningPath: The fleet carried roughly 30,000 men and was meant to escort an invasion army. Wooden ships of that era held a few hundred men each, so 30,000 divided by about 230 gives a fleet in the low hundreds, not thousands.

questions.prompt: How many Allied troops landed in Normandy on D-Day, 6 June 1944?
questions.reveal: The planners assumed they would capture no working port, so two prefabricated harbours were towed across the Channel in sections and bolted together off the beaches.
questions.reasoningPath: Five beaches, each assaulted by roughly a division - 20,000 to 30,000 men - plus airborne troops dropped inland. Five times about 30,000 lands you near 150,000 for the first day, with millions following over the months after.

questions.prompt: Zheng He's first treasure fleet sailed from China in 1405 with how many men aboard?
questions.reveal: Columbus set out 87 years later with three ships and about 90 men. Zheng He's flagship class dwarfed anything Europe would launch for centuries.
questions.reasoningPath: The fleet ran to more than 300 vessels, including dozens of enormous treasure ships plus supply, water and troop transports. At an average of roughly 90 crew per ship across 300-odd ships, the total lands in the tens of thousands.

questions.prompt: A Roman labourer earned about one denarius a day. A legionary's yearly pay under Augustus was how many denarii?
questions.reveal: Food, boots and tent were deducted from it, and after 20 years a veteran was promised a discharge bonus of 3,000 denarii - more than a decade of that pay in one payment.
questions.reasoningPath: A full year of daily labourer's wages would be roughly 300 denarii. A soldier was fed, housed and equipped by the state and could not leave, so his cash pay sat somewhat below a free labourer's annual earnings - a few hundred denarii, not tens and not thousands.

questions.prompt: The United States bought Louisiana from France in 1803 for how many million dollars?
questions.reveal: The territory covered about 2.1 million km2, which works out at roughly seven dollars per square kilometre - and it doubled the size of the country overnight.
questions.reasoningPath: The entire US federal budget in 1803 ran to about 10 million dollars a year and Jefferson had to borrow in Europe to pay. A price a government can just about borrow is the same order as a year of its spending - tens of millions, not hundreds.

questions.prompt: The Manhattan Project cost roughly how many billion dollars of 1940s money?
questions.reveal: About 90% went on factories and the industrial slog of separating uranium and breeding plutonium; the physics was the cheap part. Peak workforce: 130,000 people.
questions.reasoningPath: The United States spent something like 300 billion dollars on the whole of the Second World War. The bomb programme was enormous but still a single industrial effort - well under one percent of the war - so a couple of billion.

questions.prompt: The Titanic carried about 2,200 people. Her 20 lifeboats had seats for how many of them?

questions.reasoningPath: Ship's lifeboats of that era held roughly 40 to 70 people each. Twenty boats at about 60 apiece is around 1,200 - a little over half of everyone on board, which is exactly why the shortage became the scandal it did.

questions.prompt: How many houses did the Great Fire of London burn down in 1666?
questions.reveal: It burned out the homes of about 70,000 of the City's 80,000 residents - and the official death toll was six.
questions.reasoningPath: The fire consumed most of the walled City, which housed on the order of 80,000 people. At five or six people to a crowded timber house, that is well over ten thousand houses.

questions.prompt: How many flights did the Berlin Airlift make into the blockaded city in 1948-49?

questions.reasoningPath: The airlift ran about 15 months, roughly 460 days. Keeping two million people supplied by air needed hundreds of landings a day; at around 600 flights a day for 460 days you get close to 280,000.

questions.prompt: Magellan's expedition made the first circumnavigation: how many days from leaving Spain to getting back?

questions.prompt: The First Fleet sailed from Portsmouth to Botany Bay in 1787-88. How many days was the voyage?

questions.reasoningPath: England to Australia the long way round is some 24,000 km, and a laden sailing convoy makes perhaps 120-150 km a day, before counting weeks in port at Tenerife, Rio and Cape Town. That is roughly eight months.

questions.prompt: How many months did Darwin's voyage aboard HMS Beagle last?
questions.reveal: Darwin was taken on largely as the captain's dining companion, and spent only about 18 months of it at sea - the rest he was ashore, collecting.
questions.reasoningPath: The voyage is always described as the five-year voyage: it left in December 1831 and returned in October 1836, which is a few months short of five full years.

questions.prompt: How many years passed between the first stone and the finished Cologne Cathedral?
questions.reveal: Work stopped for some three centuries with a medieval crane left standing on the half-built south tower - a fixture of the skyline. When it was topped out, it was the tallest building in the world.
questions.reasoningPath: The foundation stone was laid in the high Middle Ages, in the 1200s, and the towers were completed in the industrial nineteenth century after a centuries-long halt. Two dates six centuries apart.

questions.prompt: At its 1920 peak, the British Empire covered how many million km2 of land?
questions.reveal: That empire ruled about 412 million people at its height - close to a quarter of everyone alive at the time.
questions.reasoningPath: Earth's land surface is about 149 million km2, and the empire is always described as covering roughly a quarter of it. A quarter of 149 is a bit under 40 million km2 - for comparison, Russia alone is 17.

questions.prompt: How many days did it take to build the Empire State Building?
questions.reveal: At the peak, 3,400 workers put up four and a half floors a week, and the building opened ahead of schedule and under budget.
questions.reasoningPath: It has 102 floors and is famous for going up at several floors a week. At four floors a week the frame alone takes about 25 weeks; add foundations, cladding and fit-out and you land a bit over a year rather than several.

questions.prompt: How many years did the Hundred Years' War actually last?
questions.reveal: It was not one war at all: long truces broke it into separate phases, and the name was coined by historians only in the 1800s.
questions.reasoningPath: The name is a historians' round number, and round numbers in history are almost always shorter than the real span. It ran from 1337 to the fall of English Gascony in 1453 - a bit more than a century, not less.

questions.prompt: How many years did the Ottoman Empire last, from its founding to its abolition?
questions.reveal: One family held it the entire time: 36 sultans of the House of Osman, in an unbroken male line from a frontier warlord to a deposed monarch on a train to exile.
questions.reasoningPath: It was already a rising power well before it took Constantinople in 1453, founded around 1300, and it was abolished just after the First World War. From about 1300 to 1922 is a bit over six centuries.

questions.prompt: How many billion people were alive on Earth in 1900?
questions.reveal: It had taken the whole of human history to reach that number. It has taken a little over a century to multiply it by five.
questions.reasoningPath: Humanity passed one billion around 1800, and growth only accelerated after 1900 with medicine and fertiliser. So 1900 sits above one billion but well short of the eight billion of today - somewhere between one and two.

questions.prompt: How tall was the Colossus of Rhodes, in metres?
questions.reveal: It stood barely 54 years before an earthquake snapped it at the knees, and the bronze lay where it fell for some 800 years before being sold off as scrap.
questions.reasoningPath: A bronze statue cast in the third century BC, standing on a harbour pedestal and counted as a wonder. It was celebrated but not superhuman: the Statue of Liberty's figure is 46 m, and the Colossus is always described as somewhat smaller - a ten-storey building, not a skyscraper.

questions.prompt: The first transatlantic telegraph message ran to 98 words. How many hours did it take to send?
questions.reveal: Three weeks later an engineer pushed 2,000 volts down the line to speed it up and killed the cable outright. The Atlantic stayed silent until a new one landed in 1866.
questions.reasoningPath: The 1858 cable was so weak that operators read faint flicks of a mirror galvanometer, taking minutes per letter. Around 500 letters at roughly two minutes each is somewhere near a full day's work, not a few minutes.

questions.prompt: How many years did the United States take to build the Panama Canal?
questions.reveal: The French had tried first and given up, with some 20,000 workers dead. The American engineers' opening move was not digging but a campaign against mosquitoes.
questions.reasoningPath: An 80 km cut through a mountain range plus three sets of giant locks, using steam shovels and railways rather than modern machines. Comparable megaprojects today take five to ten years, so with 1900s technology think roughly a decade rather than a generation.

But the closing image, 'a deposed monarch on a train to exile', is wrong: I checked the Abolition of the Ottoman sultanate article, which states Mehmed VI sought refuge aboard the British warship HMS Malaya and departed Constantinople on 17 November 1922 - by sea, on a battleship. The train to exile was ABDULMECID II, the last caliph, put on the Orient Express in March 1924 - a different man and a different event two years later. The reveal should end 'to a deposed monarch slipping out of his capital aboard a British battleship' or similar. Everything else holds: 'unbroken male line' is correct in the sense that all 36 descended in the male line from Osman, though succession frequently ran brother-to-brother rather than father-to-son. Answer and range unchanged (position 0.728 linear).
verdicts.correctedReveal: The end was quiet: sixteen days after the sultanate was abolished, Mehmed VI slipped out of Istanbul aboard a British battleship, HMS Malaya. He died in San Remo in 1926 and lies buried in Damascus; his cousin, the last caliph, was buried in Medina.

verdicts.note: Checked the claimed source rather than taking it on trust: Wikipedia's World population historical table, sourced to the UN, gives 1,650 million for 1900 - i.e. 1.65 billion, not 1.60. I considered a fix to 1.65 and decided against it. The spread across the standard series is Maddison ~1.56B, McEvedy and Jones ~1.63B, UN/HYDE ~1.65B, a range of about 6% and under your 10% threshold, and 1.6 is the common published rounding. On a 0.5-12 log track the 1.6 vs 1.65 difference moves the answer by 0.01 of track position - invisible in scoring. Reveal verified: world population first hit 1 billion in 1804 and 8 billion on 15 November 2022, so 1.6 x 5 = 8 in 'a little over a century' works, and it works better with 1.6 than with 1.65. Position 0.366 log. The answer is a fixed historical estimate, not a figure that changes year to year.

Checked Wikipedia Colossus of Rhodes: '70 cubits, or 33 metres (108 feet) high', with a second passage giving 32 m - a 3% internal spread, fine. Reveal verified: completed 280 BC, collapsed in the 226 BC earthquake, so 54 years standing is exact; remains 'lay on the ground for over 800 years' matches 226 BC to AD 653 = 879 years. Two honest caveats, neither reaching drop: (a) the height rests on ancient literary testimony (Pliny and Philo of Byzantium, both 70 cubits) with no archaeological confirmation - but the question's source field already discloses Pliny, and the figure is universally accepted rather than a fringe origin; (b) the scrap-sale story (AD 653, melted down and sold to a merchant of Edessa, 900 camels) comes solely from Theophanes the Confessor and Wikipedia flags it as possibly unreliable, so 'sold off as scrap' states a single-source tradition as fact. The reveal's load-bearing claims - 54 years, ~800 years lying there - are solid. Position 0.403 linear, and it is estimable by comparison with the Statue of Liberty.

Checked Wikipedia Transatlantic telegraph cable and both numbers in the prompt land exactly: Queen Victoria's message was '98 words' and 'took 16 hours to send'. Reveal verified against the same source: Wildman Whitehouse applied excessive voltage trying to speed up operation, the insulation degraded over several days and the cable failed altogether in September 1858, about three weeks after the first message - and the Atlantic had no working cable again until the 1866 landing (the 1865 attempt parted mid-ocean). The specific '2,000 volts' is the commonly cited figure and is consistent with the article's account of burned insulation under high voltage. Position 0.654 log. Minor nuance that does not affect the answer: 98 words refers to Victoria's message rather than the very first test signals down the line, which is the standard reading of 'first transatlantic telegraph message'.

Checked Wikipedia Panama Canal: the US took control 4 May 1904 and the canal opened 15 August 1914 - exactly 10 years, and the article states the American phase as 1904 to 1914. Reveal verified: the French effort left 'an estimated 22,000 men died from disease and accidents', so 'some 20,000 workers dead' is a fair rounding of 22,000, and the French did abandon the attempt. The mosquito claim is confirmed and is the real story, not a flourish: Gorgas's sanitation campaign against yellow fever and malaria preceded the serious digging and 'after two years of extensive work, the mosquito-spread diseases were nearly eliminated'. Position 0.188 linear - low in the band but inside it. OVERLAP FLAG: verified.json geography already asks the Panama Canal's length in km - same subject, different quantity, not a duplicate.

questions.prompt: Depth of the Challenger Deep, the deepest point in any ocean, in metres?
questions.reveal: The pressure down there is over 1,000 times what you feel at the surface — yet a 2018 dive filmed a plastic bag lying on the bottom.
questions.reasoningPath: Everest is about 8.8 km tall, and the standard comparison is that the deepest trench would swallow it with room to spare — so a bit over 10 km, not 5 and not 30.

questions.prompt: How far does the Great Barrier Reef stretch along Australia's coast, in km?
questions.reveal: It is not one reef but about 2,900 of them plus 900 islands — the largest structure on Earth built by living organisms.
questions.reasoningPath: Australia is roughly 4,000 km across; the reef runs down most of the Queensland coast, from Cape York toward Brisbane — call it half to two-thirds of that side, so a couple of thousand km.

questions.prompt: Area of the Sahara, the world's largest hot desert, in millions of km²?
questions.reveal: It was green savanna dotted with lakes as recently as 6,000 years ago, and the wobble of Earth's orbit will make it green again in roughly 10,000 more.
questions.reasoningPath: It spans Africa from the Atlantic to the Red Sea, about 4,800 km, and roughly 1,800 km north to south — multiply and you get around 9 million km², about the size of China.

questions.prompt: Maximum depth of Lake Baikal, the world's deepest lake, in metres?
questions.reveal: It holds about a fifth of all the unfrozen fresh water on Earth's surface, and at 25 million years old it is the most ancient lake there is.
questions.reasoningPath: Ordinary big lakes run tens to low hundreds of metres. Baikal sits in a continental rift that is still pulling apart, so it should be several times deeper than a normal lake — over a kilometre, but far short of ocean trenches.

questions.prompt: Total height of Angel Falls, the world's tallest waterfall, in metres?
questions.reveal: Its single unbroken plunge is 807 m — so long that in the dry season much of the water blows away as mist before it ever reaches the bottom.
questions.reasoningPath: Famous wide falls like Niagara are only about 50 m. The tallest one falls off a flat-topped tableland, so think skyscraper scale — the Burj Khalifa is 828 m and this beats it.

questions.prompt: Length of Canada's coastline, the longest of any country, in km?
questions.reveal: That is more than half of the entire world's coastline. Norway is a distant second at about 83,000 km — the total is inflated by tens of thousands of Arctic islands.
questions.reasoningPath: Earth's whole circumference is 40,000 km. A country facing three oceans with a shredded, island-strewn Arctic edge must run to several times that — hundreds of thousands of km, not tens of thousands.

questions.prompt: How many mountains on Earth rise more than 8,000 m above sea level?
questions.reveal: Every one is in the Himalaya or Karakoram. Reinhold Messner became the first person to climb all of them in 1986 — and did it without bottled oxygen.
questions.reasoningPath: You can name a few — Everest, K2, Kangchenjunga, Annapurna — and they all crowd into one corner of Asia. A single range cannot hold dozens, so somewhere around ten to twenty.

questions.prompt: Depth of the Kola Superdeep Borehole, the deepest hole ever drilled, in metres?
questions.reveal: Twenty years of drilling got only about a third of the way through the crust, and the rock at the bottom was near 180 °C — far hotter than predicted.
questions.reasoningPath: The deepest mines reach about 4 km. A drill string can go further but heat and rock flow stop it well before the mantle at 35 km — so somewhere near the height of Everest, around 12 km.

questions.prompt: Maximum depth of the Congo, the world's deepest river, in metres?
questions.reveal: Its lower canyon is so deep and dark that blind, colourless fish live at the bottom, cut off from relatives just a few hundred metres away by the current.
questions.reasoningPath: Big navigable rivers are typically 10 to 30 m deep. A record-holder squeezing an enormous flow through a narrow rocky gorge could be ten times that, but nowhere near lake depths — so a couple of hundred metres.

questions.prompt: How wide is the curtain of falling water at Victoria Falls, in metres?
questions.reveal: Its Lozi name, Mosi-oa-Tunya, means 'the smoke that thunders': the spray climbs over 400 m and can be seen from 50 km away.
questions.reasoningPath: The falls are simply the full width of the Zambezi dropping into a crack. A major African river in flood is on the order of one to two km across, so the curtain is about that.

questions.prompt: Surface elevation of Lake Titicaca, high in the Andes, in metres?
questions.reveal: At 281 m deep it stores enough summer heat to warm the air above it, letting maize ripen on the Altiplano at an altitude where it otherwise could not grow.
questions.reasoningPath: It sits on the Altiplano between Peru and Bolivia. La Paz is around 3,600 m and the lake is slightly above the city — so just under 4,000 m, well below the 6,000 m peaks around it.

questions.prompt: Area of Salar de Uyuni, the world's largest salt flat, in km²?
questions.reveal: It varies by less than a metre in height across its whole surface, so satellites point their altimeters at it to calibrate them.
questions.reasoningPath: Photographs show white stretching past the horizon in every direction, which means tens of km at least; the flat is roughly 100 km by 100 km — so about ten thousand km².

questions.prompt: If all of Antarctica's ice melted, how many metres would sea level rise?
questions.reveal: The ice averages 2.2 km thick, and its sheer weight has pressed the bedrock underneath it hundreds of metres below sea level.
questions.reasoningPath: 14 million km² of ice about 2 km thick is roughly 28 million km³. Spread over 360 million km² of ocean that is about 80 m of water; trim for ice being less dense than rock and for flooded coastline, and you land near 60 m.

questions.prompt: Average flow of the Amazon into the Atlantic, in cubic metres per second?
questions.reveal: That is roughly a fifth of all the river water reaching the world's oceans, and the freshwater plume is still detectable more than 100 km out at sea.
questions.reasoningPath: The basin covers about 6 million km² and gets some 2 m of rain a year; if half of that runs off, that is about 6,000 km³ per year. Divide by 31 million seconds and you get roughly 200,000 m³ per second.

questions.prompt: Land area of Madagascar, the world's fourth-largest island, in km²?
questions.reveal: It broke away from India about 90 million years ago, and roughly nine in ten of its plants and animals live nowhere else on Earth.
questions.reasoningPath: On a map it is a long slab about 1,600 km top to bottom and 500 km wide. That multiplies out near 600,000 km² — about the size of France or Ukraine.

questions.prompt: Area of the Gobi Desert, spanning Mongolia and northern China, in km²?
questions.reveal: It is a cold desert — winter nights drop below −30 °C and snow sometimes dusts the dunes. Its cliffs also yielded the first dinosaur nests known to science, in 1923.
questions.reasoningPath: It runs about 1,600 km southwest to northeast and 800 km across, giving something over a million km² — roughly a seventh of the Sahara, and about the size of Mongolia itself.

questions.prompt: World's biggest tides, in the Bay of Fundy: metres between low and high water?
questions.reveal: Around 100 billion tonnes of seawater move in and out on every tide — more than all the world's rivers discharge in the same span of time.
questions.reasoningPath: An ordinary coast sees one or two metres of tide. A long funnel-shaped bay whose natural sloshing period matches the tide amplifies it roughly tenfold — so around 15 m, the height of a five-storey building.

questions.prompt: Average elevation of the Tibetan Plateau, the 'roof of the world', in metres?
questions.reveal: Its 2.5 million km² of high ground steers the Asian monsoon, and the air up there carries only about 60% of the oxygen you get at sea level.
questions.reasoningPath: Lhasa sits at 3,650 m and is one of the plateau's lower points; the Himalaya rim reaches 8,000 m. The average has to sit above Mont Blanc but well below the peaks — around 4,500 m.

questions.prompt: Averaged across the whole planet, how deep is the ocean, in metres?
questions.reveal: Shrink Earth to the size of a billiard ball and the entire ocean would be a film thinner than a coat of paint.
questions.reasoningPath: Shallow continental shelves are only about 100 m deep but cover little area; the abyssal plains that dominate the sea floor run 4 to 5 km, and the deepest trench is 11 km. The average must sit near 4 km.

questions.prompt: What percentage of all the water on Earth is fresh water?
questions.reveal: About 69% of that fresh water is locked in ice caps and glaciers, and under 1% of it is the liquid surface water that rivers and lakes actually hold.
questions.reasoningPath: Oceans cover 71% of the surface and average nearly 4 km deep, while lakes and rivers are shallow puddles by comparison and ice sheets, though thick, cover little of the globe. Fresh water has to be a low single-digit percentage.

questions.prompt: Surface area of the Pacific Ocean, in millions of km²?
questions.reveal: It is bigger than every scrap of land on the planet combined — about 149 million km² — and it shrinks a little each year as the Atlantic widens.
questions.reasoningPath: Earth's surface is about 510 million km² and roughly 70% of it is ocean, so 360 million km² of sea. The Pacific looks like nearly half the globe on a map, so somewhere around 160 million.

questions.prompt: How many centimetres wider does the Atlantic Ocean grow each year?
questions.reveal: That is roughly the speed your fingernails grow — and it means the whole ocean did not exist 200 million years ago, when Brazil was pressed against West Africa.
questions.reasoningPath: The Atlantic is about 5,000 km wide and opened over roughly 200 million years. Five million metres divided by 200 million years is a few centimetres a year.

questions.prompt: What percentage of Greenland's surface is buried under its ice sheet?
questions.reveal: The ice runs up to 3 km thick and weighs so much that it has pressed the middle of the island into a bowl lying below sea level.
questions.reasoningPath: Every town on Greenland is on the coast and the interior is a blank white dome, but the fjord-cut fringe is bare rock. So most of it, with a strip left over — around four-fifths.

questions.prompt: Depth of the Calypso Deep, the deepest point of the Mediterranean, in metres?
questions.reveal: That basin dried to a salt desert about 5.5 million years ago, then refilled through the Strait of Gibraltar in a flood that may have taken only a couple of years.
questions.reasoningPath: The Mediterranean is a true ocean basin with a subduction trench south of Greece, not a shallow shelf sea. Expect something near the global ocean average of 4 km rather than a few hundred metres.

questions.prompt: How far below its entrance does the deepest explored cave reach, in metres?
questions.reveal: The two deepest known caves are in the same Caucasus massif in Abkhazia, and reaching the bottom of either takes an expedition camped underground for over a week.
questions.reasoningPath: Caves need soluble rock above the water table, so depth is capped by the height of the limestone massif they sit in — a couple of kilometres of mountain, not ten.

verdicts.note: Depth verified exactly: Wikipedia's Challenger Deep survey table gives 10,935 +/- 6 m from the 2021 study, matching the answer to the metre. Historical spread (10,920 Takuyo 1984, 10,925 Sonne 2016, 10,994 Sumner 2010) is under 1%. Track position 0.798, fine. THE REVEAL IS FACTUALLY WRONG and must be edited: I checked the Mariana Trench article and the plastic bag on the bottom was found by Victor Vescovo in 2019, not 2018 - 'In 2019, Victor Vescovo reported finding a plastic bag and candy wrappers at the bottom of the trench.' The 2018 date comes from a separate Marine Policy study of the Deep-sea Debris Database that publicised a 1998 photograph at 10,898 m; there was no 2018 dive. Change the reveal to 'a 2019 dive found a plastic bag and candy wrappers lying on the bottom.' Pressure check: ~1,086 atm, so 'over 1,000 times' is correct. No duplicate in verified.json (closest is Mauna Kea base-to-summit 10,210 m, a different quantity).

verdicts.note: Tried to break it on the length figure, since some tourism sources quote 2,600 km. Wikipedia's Great Barrier Reef article gives 'over 2,300 kilometres' and confirms 'over 2,900 individual reefs and 900 islands' plus 'the world's biggest single structure made by living organisms' - every element of the reveal checks out and the reveal adds facts rather than restating the answer. That is a 6.5% spread, inside the ~10% tolerance, and the two are just different boundary conventions (Wikipedia notes 11 million km2 if you include everything under 250 mm rainfall). Reveal verified: the African Humid Period ended ~5,500-6,000 years ago and the precession cycle (~23,000 yr) puts the next green phase roughly 10,000 years out. Track position 0.449. Not in verified.json.

Track position 0.853, inside band but near the top; acceptable. Not in verified.json.

The article also explains the 979 m includes ~400 m of sloped cascade plus a 30 m downstream plunge, so the 'total height' wording in the prompt is the correct framing (a prompt saying just 'height' would have been ambiguous). That is a genuine >10% source disagreement, definitional rather than an error, so a player using a non-CIA figure would be marked wrong on an unstated convention. verdicts.correctedPrompt: According to the CIA World Factbook, how long is Canada's coastline, the longest of any country, in km?

verdicts.note: Count and reveal both verified on the Eight-thousander article: 14 peaks, all in the Himalaya and Karakoram, Messner first to complete all 14 on 16 October 1986 and 'summited each of the 14 peaks without the aid of bottled oxygen'. The defect is the prompt wording: 'how many mountains rise more than 8,000 m' is ambiguous, because there are roughly 20+ summits above 8,000 m once subsidiary tops are counted (Lhotse Middle, Yalung Kang, Broad Peak Central and others); the canonical 14 are the peaks with sufficient topographic prominence. A player answering ~20 on the honest reading would be scored wrong and would have grounds to complain. Adding 'separate' resolves it without turning the question into jargon. Answer 14, range 2..40 linear, position 0.316 - all unchanged.

Reveal is partly loose but not wrong - the blind, unpigmented Lamprologus lethops is documented at depths to ~160 m in the lower Congo, and the rapids/current isolating populations across short distances is real published work on Lower Congo speciation. Track position 0.671. Not in verified.json.

The thermal-moderation claim (the lake's stored heat lets maize ripen on the Altiplano) is standard published Altiplano climatology. Linear range 1000..6000 with answer 3812 gives position 0.562, well centred. Not in verified.json.

Track position 0.38. Not in verified.json.

Reveal's 2.2 km average thickness checks out from NSIDC's own numbers: ~30 million km3 of ice over ~14 million km2 = 2.14 km. Wikipedia's Amazon discharge table gives 223,700 m3/s average at the delta (Obidos 172,100, Santarem 188,600 - the lower numbers are upstream gauges, not competing estimates). 220,000 sits between 209,000 and 223,700; the full spread is ~7%, inside tolerance. Reveal check: global river discharge to oceans is ~1.2 million m3/s, so 220,000 is ~18%, and 'roughly a fifth' is fair. Track position 0.434. Not in verified.json - the existing bank has Amazon LENGTH (6,400 km), which is a different quantity, so no duplication.

Wikipedia's country article gives 592,796 km2 total; the island area is 587,041 km2 and the CIA land-only figure is 581,540 km2 - a ~2% spread, well inside tolerance, and 587,000 is the island figure the prompt actually asks for. Fourth-largest island confirmed. Reveal verified: split from the Indian subcontinent 'approximately 90 million years ago' and 'over 90% of its wildlife being endemic', so 'nine in ten' is right. Track position 0.783. Not in verified.json.

Verified on the Gobi Desert article: approximately 1,295,000 km2, so 1,300,000 is 0.4% off - well inside tolerance. Reveal confirmed: the 1923 Central Asiatic Expedition uncovered 26 eggs averaging 23 cm, the first dinosaur eggs/nests recognised by science. Cold-desert framing with sub -30 C winter nights is standard. Track position 0.406. Not in verified.json.

Verified on the Bay of Fundy article: highest tidal range in the world, averaging about 16 m, and 'around 100 billion tonnes of water flows in and out' per half-tidal cycle, which the article calls twice the combined flow of all the world's rivers - so the reveal's 'more than' is true and if anything understates it. One caveat I checked and am letting through: Guinness recognises a near-tie with Ungava Bay's Leaf Basin (~16.8 m vs Burntcoat Head ~16.3 m), so the 'world's biggest' superlative is mildly contested, but the 16 m answer is unaffected either way. Track position 0.564. Not in verified.json.

Verified on the Tibetan Plateau article: 'an average elevation exceeding 4,500 metres' and an area of 2,500,000 km2, so both the answer and the reveal's area figure match. Oxygen claim checks out independently: atmospheric pressure at 4,500 m is ~57-58% of sea level, so 'about 60% of the oxygen' is right. Linear range 500..6500 puts the answer at 0.667, inside band. Not in verified.json (the bank has Everest's height, a different quantity).

Went straight to the claimed source rather than a mirror: NOAA Ocean Service states 'The average depth of the ocean is about 3,682 meters (12,080 feet)' - exact match to the answer. Reveal arithmetic verified independently: 3.682/6371 = 0.00058, so on a 57 mm billiard ball the ocean film is ~17 microns, versus ~50-100 microns for a coat of paint, so 'thinner than a coat of paint' holds. This is the one that fails. I checked the claimed source itself - the USGS Water Science School 'How much water is there on Earth' page - and its own distribution table does NOT support 2.5%: it puts oceans at 96.54% of all water, with the remaining saline groundwater and saline lakes accounting for ~0.94%, leaving fresh water at about 3.5%. The commonly quoted 2.5% comes from the Shiklomanov budget, and other sources round to 3%. That is a 2.5 vs 3.5 spread of 40%, far beyond the ~10% tolerance, and critically the claimed source contradicts the stated answer, which is exactly the situation that generates a complaint email we cannot defend. The reveal's supporting numbers are actually fine (USGS gives 68.7% of fresh water in ice caps, glaciers and permanent snow, matching 'about 69%', and surface water well under 1%), but the headline answer cannot be pinned down. Drop rather than fix - there is no defensible single value.

The shrinking-Pacific/widening-Atlantic claim is correct plate tectonics and ties to [21] without duplicating it. Track position 0.609. Not in verified.json.

Not in verified.json.

Verified on the Calypso Deep article. The article lead's loose '~5,200 m' and the older 5,267 m figure are within ~3%, inside tolerance. Reveal verified: the Messinian salinity crisis dried the basin ~5.5 Ma and the Zanclean flood refilled it through Gibraltar, possibly in a couple of years. One wording nit for the parent: the claimed source should read '2020 Limiting Factor crewed dive', not 'bathymetric survey' - it was direct sensor measurement, not sonar mapping. So the deepest explored cave is 2,224 m, not 2,220 m. The prompt is well built because it does not name the cave, so it survives the rank flip - only the number needs updating. Reveal verified: both caves are in the Arabika Massif in Abkhazia, and bottom-reaching expeditions do camp underground for over a week. Flagging for the parent that this figure has been revised in 2017, 2023, 2024 and 2025 - it is close to the 'changes year to year' drop rule, but every revision has been under ~1%, invisible on a 400..20000 log track, so it is survivable if the source is dated. Position with 2224 is 0.438, unchanged and in band. Not in verified.json.

questions.prompt: Population of Greater London, the 32 boroughs plus the City, in millions?
questions.reveal: London's population actually shrank for decades after 1939 and only clawed its way back to the pre-war peak around 2015.
questions.reasoningPath: The UK holds about 67 million people and roughly one in seven lives in the capital. London belongs in the same bracket as Bogota or Bangkok: comfortably above 5 million, nowhere near Tokyo's 37 million metro.

questions.prompt: The Danube touches more countries than any other river. How many countries?
questions.reveal: Four national capitals stand on its banks - Vienna, Bratislava, Budapest and Belgrade - more than any other river can claim.
questions.reasoningPath: Trace it from Germany's Black Forest to the Black Sea: Germany, Austria, Slovakia, Hungary, Croatia, Serbia, Romania, Bulgaria, then Moldova and Ukraine at the delta. Central Europe is a patchwork of small states, so the count runs to about ten, not three.

questions.prompt: What percentage of the world's people now live in urban areas rather than rural ones?
questions.reveal: Humanity crossed the halfway mark around 2007. In 1800, fewer than one person in ten lived in a town of any size.
questions.reasoningPath: Rich countries run about 80% urban and China passed half around 2011, but India, still the biggest single population, is only about 36%. Weighting by population lands the world a little above half rather than near 80.

questions.prompt: How many time zones does Russia span?
questions.reveal: France holds the record at 12 once its overseas territories count, and Russia briefly squeezed itself down to nine zones between 2010 and 2014.
questions.reasoningPath: Russia stretches from Kaliningrad to the Bering Strait, roughly 170 degrees of longitude. At 15 degrees per hour that is about eleven hours of difference, so the answer is nearer a dozen than a handful.

questions.prompt: What percentage of humanity lives in the Northern Hemisphere?
questions.reveal: About two-thirds of Earth's land lies north of the equator, and the entire Southern Hemisphere holds fewer people than India alone.
questions.reasoningPath: China, India, all of Europe, the Middle East, North America and most of Africa sit north of the line. The south gets Australia, southern Africa and most of South America. That is not a 60-40 split but something close to nine to one.

questions.prompt: How many billion people live on the continent of Africa (2024)?
questions.reveal: Africa's median age is about 19, the youngest of any continent, and it is projected to supply more than half of all global population growth to 2050.
questions.reasoningPath: World population is about 8.2 billion, with China and India roughly 1.4 billion each. Africa's largest country, Nigeria, is around 220 million across 54 countries, which puts the continent between one and two billion.

questions.prompt: Population of Indonesia, the fourth most populous country, in millions (2024)?
questions.source: UN World Population Prospects / Statistics Indonesia
questions.reveal: More than half of Indonesians live on Java, an island about the size of England carrying some 150 million people.
questions.reasoningPath: It ranks fourth, behind China, India and the US at about 340 million. Pakistan and Nigeria sit around 240 and 220 million, so Indonesia has to be just above them: a few hundred million, not tens of millions.

questions.prompt: Greenland is the world's largest island. How many people live on it?
questions.reveal: No road links any two Greenlandic towns; getting between them means a boat, a plane or, in winter, a sled.
questions.reasoningPath: It is an ice sheet with a thin fringe of coastal settlements, and the capital Nuuk is a small town by world standards. Think Faroe Islands scale rather than Icelandic: tens of thousands, not hundreds of thousands.

questions.prompt: Total population of Singapore, in millions (2024)?
questions.reveal: Singapore has enlarged its own territory by roughly a quarter since the 1960s, importing sand to reclaim land from the sea.
questions.reasoningPath: A single dense city-state on an island smaller than many capitals' metro areas: bigger than Oslo or Helsinki, far smaller than Jakarta. That places it in the several-million band.

questions.prompt: Population of Istanbul, Europe's largest city, in millions (rounded, 2024)?
questions.reveal: It is the only city built across two continents, and it has more than tripled in size since 1980.
questions.reasoningPath: It outranks Moscow's roughly 13 million and London's 9 million to lead Europe, but it is nothing like Tokyo's 37 million metro. That brackets it in the mid-teens.

questions.prompt: Kazakhstan, the largest landlocked country, covers how many million km²?
questions.reveal: It is the ninth-largest country on Earth yet holds only about 20 million people, roughly seven per square kilometre.
questions.reasoningPath: It ranks ninth by area: well under Australia's 7.7 million km² and India's 3.3 million, but many times France's 0.55 million. That pins it near two to three million.

questions.prompt: How many countries share a land border with China?
questions.reveal: Russia ties it at 14, and China's shortest border is the 76 km it shares with Afghanistan at the end of the Wakhan Corridor.
questions.reasoningPath: Walk the ring: North Korea, Russia, Mongolia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Afghanistan, Pakistan, India, Nepal, Bhutan, Myanmar, Laos, Vietnam. A country that large touches a dozen-plus neighbours, not four or five.

questions.prompt: The Canada-United States frontier, the world's longest land border, runs how many km?
questions.reveal: Over 2,000 km of it runs dead straight along the 49th parallel, and a separate 2,475 km stretch fences off Alaska.
questions.reasoningPath: North America is roughly 5,000 km wide, but this border is no straight line: add the Great Lakes shoreline detours and the whole Alaska section, and it comes to nearly double the continent's width.

questions.prompt: Russia and the US come closest at the Diomede Islands. How many km of sea separate them?
questions.reveal: The International Date Line runs between them, so the two are nicknamed Tomorrow and Yesterday Isles, almost a full day apart in local time.
questions.reasoningPath: The Bering Strait is about 82 km wide and the two islands sit near its middle, so the gap between them is only a few kilometres. In a hard winter the sea between them freezes solid.

questions.prompt: How many of the world's countries are landlocked, with no sea coast at all?
questions.reveal: Two are doubly landlocked, meaning every one of their neighbours is landlocked too: Liechtenstein and Uzbekistan.
questions.reasoningPath: Africa contributes about 16, Europe roughly 14 counting the microstates, Asia about a dozen with Central Asia and Mongolia, and South America just Bolivia and Paraguay. That totals around 40 out of 193.

questions.prompt: Bolivia's seat of government, La Paz, sits how many metres above sea level?
questions.reveal: Water boils there at about 88 degrees Celsius, so cooking takes noticeably longer, and the airport at El Alto stands above 4,000 m.
questions.reasoningPath: It sits on the Andean Altiplano, higher than any Alpine ski resort but still a fully functioning city with a million-plus residents. Permanent living gets hard much above 4,000 m, so it belongs in the 3,000-4,000 band.

questions.prompt: La Rinconada in Peru is the highest permanent settlement on Earth. Its altitude in metres?
questions.reveal: Some 30,000 people live up there working a gold mine, breathing air with roughly half the oxygen of sea level.
questions.reasoningPath: Everest base camp is about 5,300 m and year-round human settlement gives out just below that ceiling. La Paz manages 3,600, so the highest permanent town has to sit near 5,000.

questions.prompt: The Gotthard Base Tunnel, the longest rail tunnel, runs how many km under the Alps?
questions.reveal: Trains pass under as much as 2,300 m of rock, and the 17-year dig hauled out roughly 28 million tonnes of mountain.
questions.reasoningPath: The Channel Tunnel is 50 km under a strait about 34 km wide. The Alps are a wider barrier, but a base tunnel still only crosses one range, so tens of kilometres is the right order, not hundreds.

questions.prompt: The world's longest bridge, China's Danyang-Kunshan viaduct, stretches how many km?
questions.reveal: It carries high-speed trains between Shanghai and Nanjing, and about 9 km of it runs on piers straight across Yangcheng Lake.
questions.reasoningPath: This is not a span over a gap but a continuous viaduct holding a railway above soft delta ground, so its length is set by the distance between cities, not by a river's width. That means well past any suspension bridge.

questions.prompt: Guinness calls Tokyo's Shinjuku the busiest station on Earth: how many million passengers a day?
questions.reveal: The station has more than 200 exits, and at rush hour railway staff are still employed to push passengers into the carriages.
questions.reasoningPath: Greater Tokyo's 37 million people commute overwhelmingly by rail, and Shinjuku is the main interchange. A busy European terminus handles a few hundred thousand a day; Tokyo's biggest runs about ten times that.

questions.prompt: India's railway network covers how many km of route (2023)?
questions.reveal: It moves over 20 million passengers a day and employs about 1.2 million people, one of the largest workforces on the planet.
questions.reasoningPath: India covers 3.3 million km² and the network reaches nearly every district. France, about a sixth the area, has some 27,000 km of route, so scaling up lands in the tens of thousands, not hundreds of thousands.

questions.prompt: Australia's Dingo Fence, the world's longest fence, runs how many km across the outback?
questions.reveal: The effect is visible from orbit: on the dingo-free side kangaroo numbers boom and the vegetation is cropped visibly shorter.
questions.reasoningPath: It runs from the South Australian coast up and across to Queensland's coast to shut dingoes out of the southeastern sheep country. Australia is about 4,000 km wide and the fence zigzags, so a few thousand km.

questions.prompt: Tristan da Cunha, the remotest inhabited island, lies how many km from the nearest inhabited land?
questions.reveal: Fewer than 250 people live there sharing just eight surnames, and with no airstrip the only way in is a six-day boat trip from Cape Town.
questions.reasoningPath: It sits in the middle of the South Atlantic. The nearest land with people on it is St Helena to the north, and Africa is nearly 3,000 km east, so the gap has to be thousands of km, not hundreds.

questions.prompt: Kyiv's Arsenalna, the world's deepest metro station, sits how many metres below ground?
questions.reveal: The escalator ride alone takes about five minutes, and the station served as a bomb shelter after the 2022 invasion.
questions.reasoningPath: An ordinary deep station sits 30-60 m down. The record holders are Cold War-era tunnels built to double as shelters, so the deepest should be roughly double that: a 30-storey building turned upside down.

questions.prompt: The Philippines officially counts how many islands?
questions.source: Philippine National Mapping and Resource Information Authority (NAMRIA)
questions.reveal: Only about 2,000 are inhabited and more than 5,000 have no name at all; a 2016 survey turned up over 500 that nobody had counted before.
questions.reasoningPath: Indonesia, the largest archipelago, runs to more than 17,000 islands. The Philippines is a smaller archipelago of the same shape and geology, so its total should be thousands - roughly half Indonesia's, not hundreds.

verdicts.correctedPrompt: Population of Greater London, the 32 boroughs plus the City, in millions (2024)?
verdicts.note: Checked ONS-derived figures: Wikipedia/ONS mid-2024 estimate is 9,089,736; Trust for London states London hit 'a new high of 9.1 million' in 2024; the 2021 census was 8,799,800. The candidate's 8.9M is the mid-2022/2023 vintage and is now ~2% stale. Reveal verified independently: 1939 peak 8.6M, fell to 6.8M by 1991 (Trust for London), regained the pre-war peak in 2015 - reveal is correct. Fixing answer to 9.1 and pinning the year in the prompt, since this drifts ~1%/yr. Track position with 9.1 on log 1.5-30 = 0.60, in band.

Tried to break the '10 countries' claim. Wikipedia's Danube article states it 'connects ten European countries, running through their territories or marking a border' and enumerates them (Germany, Austria, Slovakia, Hungary, Croatia, Serbia, Romania, Bulgaria, Moldova, Ukraine) - count checks out at exactly 10. Attempted counter-example: the Nile basin spans 11 states but the Nile's own course touches far fewer, so the Danube's 10 stands as the record for a river's course. Reveal verified verbatim on the same source: 'four national capitals: Vienna, Bratislava, Budapest, and Belgrade' - and no other river has four. Note for the editor: verified.json geography #22 already asks the Danube's LENGTH (2,850 km). Different quantity so not a duplicate, but it is the second Danube question in the category.

This fails on definition, not on precision. World Bank/UN national-definitions series (SP.URB.TOTL.IN.ZS, fetched from the World Bank API) gives world urban share 57.31% (2023) and 57.57% (2024) - so 57 is right under that definition. But Our World in Data's urbanization page, using the EU/UN Degree of Urbanisation, reports the split as 44% cities + 36% towns and suburbs + 20% rural - i.e. 80% urban vs 20% rural, which is exactly how this prompt words it ('urban areas rather than rural ones'). Two reputable, heavily-cited sources answering the identically-worded question differ by 57 vs 80, roughly 40% relative - far outside the ~10% tolerance. Worse, 80 is the top of the stated 20-80 range, so a player who read OWID lands at maximum penalty while being defensibly right. Not salvageable by tightening the range.

Checked Wikipedia 'Time in Russia': 11 zones, UTC+02:00 to UTC+12:00, confirmed. Reveal checked in two parts against separate pages: (a) the same article confirms the 28 March 2010 change abolished two of the eleven zones, giving 9 zones from 2010 until the October 2014 restoration - reveal correct; (b) 'List of time zones by country' states 'France, including its overseas territories, has the most time zones with 12 (13 including its claim in Antarctica)', which confirms the France-at-12 claim exactly as worded. Same table gives US 11 and UK 9, so no rival at 12. Answer 11 at linear position 0.38.

Wikipedia 'Northern Hemisphere' gives '87.0% of the Earth's total human population' and '67.3% of Earth's land'. Two adversarial checks: (1) the article's own 6.4 billion figure is stale against today's 8.2B total (6.4/8.2 = 78%), so the 87% is a ratio carried forward from an older total - but the ratio itself is corroborated by the independent range of published estimates (87-90%, the 90% figure being the common textbook one), a spread of only 3.4%, inside tolerance, and the 40-100 range makes that spread ~5% of track. (2) Reveal checked arithmetically: 67.3% land is 'about two-thirds' - correct; and 13% of 8.2B = ~1.07B for the Southern Hemisphere versus India's 1.45B, so 'fewer people than India alone' holds. Weakest keep in the set, but I could not find a source outside the 87-90 band.

Cross-checked two ways since Worldometers returned 403. Wikipedia's 'List of continents by population' gives Africa 1,393,676,444 for 2021 (UN WPP); compounding at Africa's ~2.35%/yr growth reaches ~1.49B for 2024, matching the UN WPP 2024 revision's ~1.52B. Candidate 1.5B is correct to within 1-2%. Reveal checked: same-source median age 19.7 in 2012 (world 30.4), now ~19, youngest of any continent - correct; and the UN projection that Africa supplies more than half of global population growth to 2050 is a standard WPP finding, consistent with Wikipedia's cited 3.8bn-by-2100 projection. Linear position 0.31.

Checked 'Demographics of Indonesia': the 2025 Kemendagri civil-registration total is 288,315,089, and Java is 54.4% of the national population. Working back, the mid-2024 BPS figure (281.6M) and UN WPP 2024 (~283.5M) bracket the candidate's 282M within 0.7% - the prompt correctly pins 2024. Tested the reveal hard because the England comparison is the kind of thing that is usually wrong: Java is 129,904 km2 against England's 130,279 km2, so 'about the size of England' is unusually accurate, and 54.4% of ~288M is ~157M, so 'some 150 million' holds. Indonesia is 4th most populous behind India, China, USA - correct. Log position 0.68.

Wikipedia 'Greenland' gives 56,583 (2022) and a 2025 estimate of 56,831, confirming Statistics Greenland's ~56k and making it the least densely populated country - candidate 56,000 is within 1.5% and the figure is unusually stable year to year (Greenland's population has sat in the 55-57k band for two decades), so the 'changes annually' objection does not bite. Reveal: the Greenland article confirms all towns sit on the ice-free coast but does not itself cover roads; the no-inter-town-road fact is separately well established (Greenland has roughly 150 km of road in total, none of it linking two towns). Log position 0.35.

Checked 'Demographics of Singapore': total population 6.11 million as of June 2025 (4.20M residents - 3.66M citizens plus 540k PRs - and 1.91M non-residents), which puts the June 2024 total at 6.04M. Candidate 6M for 2024 is correct. I specifically checked the residents-vs-total trap: 'total population' is the right frame and the prompt says 'total', so a player is not being scored against the 4.2M resident figure. Reveal checked: Singapore's land area grew from ~581.5 km2 in the 1960s to ~735 km2, an increase of ~26%, matching 'roughly a quarter', and the imported-sand reclamation is well documented. Log position 0.34.

The number is fine but the reveal contains a false claim. TUIK via Wikipedia: 15,754,053 at 31 Dec 2025 (15.66M in 2023, 15.70M in 2024), so 16M rounded is defensible at ~1.6% error. The reveal, however, asserts Istanbul 'is the only city built across two continents' - that is wrong, and Wikipedia pointedly does not make the exclusivity claim ('It is a city on two continents'). Atyrau and Oral in Kazakhstan and Orenburg and Magnitogorsk in Russia all straddle the Europe-Asia line. Second soft spot: 'Europe's largest city' only holds if you count Istanbul's Asian side, since Moscow (13.1M) beats Istanbul's European side (~10.6M) - Wikipedia hedges to 'among the largest cities in Europe'. Reveal-wrong is a drop under the rules. Salvageable if the reveal is rewritten (e.g. the two-thirds-in-Europe split) and the answer set to 15.7.

Wikipedia 'Kazakhstan' confirms all four load-bearing claims: area 2,724,910 km2 (candidate 2.7M correct to 0.9%), explicitly 'the world's ninth-largest country by land area and the largest landlocked country', and population ~20.5 million. Checked the reveal's density arithmetic myself: 20.5M / 2.72M km2 = 7.5 per km2, matching 'roughly seven per square kilometre' and the article's own 'fewer than 8 people per square kilometre'. Area is a fixed figure so there is no year-drift problem. Linear position 0.63.

Wikipedia 'Borders of China' states 14 land neighbours, 'tied with Russia for the most in the world', and I counted the enumerated table myself: Mongolia, Russia, India, Myanmar, Nepal, North Korea, Vietnam, Kazakhstan, Pakistan, Laos, Tajikistan, Kyrgyzstan, Bhutan, Afghanistan = exactly 14. Both reveal claims verified on that same table: the Russia tie at 14, and Afghanistan as the shortest border at 76 km (the Wakhan Corridor) - the table's next-shortest is Laos at 423 km, so the 76 km really is the outlier it is presented as. Linear position 0.32.

Wikipedia's Canada-United States border infobox gives 8,891 km, matching the International Boundary Commission; the CIA Factbook's 8,893 km differs by 0.02%, so there is no meaningful source disagreement. Verified the reveal's straight-line claim on a separate page ('49th parallel north'): 'Roughly 2,030 kilometres of the Canada-United States border was designated to follow the 49th parallel', from the Lake of the Woods to the Strait of Georgia - so 'over 2,000 km' is right. The Alaska-Canada figure of 2,475 km is the standard IBC/Factbook segment length and is consistent with the 8,891 total. Log position 0.42.

Wikipedia 'Diomede Islands' confirms the islands are '2.4 miles (3.8 km) apart at their closest points' - candidate 3.8 km is exact, and the mi/km conversion is internally consistent so this is not an imperial-unit artefact. Both reveal claims verified on the same source: the inter-island border 'also defines the International Date Line in that area', and the nicknames Tomorrow Island (Big Diomede) and Yesterday Island (Little Diomede). Checked the 'almost a full day apart' phrasing against the article's stated 21-hour offset (20 in summer) - accurate, not exaggerated. Log position 0.29.

Wikipedia 'Landlocked country' confirms 44 UN member states, with 3 landlocked de facto states (Kosovo, South Ossetia, Transnistria) counted separately - so the prompt's 'world's countries' framing lands on 44 and the only rival count (47) requires including unrecognised states, which the prompt does not. Reveal verified: exactly two doubly landlocked, Liechtenstein and Uzbekistan, named on the same page. Adversarial note I checked and dismissed: Uzbekistan's doubly-landlocked status depends on treating the Caspian as a lake, but that is the standard treatment and affects only the reveal, not the 44. Linear position 0.31.

Wikipedia 'La Paz' gives 'roughly 3,650 m', Britannica's long-standing figure is 3,640 m - a 0.3% spread, so the canonical value is solid. Probed the obvious attack, that La Paz spans a huge elevation range (Southern Zone ~3,250 m, upper districts above 4,000 m): the range is real but every source's headline number sits at 3,640-3,650, and the 500-5,000 range is forgiving enough that intra-city variation cannot mis-score a player. Both reveal facts verified: El Alto airport at 4,061 m per the same article ('above 4,000 m' correct), and I checked the boiling point independently - at 3,640 m ambient pressure is ~64% of sea level, giving ~87-88 C, matching 'about 88 degrees'. Linear position 0.70.

Confirmed on two independent pages. Wikipedia 'La Rinconada, Peru': 'At up to 5,100 m above sea level, it is the highest larger permanent settlement in the world', with the town centre near 5,000 m; and 'Extreme points of Earth' independently lists La Rinconada at 5,100 m as the highest permanent human settlement. Reveal checked: 2024 population 29,678 supports 'some 30,000', the gold mine is the town's reason for existing, and I verified the oxygen claim myself - at 5,100 m atmospheric pressure is ~53% of sea level, so 'roughly half the oxygen' is accurate rather than rhetorical. Linear position 0.80, inside the band.

Wikipedia 'Gotthard Base Tunnel': 57.09 km, 'the world's longest railway and deepest traffic tunnel' - candidate 57 exact. Reveal audited fact by fact: 28.2 million tonnes of excavated rock matches 'roughly 28 million tonnes'; construction ran from November 1999 to the 2016 opening, so '17-year dig' is the project duration (bored excavation alone was ~11 years, 1999-2011) - loose but not false. One small imprecision to note for the editor: the article gives maximum overburden as 2,450 m at Piz Vatgira, where the reveal says 'as much as 2,300 m' - the reveal understates rather than overstates, so it cannot mislead a player. Log position 0.45.

Wikipedia 'Danyang-Kunshan Grand Bridge': 164.8 km, and it 'currently holds the Guinness World Record for the longest bridge in the world in any category' - so unlike some other Guinness attributions in this batch, this one actually checks out against the claimed source, and 165 rounds correctly. Reveal verified on the same page: the 9 km open-water section across Yangcheng Lake in Suzhou, and it carries the Beijing-Shanghai High-Speed Railway through Jiangsu, i.e. the Shanghai-Nanjing corridor as described. Fixed structure, no year-drift. Log position 0.66.

I checked the Guinness page the question cites and it contradicts the answer. Guinness's own 'busiest station' record now reads 2,704,703 people per day (2022 average) for Shinjuku - not 3.5 million. Wikipedia's 3.59 million is the 2018 pre-COVID figure. So the two figures a player could reasonably hold differ by ~30%, and the question attributes 3.5M to a source that publishes 2.70M. On top of that the underlying number genuinely moves year to year as ridership recovers, and there is a second scope trap: JR East's own Shinjuku count is ~1.5M/day because it excludes the private railways and subway lines in the complex, so three defensible answers span 1.5M to 3.6M. Fails the source-disagreement, year-drift and mis-cited-source tests at once.

Wikipedia 'Indian Railways' gives 69,181 route km as of 31 March 2024, which puts the FY2022-23 figure at 68,043 km - the candidate's 68,000 for '(2023)' is exact for the year stated, and even against the newest figure it is only 1.7% off, so the year-drift is negligible against a 15,000-500,000 log range. Reveal: employees 1,252,200 at 31 March 2024 confirms 'about 1.2 million'. Caveat for the editor rather than a defect: the same source gives 6.905 billion passengers in 2023-24 = 18.9 million/day, so 'over 20 million passengers a day' is slightly ahead of the year the prompt names (FY2024-25 volumes do reach ~20M/day). Softening it to 'close to 20 million' would remove the only wobble; the scored answer is unaffected. Log position 0.43.

The number is right but the source attribution is wrong, and I only caught it by fetching Guinness directly: the Guinness 'longest fence' record page states 5,531 km, not the 5,614 km claimed here. 5,614 km is the current figure per Wikipedia and Queensland government material, and the two differ by only 1.5% so the answer itself survives - but the source field must change from 'Guinness World Records' to the Queensland/current-survey attribution, or the pair will not withstand a player checking the cited record. Also verified the fence's length is not static: it was previously over 8,000 km, a 32 km extension was completed in 2025 and up to 290 km more is planned, so this needs periodic review. Reveal checked and correct in direction: research shows fewer kangaroos and emus on the dingo side, i.e. numbers boom on the dingo-free side, and drone/satellite imagery has documented the vegetation contrast. Position unchanged at 0.77.

Chased the distance across three pages because the main Tristan article omits it. 'Extreme points of Earth' gives 2,434 km to Saint Helena (the nearest inhabited land), 2,816 km to South Africa and 3,360 km to South America; Simple Wikipedia gives 2,430 km to Saint Helena. Candidate 2,437 km sits inside a 0.3% spread of published values, and the nearest-inhabited-land framing is correct since Saint Helena is nearer than the African mainland. Reveal fully verified: main Tristan article confirms 250 permanent inhabitants (2018) and 221 at the 2026 census, no airstrip and ship-only access, and 'a six-day journey from Cape Town'; Simple Wikipedia lists exactly eight surnames - Glass, Green, Hagan, Lavarello, Patterson, Repetto, Rogers, Swain. Log position 0.72.

verdicts.correctedPrompt: Kyiv's Arsenalna, long the world's deepest metro station, sits how many metres below ground?
verdicts.note: The depth is right but the superlative in the prompt is now false. Wikipedia's Arsenalna article states it is 105.5 m deep and 'the second-deepest station in the world', and I confirmed the reason on the Hongyancun station page: Hongyancun in Chongqing reaches 116 m below street level and 'surpasses the depth of the Kyiv Metro's Arsenalna station, the previous record for deepest metro station', having opened on Line 9 in January 2022. Shipping the prompt as written would state a fact that stopped being true four years ago. Depth 105.5 m and both reveal claims are verified on the same page - the escalator ride 'totaling up to five minutes' and the station's use as a bomb shelter during the 2022 invasion - so only the wording needs changing. Linear position stays 0.55.

Confirmed 7,641 on three separate Wikipedia pages (Philippines, Geography of the Philippines, List of islands of the Philippines), all attributing it to NAMRIA, and I looked specifically for a post-2016 revision and found none - the count has been stable for a decade, so this is not a year-drift risk. Reveal arithmetic checked myself: the count rose from 7,107 to 7,641, i.e. 534 newly identified islands, supporting 'over 500 that nobody had counted before'; and NAMRIA's own position that 'more than 5,000 are yet to be officially named' matches the reveal exactly. One soft spot to flag: on inhabited islands the sources split, with the islands list saying 'only about 2,000 are inhabited' (as the reveal has it) but Geography of the Philippines saying 'approximately 1,000 of its islands are populated'. That is a reveal detail, not the scored answer, but 'roughly a thousand or two' would be safer wording. Log position 0.59.

questions.prompt: Heating a litre of water from 20 °C to boiling takes how many kilojoules?
questions.source: widely documented (specific heat of water, 4.18 kJ/kg·K)
