questions.reveal: Water is unusually stubborn to heat. The same energy would raise a litre of olive oil by about 180 °C, or a kilogram of iron by 740 °C — which is why coastlines have milder weather than inland plains.
questions.reasoningPath: A litre of water is 1 kg. Raising 1 kg of water 1 °C takes about 4 kJ (the calorie, times 1000). Going from 20 °C to 100 °C is an 80-degree climb, so 4 × 80 ≈ 320-340 kJ. Sanity check: a 2 kW kettle boils a litre in roughly 3 minutes, i.e. 2000 W × 170 s ≈ 340 kJ.

questions.prompt: The air filling a 3 m by 4 m room with a 2.5 m ceiling weighs how many kilograms?
questions.reveal: Air weighs roughly 1.2 kg per cubic metre, and the whole atmosphere stacked above a single square metre of that floor weighs about 10 tonnes. You never feel it because the same pressure pushes from every direction at once.
questions.reasoningPath: Room volume is 3 × 4 × 2.5 = 30 m³. Air is roughly a thousand times lighter than water, and water is 1000 kg per cubic metre, so air is about 1 kg per cubic metre. 30 m³ × ~1.2 kg ≈ 36 kg — about the weight of a ten-year-old child.

questions.prompt: A resting adult gives off body heat at about how many watts?
questions.reveal: That is roughly one old filament bulb per person, so thirty people warm a hall about as well as a 3 kW heater — the reason packed rooms get stuffy long before anyone turns the heating up.
questions.reasoningPath: A person eats about 2000 kcal a day and, at rest, all of it eventually leaves as heat. 2000 kcal ≈ 8,400 kJ spread over 86,400 seconds ≈ 0.1 kJ per second, which is 100 joules per second — 100 watts.

questions.prompt: A one-litre jar of honey: how many grams does the honey weigh?
questions.reveal: Honey is roughly four-fifths dissolved sugar and under a fifth water. That same sugar concentration sucks water straight out of any bacterium that lands in it, which is why sealed honey never spoils.
questions.reasoningPath: A litre of water weighs 1000 g. Honey sinks in water and is visibly denser and thicker, but it is not stone — it is mostly dissolved sugar, and sugar syrup tops out near 1.4 times water. So somewhere around 1.3-1.5 kg.

questions.prompt: How many grams of table salt dissolve in 100 mL of room-temperature water?
questions.reveal: Sugar is far more soluble — over 200 g will vanish into the same 100 mL. Salt is also odd in that heating barely helps: boiling water takes only a few grams more than cold water does.
questions.reasoningPath: A teaspoon of salt is about 6 g, and you can keep stirring several teaspoons into a small glass of water before the last grains refuse to go. Half a cup of water taking five or six teaspoons puts the answer in the 30-40 g range, not 5 g and not 200 g.

questions.prompt: How many drops of water add up to one millilitre?
questions.reveal: The 20-drop convention is a pharmacist's agreement, not a law of nature: drop size depends on surface tension, so hospital drip sets are calibrated separately at 10, 15, 20 or 60 drops per millilitre.
questions.reasoningPath: A drop of water sitting on a table is a few millimetres across, so a cube of about 3-4 mm a side — that is roughly 0.05 mL. One millilitre is a cube 10 mm a side, so it should take somewhere in the tens of drops to fill it, not hundreds.

questions.prompt: A home hot-water tank should be kept at what temperature in Celsius?
questions.reveal: 60 °C is the point at which Legionella bacteria die off in the tank — but water that hot burns adult skin in about five seconds, so taps are usually blended back down to around 45 °C before they reach you.
questions.reasoningPath: It has to be too hot to touch comfortably (a hot bath is 40 °C) but there is no point storing it at boiling, since that wastes energy and scalds instantly. Bath-hot plus a safety margin for killing bacteria lands around 55-65 °C.

questions.prompt: Water hits the grounds in a well-set espresso machine at what temperature in Celsius?
questions.reveal: The accepted brewing window is 90.5–96.1 °C. Boiling water would strip out bitter compounds; espresso also runs at about 9 bar of pressure, nine atmospheres, which is what pulls the shot in 25 seconds.
questions.reasoningPath: Coffee is made with water that has just come off the boil, never with lukewarm water and never with water still boiling in the cup. That puts it a handful of degrees under 100 °C.

questions.prompt: How many millilitres of air move in and out with one relaxed breath?
questions.reveal: Even after breathing out fully, about 2.4 litres of air stays behind — the lungs never empty. Total capacity is around 6 litres, so quiet breathing uses less than a tenth of what you have.
questions.reasoningPath: You breathe roughly 12-15 times a minute at rest, and a deep forced breath is a few litres. A quiet breath is obviously a small fraction of that — about the volume of a small glass of water, so a few hundred millilitres rather than litres.

questions.prompt: A 4,500 mAh phone battery at 3.85 volts stores how many watt-hours?
questions.reveal: That is about 62 kilojoules — roughly the food energy in a single teaspoon of sugar. Petrol packs some 50 times more energy per kilogram than a lithium-ion cell, which is why electric flight is so hard.
questions.reasoningPath: Watt-hours are amp-hours times volts. 4,500 mAh is 4.5 Ah, and 4.5 × 3.85 ≈ 17. Cross-check: a phone charger delivering about 5 W refills a flat battery in roughly three hours, so 5 × 3 ≈ 15 Wh.

questions.prompt: Boil away one litre of water: how many litres of steam does it become?
questions.reveal: That expansion is the entire trick of the steam engine — and the reason a few drops of water dropped into hot oil erupt so violently.
questions.reasoningPath: Gases at everyday pressure are about a thousand times less dense than the liquids they came from. A litre of water is 1 kg; as steam at 100 °C that same kilogram spreads across roughly one and a half to two cubic metres, so 1,500-2,000 litres.

questions.prompt: Ethanol, the alcohol in drinks, boils at what temperature in Celsius?
questions.reveal: Distilling cannot get past 95.6% ethanol: at that mixture alcohol and water boil together as one vapour, so the last few percent of water has to be removed by other means entirely.
questions.reasoningPath: Distillation works because alcohol boils before water does, so it must be under 100 °C. It also evaporates fast off skin at room temperature but does not boil in a warm room, so it must be well above 40 °C. Somewhere in the 70s or 80s.

questions.prompt: About how many litres of milk go into one kilogram of hard cheese?
questions.reveal: One wheel of Parmigiano-Reggiano swallows around 550 litres — roughly a day's milk from twenty cows. The leftover whey is 90% of what went in, and in Parma it traditionally goes to feed the pigs.
questions.reasoningPath: Milk is about 3.5% fat and 3.2% protein — call it 10% solids in total, and cheese is essentially those solids with some water still held in. So a kilogram of cheese needs something like ten times its weight in milk, and milk weighs about a kilogram per litre.

questions.prompt: The WHO's recommended minimum indoor temperature for a home, in Celsius?
questions.reveal: Cold homes kill: excess winter deaths run highest not in Scandinavia but in mild-winter countries like Portugal and Ireland, where houses are built for summer and barely insulated.
questions.reasoningPath: A comfortable living room sits around 20-22 °C, and the guideline is a health floor rather than a comfort target — cool enough to want a jumper, warm enough not to harm you. That points a couple of degrees below normal room temperature.

questions.prompt: How many kilocalories of energy are stored in one kilogram of body fat?
questions.reveal: Pure fat carries 9 kcal per gram, but fat tissue is only about 87% lipid — the rest is water and protein. A 15 kg fat reserve still holds over 100,000 kcal, some fifty days of fuel.
questions.reasoningPath: Fat delivers about 9 kcal per gram, so a kilogram of pure fat would be 9,000 kcal. Body fat is tissue, not oil, so knock off the water and connective material and land a bit under that — around 7,000-8,000.

questions.prompt: A pendulum clock that ticks once a second needs a pendulum how many centimetres long?
questions.reveal: In 1791 the French Academy nearly defined the metre as exactly this length before choosing a fraction of the Earth's meridian instead. The two candidate definitions landed within a centimetre of each other.
questions.reasoningPath: Grandfather clocks are tall for a reason: the pendulum in one runs nearly the height of the case. A short pendulum swings much faster than once a second, so this one has to be a substantial fraction of a metre — call it about a metre.

questions.prompt: Burning one litre of petrol puts how many kilograms of CO2 into the air?
questions.source: US EPA and UK DEFRA emission factors
questions.reveal: Most of that mass is air, not fuel: carbon makes up only 27% of a CO2 molecule, so the gas leaving the exhaust weighs about three times what the petrol did.
questions.reasoningPath: A litre of petrol weighs about 0.75 kg and is nearly all carbon and hydrogen. Every carbon atom (mass 12) picks up two oxygens (mass 32) to become CO2 (mass 44), tripling its weight. So expect roughly three times 0.75, a bit over 2 kg.

questions.prompt: The longest straw anyone could ever drink water through, in metres?
questions.reveal: Suction cannot pull; the atmosphere pushes. The same limit stops well pumps lifting water from more than about ten metres down — a puzzle that led Torricelli to explain it in 1643 and invent the barometer.
questions.reasoningPath: Sucking cannot do more than remove the air above the water; the atmosphere then does the lifting. Atmospheric pressure is famously 760 mm of mercury, and mercury is about 13.6 times denser than water, so the same pressure supports 0.76 × 13.6 ≈ 10 metres of water.

questions.prompt: Household food waste worldwide: how many kilograms per person per year?
questions.reveal: That is close to a fifth of all the food that ever reaches consumers, and the per-person figure barely differs between rich and poor countries — what changes is where along the chain the loss happens.
questions.reasoningPath: Think of one household bin: a bag of forgotten salad, some bread, scraps — easily 1-2 kg a week per person. Multiply by 52 and you get 50-100 kg a year, against the roughly 500 kg of food a person actually eats.

questions.prompt: How many grams of tea leaves does a standard tea bag hold?
questions.reveal: Tea loses about three-quarters of its weight during processing, so those few grams began life as roughly 8 grams of fresh green leaf, picked as two leaves and a bud.
questions.reasoningPath: A tea bag is a flat sachet holding a pinch of dried leaf, and dried leaf is very light. A teaspoon of sugar is 4 g and is visibly more material than a tea bag contains, so a couple of grams.

questions.prompt: How many litres of maple sap boil down into one litre of syrup?
questions.reveal: Sap is only about 2% sugar and finished syrup is 66%, so nearly everything boiled off is water vapour. A single tap on a single maple yields about that much sap over an entire season.
questions.reasoningPath: Sap tastes barely sweet — a couple of percent sugar at most — while syrup is roughly two-thirds sugar. Concentrating from 2% to 66% means removing about 97% of the water, a reduction of something like 30 or 40 to one.

questions.prompt: Humanitarian standards set a minimum of how many litres of water per person per day?
questions.reveal: Only 2.5–3 litres of that is drinking and cooking; the rest is washing and sanitation. Households in western Europe typically get through about ten times the figure per person every day.
questions.reasoningPath: Drinking accounts for 2-3 litres. Add a bucket wash, cooking and cleaning and you need a few buckets, not a bathtub — a shower alone would blow the budget at 50 litres. So low tens of litres.

questions.prompt: A traditional incandescent light bulb is rated to last how many hours?
questions.reveal: The 1,000-hour figure was a business decision, not a technical limit: the Phoebus cartel of bulb makers agreed it in 1924 and fined any member whose lamps lasted longer.
questions.reasoningPath: An old bulb in a regularly used room burned out roughly once a year. At about three hours of use per evening, a year is around 1,000 hours.

questions.prompt: EU rules cap a new vacuum cleaner's motor at how many watts?
questions.reveal: Suction depends on airflow design rather than raw wattage: testing found the capped machines cleaned as well as the 2,000-watt models they replaced, on under half the electricity.
questions.reasoningPath: A vacuum is one of the hungrier household appliances but nowhere near a kettle or oven, which run at 2-3 kW. A cap has to bite without crippling the machine, so it sits below the old typical 1,600-2,000 W and above a toaster's few hundred.

questions.prompt: How many sheets of A4 paper does it take to cover one sheet of A0?
questions.reveal: A0 is defined as exactly one square metre, and every A size keeps identical proportions when halved — the √2 ratio Lichtenberg described in a letter in 1786, standardised in Germany in 1922.
questions.reasoningPath: Each step down the A series halves the sheet: A0 to A1 to A2 to A3 to A4 is four halvings. Two to the power of four is 16.

verdicts.note: Recomputed from scratch: 1 kg x 4.18 kJ/kg.K x 80 K = 334.4 kJ, so 335 is right. Attacked the reveal's two comparisons and both survive: olive oil (c approx 2.0 kJ/kg.K, density 0.91 kg/L) gives 334.4/(0.91x2.0) = 184 C, matching 'about 180'; iron (c = 0.449 kJ/kg.K) gives 334.4/0.449 = 745 C, matching 740. The maritime-climate explanation follows correctly from water's high specific heat. Track position 0.61. No disqualifying issue found.

3 x 4 x 2.5 = 30 m3; at the standard 1.204 kg/m3 for dry air at 20 C that is 36.1 kg, so 36 is correct. Checked the reveal's second claim independently: 101325 Pa / 9.81 m/s2 = 10330 kg per square metre, i.e. about 10 tonnes, confirmed. Fully metric, no brand or country dependence. Position 0.63.

Tried to disprove via basal metabolic rate and nearly did: Wikipedia's BMR page gives a mean of 1500 kcal/day = 73 W (range 1027-2499 kcal/day = 50-121 W), which is below 100. But the question says 'resting', not 'basal', and the thermal-comfort literature settles it: 1 met is defined as the output of an average person seated at rest, 58.2 W/m2, which over a 1.8 m2 body surface is 105 W. So 100 W is the correct, sourced figure. Reveal arithmetic checks: 30 x 100 W = 3 kW. Position 0.73; the BMR-vs-resting gap is negligible on a 5-300 log track.

Verified density directly against Wikipedia's Honey article: 'The density of honey typically ranges between 1.38 and 1.45 kg/L at 20 C', so a litre is 1380-1450 g and 1420 sits at the midpoint. Spread is about 5%, well inside the 10% bar. Reveal composition also confirmed there: roughly 82 g of sugars per 100 g and 15.5-18% water, matching 'four-fifths sugar, under a fifth water'; the osmotic/never-spoils mechanism is standard. One suggestion, not a defect: lo = 500 g/L is below water's own 1000 g/L and is physically implausible for any liquid food, so the bottom third of the track is dead. lo = 900 would make it a better guess (position would be 0.74 instead of 0.84).

Checked against Wikipedia's Sodium chloride data: solubility 360 g/L at 25 C = 36 g per 100 mL, matching the answer exactly. Attacked both reveal claims: sucrose solubility at 20 C is about 200 g/100 mL, so 'over 200 g' holds; and NaCl runs 35.7 g/100 mL at 0 C to 39.1 g at 100 C, so 'boiling water takes only a few grams more' is correct and is genuinely the interesting part. Position 0.72.

Verified line by line against Wikipedia's Drop (unit) article: modern pharmacy rounds a drop to exactly 0.05 mL, i.e. 20 drops per mL, and 'IV drips deliver 10, 15, 20, or 60 drops per ml' with micro-drip sets at 60 - the reveal's list is exactly right, including the surface-tension dependence. I considered dropping this as pure convention/memorisation, but the reveal itself discloses that it is a convention, and 0.05 mL is also the real physical size of a water drop from a dropper, so a player can reason to it rather than recall it. Position 0.33.

Checked the Legionella evidence rather than the WHO citation: at 60 C, 90% of Legionella die in 2 minutes (vs 80-124 minutes at 50 C), and CDC guidance is to hold potable hot water between 49 and 60 C - so 60 C is the standard storage figure and the reveal's mechanism is right. Scald data independently support 'about five seconds' for an adult third-degree burn at 60 C, and blending down to mid-40s C at the tap matches thermostatic-mixing-valve practice. Metric, no brand dependence. Position 0.67.

The claimed source does not say what the question says it says. The SCA figure quoted in the reveal (90.5-96.1 C) is 195-205 F, which is the SCA Golden Cup standard for BREWED/drip coffee, not an espresso specification. The actual espresso authority contradicts it: the Istituto Nazionale Espresso Italiano specifies water at 88 +/- 2 C at the group exit (with 67 +/- 3 C in the cup), i.e. 86-90 C, which puts the stated answer of 93 C outside the Italian standard entirely. So the reveal's 'the accepted brewing window is 90.5-96.1 C' is a misattribution, and the underlying number is measurement-point dependent (boiler vs group exit vs cup), meaning there is no single verifiable answer. The 9 bar and 25 s figures in the reveal are correct (INEI: 9 +/- 1 bar, 25 +/- 5 s), so the salvage path is to re-aim the prompt at SCA drip-brew temperature and rewrite the reveal without the espresso claims - but as written it should not ship.

The answer is solid - Wikipedia's Lung volumes table gives tidal volume 500 mL - but the REVEAL contains a hard numerical error. It says 'even after breathing out fully, about 2.4 litres of air stays behind'. 2.4 L is functional residual capacity, the volume left after a NORMAL relaxed exhale. After breathing out fully (maximal exhalation) the residual volume is only 1100-1200 mL. Fix the reveal to something like: 'Even after a normal breath out, about 2.4 litres is still sitting in your lungs, and forcing everything out still leaves 1.2 litres - the lungs never empty.' The third sentence is fine: total capacity about 6 L, and 500/6000 = 8%, so 'less than a tenth' checks out. Prompt, answer 500 mL and the 20-5000 log range (position 0.58) all stay as they are.
verdicts.correctedReveal: Roughly a third of each relaxed breath never reaches the alveoli — it stays in the windpipe and bronchi, where no gas exchange happens. The lungs never fully empty either: even after the hardest exhale, over a litre of air stays behind.

verdicts.note: Arithmetic verified: 4.5 Ah x 3.85 V = 17.325 Wh, rounds to 17. Reveal checked independently: 17.325 Wh x 3600 = 62.4 kJ, correct; a teaspoon of sugar is about 4 g x 4 kcal/g = 16 kcal = 67 kJ, so 'roughly' holds; petrol at about 46 MJ/kg against lithium-ion at 0.7-0.95 MJ/kg (200-265 Wh/kg) gives a 48-64x ratio, so 'some 50 times' is fair. The question hands the player both inputs, so it is a multiplication rather than a recall, which is legitimate for an estimation track. Position 0.62.

Checked against steam-table values rather than the claimed source: saturated steam at 100 C and 1 atm has a specific volume of 1.672 m3/kg, so 1 kg (1 L) of water becomes 1672 L, confirming 1700. The commonly repeated rival figure of '1600 times' is only 4% away, well inside tolerance and invisible on a 50-20000 log track. Both reveal claims are sound physics: the expansion is what drives a steam engine, and it is the correct mechanism for water flashing to steam in hot oil. Position 0.59.

Verified against Wikipedia's Ethanol article: boiling point 78.23 +/- 0.09 C, so 78 is right. The reveal is the strongest part and it checks out precisely: the ethanol-water azeotrope is 95.6% ethanol by mass (89.4 mol%, 97% ABV) boiling at 78.2 C, and it genuinely cannot be broken by ordinary distillation - entrainers or molecular sieves are required. Position 0.64.

The reveal contradicts the answer. I verified the reveal against Wikipedia's Parmigiano Reggiano page: 1100 L of milk per vat producing two cheeses, i.e. 550 L per wheel, with a finished wheel of 38 kg - that works out to about 14 L of milk per kg, not the 10 L given as the answer. A player who reads the reveal and does the division gets a different number from the one they were scored against, which is exactly the complaint-generating case. The underlying problem is that 'hard cheese' is too loose: cheddar yields about 10% (10 L/kg) while Parmigiano yields about 7% (14 L/kg), a 40% spread. Cleanest fix is to name the cheese so the answer and the reveal agree - correctedPrompt and correctedAnswer 14 below, which lands at position 0.42 on the existing 2-200 log range. The reveal's other claims survive: whey is about 90% of the input and does traditionally feed the Parma prosciutto pigs, and 550 L is roughly a day from twenty modern dairy cows. Note for the parent: the everyday set already has 'A whole wheel of Parmigiano-Reggiano weighs about how many kilograms? 40 kg', so this fix creates a second Parmigiano item - adjacent, not duplicate, but worth knowing. Alternative fix is to say 'cheddar' and keep 10, but then the reveal has to be rewritten entirely.
verdicts.correctedPrompt: About how many litres of milk go into one kilogram of Parmigiano-Reggiano?

verdicts.note: Confirmed the exact wording: WHO recommends 18 C as a 'safe and well-balanced indoor temperature to protect the health of general populations during cold seasons', with a higher minimum for children, the elderly and people with cardiorespiratory disease. The one competing figure I found is the older 1987 WHO guidance (18-24 C comfortable, 20 C minimum for vulnerable groups), but that does not touch the general-population answer of 18. I could NOT independently fetch a source for the reveal's Portugal/Ireland claim (the WHO and excess-winter-death pages 403'd or 404'd); it matches the well-established Healy 2003 finding that excess winter mortality is highest in mild-winter, poorly-insulated southern and western European countries and lowest in Scandinavia, so I am letting it through, but it is the one unsourced sentence in this item. Position 0.25.

7700 kcal/kg is the standard figure (the 3500 kcal/lb rule, which converts to 7716 kcal/kg) and the reveal's derivation is internally consistent: 0.87 x 9000 = 7830. I tried hard to break it and found one real caveat: Wikipedia's Adipose tissue page says human fat tissue is 61-94% lipid, not a uniform 87% - the 87% figure traces to Wishnofsky (1958), a single origin. Taken literally that range implies 5500-8500 kcal/kg. I am still keeping it because (a) 7700 is the near-universal published value for the energy content of a kg of adipose tissue, (b) on a 500-50000 log track even 9000 (pure fat) sits essentially on top of 7700, and (c) the reveal makes an energy-storage claim, not the discredited linear weight-loss prediction. Reveal arithmetic checks: 15 kg x 7700 = 115,500 kcal, 'over 100,000', and about 52 days at 2200 kcal/day. Position 0.59.

Derived it myself first: L = gT2/4pi2 with T = 2 s gives 0.994 m, and Wikipedia's Seconds pendulum article confirms 993.6 mm, 'less than a centimetre short of one metre everywhere on Earth' - which independently confirms the reveal's closing line about the two candidate definitions landing within a centimetre. History also checks: Talleyrand proposed the seconds-pendulum metre in 1790, the Academy of Sciences instead chose one ten-millionth of the pole-to-equator distance in 1791. The one thing I checked carefully was the 'ticks once a second' phrasing, since a seconds pendulum has a two-second period and ticks at each extreme - the phrasing is correct as written. Position 0.74.

Verified the number independently of the claimed source: burning ethanol-free petrol produces 2.353 kg CO2 per litre, which matches EPA's 8.887 kg/US gallon (= 2.348 kg/L) and DEFRA's 2.31. Reveal checked in both halves: carbon is 12/44 = 27% of a CO2 molecule, and at a petrol density of 0.755 kg/L the exhaust CO2 is 2.353/0.755 = 3.1x the fuel mass, so 'about three times' is right. One nuance I checked and dismissed: E10 pump fuel emits 2.119 kg/L of FOSSIL CO2, but the question asks about burning a litre of petrol, for which 2.3 is correct. Position 0.40.

Computed the limit rather than trusting it: 101325 Pa / (998 kg/m3 x 9.81 m/s2) = 10.35 m, confirming 10.3. Torricelli's 1643 barometer and the well-pump puzzle that prompted it are correctly told. The one attack that has any force is that the phrasing 'anyone could ever' invites a practical reading - real human suction can only manage about a metre or so, and the physics limit needs a perfect vacuum - but 'could ever' plus the log range 3-150 clearly signals the theoretical ceiling, and that is the version every source discusses. Position 0.32.

This is the one that will age into a complaint. The figure is not stable: the 2021 Food Waste Index Report put household waste at 74 kg per capita, the 2024 edition at 79 kg - a revision driven as much by methodology as by behaviour, and UNEP itself flags low or medium data confidence for most countries, since only a minority have measured household estimates and the rest are modelled. That is a single modelled origin that is restated with a different number each edition, which is squarely inside the 'answer changes' and 'single origin' drop criteria for a fixed answer bank. Compounding it: I could not verify 79 kg from any accessible primary source in this session - unep.org returned 403 on three separate URLs and no encyclopedia page carries the household-only per-capita split (they carry only the 121 kg all-sectors figure from the 2021 edition). The reveal's other claims (about a fifth of consumer-available food; little difference between income groups) are consistent with the 2024 report, but I cannot stand behind the headline number, and neither should the game.

Brand- and country-dependent, with a spread far over the 10% bar. UK supermarket tea bags run about 2.9-3.1 g (the standard 240-bag boxes from Yorkshire and Tetley weigh 750 g, i.e. 3.1 g per bag; PG Tips 240 at 696 g is 2.9 g), while US and international bags run about 2.0-2.5 g (Lipton 100 bags at 200 g is 2.0 g; Twinings 80 at 200 g is 2.5 g). That is a 55% spread between two ordinary supermarkets, and a British player answering 3 would be marked down against 2. I also traced where the '2 g' actually comes from: ISO 3103, which I verified specifies '2 grams of tea per 100 ml boiling water' - that is a BREWING RATIO for a standardised tasting pot, not the mass of tea in a commercial bag, so the answer is sourced to a document that is not about the thing being asked. The reveal's processing claim (fresh leaf loses roughly three-quarters of its weight, about 4-5 kg green leaf per kg of made tea) is correct and could be reused elsewhere.

Checked every number in the item against Wikipedia's Maple syrup article and all four hold: 'Maple syrup is made by boiling between 20 and 50 volumes of sap', with 40:1 the classic figure for the usual sugar content; sap is 2-5% sugar (2% for sugar maple, and 40:1 is what the rule of 86 gives at 2%); Canadian syrup must be at least 66% sugar; and 'the average maple tree will produce 35 to 50 litres of sap per season', confirming the reveal's 'about that much from a single tap over a season'. The 20-50 range is wide, but 40 is the consensus rule of thumb and the 3-150 log track absorbs it. Position 0.66.

Answer and prompt are right - Sphere's WASH standard is at least 15 litres per person per day - but the REVEAL misdescribes Sphere's own breakdown. Sphere lists three separate rows: water intake (drinking and food) 2.5-3 L/day, basic cooking needs 3-6 L/day, and basic hygiene practices 2-6 L/day. The reveal says 'Only 2.5-3 litres of that is drinking and cooking; the rest is washing and sanitation', which folds cooking into the 2.5-3 L row and then assigns the remaining 12 L entirely to washing - both wrong. Fix the reveal to something like: 'Only 2.5-3 litres of that is drinking water; another 3-6 goes to cooking and the rest to washing and sanitation.' The closing comparison is fine - western European household use is around 150 L per person per day, about ten times the figure. I could not reach spherestandards.org (403), so this rests on the well-known Sphere 2018 table rather than a fetched primary source. Keep answer 15 and the 5-400 log range, position 0.25.
verdicts.correctedReveal: Drinking accounts for only about 3 litres of it — cooking and washing take the rest. Sphere pairs the volume with reach, too: no household over 500 metres from a water point, and under 30 minutes queuing.

verdicts.note: Verified the reveal, which is the load-bearing part: the Phoebus cartel standardised bulb life at 1000 hours, down from the previous 2500, it tested members' bulbs and fined manufacturers whose lamps lasted longer, and a 1929 table set the Swiss-franc penalties by how many hours the lamp exceeded the limit. The cartel's 1924 founding date is standard. The 1000-hour rating survived as the industry norm long after the cartel, so the answer is not merely a historical artefact. Position 0.37 on a 100-50000 log track that sensibly spans LED lifetimes at the top end.

Went to the primary source rather than trusting the citation - the EUR-Lex text of Regulation 666/2013 - and it states rated input power 'shall be less than 1600 W' from 1 September 2014 and 'less than 900W' from 1 September 2017. So the answer and the cited regulation number are both correct. I checked the obvious attack, that the vacuum rules were struck down after Dyson's litigation: the EU General Court annulled the energy LABELLING regulation (665/2013) in 2018, not the ecodesign regulation 666/2013, so the 900 W cap stands. Reveal is fair - pre-2014 machines were routinely 2000 W+, and 900/2000 is 'under half the electricity'. Position 0.65.

Confirmed against ISO 216: A0 is 841 x 1189 mm = 0.999949 m2, defined as one square metre, and four halvings (A0-A1-A2-A3-A4) give 2^4 = 16 A4 sheets. Lichtenberg's 1786 letter to Beckmann describing the root-2 ratio is confirmed. One small discrepancy worth knowing: the ISO 216 article dates the German DIN 476 standard to 1921, while the reveal says 1922 - both dates circulate (Porstmann's proposal 1921, DIN 476 issued 1922), so it is not an error but it is the softest fact in the item. Also flagging, not as a duplicate: the everyday set already contains 'One sheet of standard 80 gsm A4 printer paper weighs how many grams?', so this is a second A4-paper item - different quantity, but the parent may want them spaced apart in the rotation. Position 0.60.

questions.prompt: One relaxed breath moves how many millilitres of air in and out of an adult's lungs?
questions.reveal: Even after the hardest exhale about 1.2 litres stays behind, so every fresh breath mixes with stale air — the lungs never actually empty.
questions.reasoningPath: A big deliberate lungful is a couple of litres, and a resting breath is obviously a small fraction of that — you barely feel it. A quarter of a litre to half a litre is the natural landing zone; 500 mL is the textbook figure.

questions.prompt: Roughly how many alveoli, the tiny air sacs, fill a pair of adult human lungs?
questions.source: Ochs et al., 2004, Am. J. Respir. Crit. Care Med.
questions.reveal: Each sac is about 0.2 mm wide, and the barrier oxygen crosses to reach the blood is under a thousandth of a millimetre thick — thinner than the wall of a soap bubble.
questions.reasoningPath: Lungs hold roughly 5 litres = 5,000 cm3. A sac 0.2 mm across has a volume near 4 millionths of a cm3. Dividing gives about a billion, and since tissue and airways take up much of the space, the true count lands a couple of times lower — hundreds of millions.

questions.prompt: At rest, an adult blinks about how many times per minute?
questions.source: clinical studies of spontaneous blink rate
questions.reveal: Reading or staring at a screen cuts the rate to roughly a quarter of that, which is the real cause of dry, gritty eyes — and the brain suppresses vision during each blink so you never notice the darkness.
questions.reasoningPath: Count your own for ten seconds and you get two or three. That is one every three or four seconds, so somewhere between 15 and 20 a minute — far more often than tear film alone would need.

questions.prompt: How many minutes does one complete cycle of human sleep last?
questions.reveal: The cycles are not identical: deep sleep dominates the early ones and REM the late ones, which is why the dream you remember is almost always from just before you woke.
questions.reasoningPath: A night is about eight hours and people are told they pass through four or five cycles. 480 minutes divided by five gives roughly 90 minutes per cycle.

questions.prompt: Best-documented case of staying awake: how many hours did a 17-year-old manage in 1964?
questions.reveal: Guinness later stopped ratifying sleep-deprivation attempts on safety grounds. He was hallucinating and paranoid by day four, yet recovered after a single 14-hour sleep.
questions.reasoningPath: One night awake is easy, two is grim, and the famous record is talked about in days rather than hours. Eleven days is the number people half-remember, and 11 x 24 is 264.

questions.prompt: Sealed away from clocks and daylight, the human body clock runs longer than 24 hours — by how many minutes?
questions.reveal: That small overshoot is why flying west feels easier than flying east. Blind people with no light signal to reset the clock can drift right out of phase with the day.
questions.reasoningPath: If the internal day were off by an hour or more, people in caves would invert within a fortnight and jet lag would be far worse than it is. The drift must be small — minutes, not hours — but big enough to matter over weeks.

questions.prompt: How many hours does the body take to clear half the caffeine from a cup of coffee?
questions.reveal: A coffee at 16:00 still leaves a quarter of its caffeine circulating at midnight. Smoking roughly halves the half-life; pregnancy can triple it.
questions.reasoningPath: Coffee kicks in within half an hour and is clearly wearing off after a few hours, yet an evening cup can still wreck sleep hours later. A half-life of minutes is far too short and a day far too long: a handful of hours fits both observations.

questions.prompt: A healthy adult takes about how many minutes to fall asleep after lights out?
questions.reveal: Dropping off in under five minutes is a sign of serious sleep debt — the clinical test for narcolepsy flags an average nap latency of eight minutes or less.
questions.reasoningPath: Instant sleep is unusual and an hour of lying awake counts as insomnia. Normal is the quiet stretch in between where you lose track of your own thoughts — ten to twenty minutes.

questions.prompt: An adult's comfortable walking pace, in km/h?
questions.reveal: That is 1.4 metres per second. Studies comparing cities find pedestrians in larger, wealthier ones walk measurably faster than the same people would elsewhere.
questions.reasoningPath: A kilometre on foot takes about twelve minutes, so five kilometres take an hour. Cross-check: a fit runner does 10-12 km/h, and walking is roughly half a jog.

questions.prompt: Above roughly what speed, in km/h, does running actually cost less energy than walking?
questions.source: biomechanics research on preferred transition speed
questions.reveal: Race walkers cheat that limit by locking the knee straight and swinging the hips, holding over 14 km/h for 20 km without ever leaving the ground.
questions.reasoningPath: Strolling is 5 km/h and a slow jog is about 8. The switch happens where hurrying on foot starts to feel silly — a bit faster than a brisk walk, well below jogging pace.

questions.prompt: Typical human reaction time to a visual signal, in milliseconds?
questions.reveal: Sound beats sight: reacting to a beep takes about 170 ms, because a sound reaches the brain through fewer processing steps than an image does.
questions.reasoningPath: A dropped ruler falls about 30 cm before you catch it, which takes a quarter of a second. Nerve signals travel the arm in a few milliseconds, so nearly all of the delay is the brain deciding.

questions.prompt: A sprint start counts as a false start if the runner reacts faster than how many milliseconds?
questions.reveal: The threshold is a rule of thumb, not a measurement. Laboratory studies have found sprinters who genuinely respond faster than it, so an honest start can still be disqualified.
questions.reasoningPath: Ordinary reaction is around 250 ms, and a primed sprinter waiting for one known sound is much quicker. The rule has to sit below any believable human response — a round tenth of a second.

questions.prompt: How many milliseconds does an image need to be shown for the brain to identify what it is?
questions.reveal: Cinema runs at 24 frames a second, 42 ms each, so the eye is comfortably faster than film. What takes longer is deciding what to do about what you saw.
questions.reasoningPath: Film at 24 frames a second looks continuous, so single frames of 42 ms are already below conscious flicker yet clearly recognisable. Recognition must therefore work at or under one frame — a few to a few tens of milliseconds.

questions.prompt: How many centimetres does scalp hair grow in a year?
questions.reveal: Each follicle grows for a few years, then rests and sheds, which sets a natural maximum length — for most people somewhere around the waist.
questions.reasoningPath: A haircut every couple of months takes off two or three centimetres, so roughly a centimetre or so a month. Twelve months gives something in the mid-teens of centimetres.

questions.prompt: How many millimetres does a fingernail grow in a year?
questions.reveal: Toenails crawl at less than half that rate. Nails also grow faster on your dominant hand, faster in summer than winter, and faster on longer fingers.
questions.reasoningPath: A nail needs clipping every week or two and you take off a couple of millimetres. That is roughly 3-4 mm a month, so about 40 mm a year — which matches the half-year it takes a bruised nail to grow out from base to tip.

questions.prompt: Longest documented head of human hair (Guinness): how many metres?
questions.reveal: Xie Qiuping had been growing it since 1973, from the age of 13 — hair reaches that length only when a follicle's growth phase runs for decades rather than a few years.
questions.reasoningPath: Hair grows about 15 cm a year, so 30 years of never cutting gives around 4.5 m if nothing sheds. The record must sit near that ceiling: several metres, not tens.

questions.prompt: A resting adult gives off body heat at roughly how many watts?
questions.reveal: Building engineers budget about that much per seated person, which is why a packed lecture hall needs cooling in midwinter.
questions.reasoningPath: Eating 2,000 kcal a day means burning about 8.4 million joules over 86,400 seconds. That works out to just under 100 joules per second — a person idles at about the power of an old filament bulb.

questions.prompt: The brain is 2% of body weight but burns what percentage of the body's energy at rest?
questions.reveal: In a newborn the brain's share is nearer 60%, and human brain metabolism peaks around age five — one leading theory for why children grow so slowly.
questions.reasoningPath: Brain tissue is famously the most energy-hungry in the body, so its share must far exceed its 2% of mass. Thinking hard does not visibly burn calories, so it cannot be most of the budget either — a fifth is the classic answer, ten times its weight share.

questions.prompt: How many trillion bacterial cells live in and on the average human body?
questions.reveal: That is roughly one bacterium per human cell. The famous 'ten microbes for every cell of you' came from a 1972 back-of-the-envelope estimate that went unchallenged for forty years.
questions.reasoningPath: Most of them live in the colon, which holds about a litre of contents at roughly 100 billion bacteria per millilitre. A thousand millilitres times 100 billion is 100 trillion as an upper bound, and the careful modern count comes in a few times below that.

questions.prompt: How many millilitres of blood does an adult heart push out with each resting beat?
questions.reveal: Hard exercise more than doubles that volume while the rate triples, lifting total output from about 5 litres a minute to over 20.
questions.reasoningPath: The whole body holds about 5 litres of blood and circulates it roughly once a minute at about 70 beats. Five litres shared across 70 beats is a bit under 100 mL per beat.

questions.prompt: How many centimetres does a baby grow in its first year of life?
questions.reveal: It is the fastest growth of an entire life, and never matched again — the same twelve months also roughly triple a baby's birth weight.
questions.reasoningPath: Newborns are about 50 cm long and a one-year-old is around 75 cm — knee-height on an adult. The difference is about half the birth length again.

questions.prompt: Average adult silent reading speed for ordinary prose, in words per minute?
questions.reveal: Reading aloud drops to about 180 words a minute, and comprehension collapses beyond roughly 500 — the eye can only fixate so fast, whatever a speed-reading course promises.
questions.reasoningPath: A paperback page holds roughly 300 words and takes a bit over a minute to read. That puts a comfortable pace in the low hundreds of words per minute, a little faster than speech at about 150.

questions.prompt: A normal conversation one metre away measures roughly how many decibels?
questions.reveal: Decibels are logarithmic, so a 70 dB vacuum cleaner carries ten times the sound energy of that conversation. Damage starts around 85 dB with long exposure.
questions.reasoningPath: A whisper sits near 30 dB and a rock concert near 110. Conversation is unremarkable, comfortably below traffic noise at 80 — so a bit above the middle of the quiet end.

questions.prompt: The highest pitch a healthy young adult can hear, in kilohertz?
questions.reveal: The ceiling falls with age: most 50-year-olds top out near 12 kHz, which is why some alarms and ringtones are piercing to teenagers and silent to their teachers.
questions.reasoningPath: Audio equipment and music files are built to reproduce everything humans can hear, and they stop at about 20 kHz. Dog whistles start just above that, which is what makes them inaudible.

questions.prompt: How many seconds does an average yawn last?
questions.reveal: Yawns are contagious across species — dogs yawn back at their owners — and fetuses yawn in the womb, long before there is anyone to copy.
questions.reasoningPath: A yawn is clearly longer than a breath or a sneeze but you could not hold one for a quarter of a minute. Counting through one puts it in the region of five or six seconds.

verdicts.note: Fetched Wikipedia Tidal volume: 'approximately 500 ml per inspiration at rest or 7 ml/kg of body mass' - matches exactly. Reveal's residual-volume claim independently checked against Wikipedia Lung volumes table: RV = 1.2 L (male) / 1.1 L (female), so 'about 1.2 litres stays behind' is correct and the reveal adds a genuinely non-obvious fact rather than restating the answer. Track position 0.642 (log 20-3000). No duplicate in verified.json - the existing body questions are bones, chromosomes, cardiac output, red-cell lifespan, neurons, nerve speed; nothing on respiration. Tried to disprove via the per-kg route (7 mL/kg x 70 kg = 490 mL) and it converges on the same number.

Did not take the claimed source on trust: PubMed was cookie-blocked, so I verified via Wikipedia Pulmonary alveolus, which states 'approximately 480 million alveoli' and cites Ochs 2004 explicitly - the claimed citation is real and the number matches. Same page gives alveolus diameter 200-500 um, so the reveal's 'about 0.2 mm wide' is the low end of the true range but defensible, and blood-air barrier 0.2-0.6 um, i.e. under 0.001 mm, so 'under a thousandth of a millimetre' checks out. Caveat for the editor: the 'thinner than the wall of a soap bubble' simile is not sourced anywhere I could find and soap-film thickness varies from ~10 nm to several um, so that clause is rhetorical, not factual - I would cut it, but it does not affect the scored answer. Position 0.670.

Wikipedia Blinking confirms 'averaging around 17 blinks per minute in a laboratory setting' - matches the answer exactly. Reveal checked separately: same source says the rate 'decreases to about 4 to 5 times per minute' when reading, and 4.5/17 = 0.26, so 'roughly a quarter' is arithmetically right, and it names reduced blinking as 'the major reason that eyes dry out' when reading. Blink-related visual suppression is separately well established in the perception literature. Position 0.349 (linear 2-45). No overlap with verified.json.

Wikipedia Sleep cycle confirms ~90 minutes for adults (figure popularized by Kleitman, 1963) and lists the competing published ranges 70-110, 80-120 and 90-110 min - every one of those brackets 90, so this is individual variation rather than sources disagreeing about a central value. Reveal verified on the same page: 'REM takes up more of the cycle as the night goes on', with deep non-REM concentrated early, so the claim that a remembered dream comes from just before waking follows. Position 0.400 (linear 30-180) - the wide range absorbs the 70-120 min spread. No duplicate.

Checked every factual claim against Wikipedia's Randy Gardner article rather than the 'widely documented' hand-wave. Confirmed: 264.4 hours (11 days 25 min), Dec 1963 - Jan 1964, age 17. Reveal confirmed too: he slept 14 hours 46 minutes afterwards ('a single 14-hour sleep' is right), and Guinness World Records did stop accepting sleep-deprivation attempts, in 1997, for safety reasons. Paranoia and hallucinations are documented by Lt Cmdr John J. Ross, though the source I reached does not pin the onset to day four specifically - that clause is the weakest part of the reveal but is the standard account. Position 0.705 (log 24-720). Note the record is 'best documented', not the longest ever claimed, and the prompt says so - good.

Verified the claimed Czeisler 1999 figure independently: Wikipedia Circadian rhythm states 'A more stringent study conducted in 1999 by Harvard University estimated the natural human rhythm to be closer to 24 hours and 11 minutes' - 24.18 h, matching the answer of 11 minutes. The west-vs-east jet lag asymmetry following from a period longer than 24 h is the standard chronobiology explanation, and free-running drift in totally blind people is the recognised basis of non-24-hour sleep-wake disorder. Position 0.183 (linear 0-60) - low but comfortably inside the band. No duplicate in verified.json.

Wikipedia Caffeine: 'In healthy adults, caffeine's half-life is between 3 and 7 hours' - 5 h is the exact midpoint and matches the FDA's commonly quoted 4-6 h. I considered dropping this under the >10% disagreement rule, but the spread is inter-individual biological variation around an agreed central figure, not sources contradicting each other, and on a log 0.5-24 track a guess anywhere in 3-7 h scores within ~7 track-percent, so no player can be unfairly punished. Both reveal claims verified on the same page: smoking cuts the half-life by 30-50% ('roughly halves' is at the aggressive end but fair) and pregnancy can extend it to ~15 h versus 2.5-4.5 h non-pregnant, i.e. triple. Not a duplicate of the existing 'mg of caffeine in a cup of coffee' question - different quantity, not derivable from it. Position 0.595.

Wikipedia Sleep onset latency confirms 15-20 min is 'indicative of little or no sleep debt', so 15 min is the low-normal end of the healthy figure and is the value sleep-medicine texts give. Reveal checked: same source states '0 to 5 minutes means severe sleep deprivation', confirming the under-five-minutes claim. The 8-minute MSLT threshold is not on that page, but it is the actual ICSD-3 narcolepsy criterion (mean sleep latency <=8 min plus >=2 sleep-onset REM periods), so the reveal is right. Position 0.237 (linear 1-60). No duplicate.

Wikipedia Preferred walking speed gives the human range as 1.10-1.65 m/s and singles out ~1.4 m/s (5.0 km/h) as the commonly recommended pace - the answer and the reveal's '1.4 metres per second' both check out and are consistent with each other. The pace-of-life claim is real and attributable: Levine and Norenzayan (1999) measured pedestrian speed in 31 countries and found it correlates with economic prosperity, and the same page notes denser urban settings produce faster walking. Metric-native, no brand or US dependency. Position 0.589 (log 0.5-25). No duplicate.

This is the one where the prompt and its own claimed source contradict each other. The prompt asks where running 'actually cost less energy than walking' - that is the energetically optimal transition speed (EOTS) - but the claimed source says 'preferred transition speed' (PTS), and 7 km/h (1.94 m/s) is the PTS value. PubMed's own listing of the transition-speed literature confirms the two are distinct and that PTS is consistently LOWER than EOTS: humans switch to running before it becomes metabolically cheaper (studies comparing PTS and EOTS in adolescents, and in runners vs nonrunners, exist precisely because they diverge). EOTS is typically ~2.2-2.3 m/s, i.e. ~8 km/h, so 7 km/h is the wrong answer to the question as written. Cheapest repair is to make the prompt ask what the answer actually measures; answer stays 7 km/h. Reveal survives: race-walking rules verified on Wikipedia (supporting leg must straighten and stay straight until the body passes over it; back toe cannot leave the ground before the front heel lands), and the men's 20 km walk record pace is ~15.7 km/h, so 'over 14 km/h for 20 km' holds - though strictly, judges only enforce contact by unaided eye and film shows millisecond flight phases, so 'without ever leaving the ground' is the rule rather than the physics. Position with 7 on log 3-40 is 0.327, unchanged.
verdicts.correctedPrompt: At roughly what speed, in km/h, do people naturally switch from walking to running?

verdicts.note: Tried to source the 250 ms figure and it does not survive. Wikipedia Mental chronometry, drawing on the standard simple-reaction-time literature, gives 'about 160 milliseconds to detect an auditory stimulus and approximately 190 milliseconds to detect visual stimulus' for college-age adults, and gives afferent conduction times of 20-40 ms visual vs 8-10 ms auditory - which is the real mechanism behind the reveal. The 250 ms figure traces to popular click-test sources (Human Benchmark medians ~270 ms) that bundle in mouse and motor lag, not the neural reaction time the prompt asks about. So the lab literature says ~190, the popular number says ~250: a >30% gap that the answer should not sit at the top of. Setting 200 ms keeps the sight-vs-sound gap at ~30 ms, matching the literature's 190 vs 160. EDITOR ACTION NEEDED that I cannot express in this schema: the reveal's '170 ms' for a beep should read about 160 ms. New position 0.301 on log 50-5000 (was 0.349), still well inside the band, and note the log range is so wide that this correction barely moves scoring - I am fixing it for accuracy, not fairness.

Verified against the actual rule rather than the claimed source: World Athletics treats any movement within 0.1 s after the gun as a false start, on the basis that the brain cannot hear and process the start signal faster. Critically, the reveal's contrarian claim also checks out - an IAAF-commissioned 2009 study found top sprinters can sometimes react in 0.08 s, and Beijing 2008 analysis found reaction times of 0.109 s (men) and 0.121 s (women) occurring about once in 1,000 starts, so an honest start genuinely can be disqualified. I checked the year-to-year-change risk since that is a drop criterion: the 100 ms threshold has not moved (the 2009 change was to immediate disqualification, not to the threshold), so this is stable. Position 0.253 (log 40-1500). No duplicate.

Springer was paywalled, so I verified the claimed Potter et al. 2014 result through MIT News' report of the study: subjects viewed sequences of 6-12 images at 13-80 ms each searching for a named target, and 'as the researchers decreased exposure time down to the fastest rate of 13 ms, subjects continued to perform better than chance'. The citation is real and the number is right. Reveal arithmetic checked by hand: 24 fps = 41.7 ms per frame, so 'cinema... 42 ms each' is correct and the eye is indeed faster than film. Position 0.159 (log 5-2000) - lowest of the set but above the 0.08 floor. Flag for the editor, not a defect: this set already contains two other reaction/perception-timing items ([10], [11]); consider spreading them across days.

The claimed source is 'widely documented dermatology' and the dermatology literature does not support 15 cm. Wikipedia Human hair growth, citing that literature, gives 'about 1 cm per month on average' (12 cm/yr), with a measured spread of 0.6-3.36 cm/month by hair thickness; the standard cited rate of 0.35 mm/day works out to 12.8 cm/yr. The 15 cm figure comes from the popular 'half an inch a month / six inches a year' formulation - an imperial-rounded number, which is exactly the kind of origin the brief says to distrust. 13 cm/yr is the defensible central value across the sources I checked. Reveal survives and is verified: the anagen phase lasts three to five years and 'scalp hair growth will halt due to follicle devitalization after reaching a length of generally two or three feet (60-90 cm)', which is roughly waist length. New position 0.406 on log 2-200 (was 0.438) - the correction is about accuracy, not scoring, since both land within 4 track-percent.
verdicts.correctedReveal: Each follicle grows for only two to six years, then rests and lets that hair go — which is why everyone has a natural maximum length, and why around 100 hairs leave your head daily. At any moment, 85–95% of scalp follicles are in that growing phase.

verdicts.note: Checked the claimed Yaemsiri 2010 citation and it is real and correctly used: Wikipedia Nail (anatomy) cites Yaemsiri et al. 2010 for fingernails at ~3.5 mm/month and toenails at ~1.6 mm/month. 3.5 x 12 = 42 mm/yr, matching the answer exactly, and 1.6/3.5 = 0.46, so the reveal's 'less than half that rate' for toenails is arithmetically correct. Reveal's finger-length claim confirmed on the same page (index-finger nail grows faster than little-finger nail, tracking terminal phalanx length), and season is listed among the documented determinants; the dominant-hand and summer-vs-winter specifics are in the Yaemsiri paper itself. Position 0.573 (log 3-300). No duplicate.

Guinness's own page 404'd, so I verified against Wikipedia's Xie Qiuping article: hair measured at 5.627 m on 8 May 2004, grown since 1973 from the age of 13. Answer 5.6 m, the 1973 date and the age of 13 in the reveal are all confirmed - every checkable claim in the reveal is right rather than a restatement of the answer. Record still stands as the longest documented. Position 0.655 (log 0.5-20). Consistent in kind with the Guinness items already in verified.json (heaviest watermelon, heaviest pumpkin, biggest bubble), so it fits the game's established style and does not duplicate any of them.

Tried hard to disprove this one. Wikipedia Basal metabolic rate gives a measured mean BMR of 1,500 kcal/day, which is only ~72 W, so if the question meant BMR the answer would be ~30% too high. But the prompt asks what a resting adult 'gives off' in heat, which is total heat emission for a seated person - the quantity building engineers use - and that is the ~100 W figure ASHRAE budgets per seated occupant (roughly 60 W sensible + 40 W latent). The reveal explicitly frames it that way ('Building engineers budget about that much per seated person'), so prompt, answer and reveal are all measuring the same thing consistently, and the packed-lecture-hall consequence follows. Editor should be aware 100 W is the upper-central value and 70-80 W is the BMR-only figure; on log 5-300 that difference is ~6 track-percent, so no player is harmed. Position 0.732. No duplicate.

The scored answer is solid: Wikipedia Human brain confirms the brain is 'about 2% of the total body weight', and the ~20% share of resting energy/oxygen is the standard Clarke and Sokoloff textbook figure, consistent across physiology sources. Partial verification only on the reveal: PNAS and the Kuzawa 2014 press coverage were 403/404 for me, so I could NOT independently confirm 'nearer 60%' for newborns - published figures for the infant brain's share of resting metabolism range from roughly 50% to 87% depending on age and method, so that specific number is the soft spot. The peak-around-age-five claim and the growth-tradeoff theory are Kuzawa's central, widely reported findings (brain glucose uptake peaking near 4.5-5 years at ~66% of resting metabolic rate). Recommend the editor either sources or softens the newborn figure. Position 0.310 (linear 2-60). Does not duplicate the existing '86 billion neurons' question.

Verified the claimed citation directly: Wikipedia Human microbiome attributes ~38 trillion bacterial cells to Sender, Fuchs and Milo (2016) against 30-40 trillion human cells, i.e. the same order of magnitude - so the reveal's 'roughly one bacterium per human cell' is right and is the paper's headline correction. The 10:1 claim originating in a 1972 back-of-the-envelope estimate (Luckey) that stood unchallenged for decades is the framing of the Sender et al. paper itself. This is the rare case where the reveal overturns a myth rather than restating the answer. Position 0.645 (log 0.1-1000). No duplicate - verified.json has neurons, red blood cells and chromosomes but nothing microbial.

DUPLICATE by derivation. verified.json already contains 'How many litres of blood does a resting adult heart pump every minute?' (5 L/min) and 'Roughly how many times does an average adult human heart beat in a single day?' (100,000), both in the space category. Stroke volume is fully determined by those two: 5,000 mL/min divided by 100,000/1440 = 69.4 beats/min gives 72 mL - i.e. this question's answer of 70 mL. Worse, this question's own reveal states 'total output from about 5 litres a minute', which hands a player the answer to the already-published cardiac-output question. The physiology itself is correct (70 mL is the standard stroke volume, and exercise roughly doubling stroke volume while rate triples to exceed 20 L/min is accurate), so this is a drop purely on duplication, not on fact. Position was 0.573 and fine.

The claimed WHO source supports the number: WHO median length-for-age runs ~49.9 cm at birth to ~75.7 cm at 12 months for boys (49.1 to 74.0 for girls), i.e. 25-26 cm, and AAP states about 10 inches in the first year. I did find a lower competing figure - Wikipedia's Child development stages puts first-year growth at roughly 7-9 inches (18-23 cm) - but that is a loose secondary against the definitive growth standard the question actually cites, so I am not dropping on it. Reveal verified on that same page: 'Weight is now approximately three times the child's birth weight' at 12 months (WHO medians give 2.9x, so 'roughly triple' is right), and first-year growth being the fastest of life and never matched again is uncontested. Position 0.682 (linear 10-32); the range is on the tight side given the 18-25 cm spread in secondary sources, so if the editor wants extra safety, widening hi to ~35 would cost nothing. No duplicate.

Could not open the Brysbaert 2019 meta-analysis itself, so I bracketed it: Wikipedia Reading gives 175-320 wpm for adult English silent reading and Speed reading gives ~200-230 wpm for normal reading with comprehension - 238 sits squarely inside both, and it is the exact non-fiction figure from that meta-analysis (fiction 260, reading aloud 183). The reveal's 'about 180 words a minute' aloud therefore matches the same paper, and the comprehension claim is independently confirmed: 'comprehension declines sharply when the reading speed exceeds 400-500 words per minute', with the eye-movement limit being the reason speed-reading claims fail. Position 0.342 (linear 50-600). No duplicate.

Wikipedia Sound pressure's table puts normal conversation at 1 m at 40-60 dB SPL; CDC and NIOSH put it at 60-70 dB. 60 dB is the value both brackets share and the single most-repeated figure, so it is the right anchor even though the surrounding ranges differ. Reveal's physics checked by hand and is correct: 70 dB is exactly ten times the sound intensity of 60 dB on a logarithmic scale, and the 85 dB damage threshold for long exposure is confirmed on the same page (it is the EU workplace hearing-protection trigger). One soft spot for the editor: that page lists a vacuum cleaner at 85 dBA at 1.8 m, and other sources put vacuums anywhere from 70 to 80 dB, so 'a 70 dB vacuum cleaner' is a loose illustration - the 10x arithmetic is right regardless, but a dishwasher or a normal office would be a safer example. Position 0.400 (linear 20-120). No duplicate.

Wikipedia Hearing range confirms ~20 kHz as the upper limit for young healthy adults, while noting the threshold rises sharply above 15 kHz and that ideal laboratory conditions can push detection to 28 kHz - so 20 kHz is the correct conventional answer, not an inflated one. Age-related decline of the upper limit starting from about age eight is confirmed on the same page, supporting the reveal, and the Mosquito deterrent (operating around 17.4 kHz, audible to teenagers and not to older adults) is the real device behind the ringtone claim. I considered dropping this as too-well-known memorisation given 20 Hz-20 kHz is a famous pair, but it is a genuine magnitude estimate on a log 1-100 track and no more memorised than several items already in verified.json. Position 0.651. No duplicate - the existing microwave-frequency question is unrelated.

Wikipedia Yawn confirms an average yawn duration of approximately 6 seconds, matching the answer. Both reveal claims verified on the same page rather than assumed: fetal yawning is documented from 24-36 weeks gestation (with imaging at 30 weeks), and cross-species contagion is real - one study found 21 of 29 dogs yawned when a stranger yawned at them, with the response appearing only in dogs older than about seven months. That makes the reveal genuinely additive. Position 0.647 (linear 0.5-9); hi=9 is tight but the answer sits well inside the band and real yawns cluster at 4-7 s, so the range is honest rather than gamed. No duplicate.

questions.prompt: The full original cut of Kurosawa's Seven Samurai (1954) runs how many minutes?
questions.reveal: Kurosawa shot for nearly a year and overran so badly that the studio twice halted production; the 'recruit a team of specialists' plot has been reused ever since.
questions.reasoningPath: A feature is usually 90-120 min; this is famously an epic with an intermission, so roughly double a normal film: 180-220 min.

questions.prompt: Runtime of Hayao Miyazaki's Spirited Away (2001), in minutes?
questions.reveal: It outgrossed Titanic in Japan and held the country's box-office record for 19 years, until an anime about a demon-slaying swordsman took it in 2020.
questions.reasoningPath: Animated features run short, typically 80-100 min; this one is known as a longer, denser film for older children, so a bit over two hours.

questions.prompt: Runtime of the Indian blockbuster RRR (2022), in minutes?
questions.reveal: Its song 'Naatu Naatu' was filmed outside the presidential palace in Kyiv months before the invasion, and became the first song from an Indian production to win an Academy Award.
questions.reasoningPath: Indian mainstream cinema is built around an interval, so films run near three hours rather than the two-hour international norm: about 170-190 min.

questions.prompt: Béla Tarr's Sátántangó, one of cinema's longest features, runs how many minutes?
questions.reveal: Tarr covered the whole film in roughly 150 shots; the opening, of cattle wandering through a ruined village, lasts more than eight minutes without a cut.
questions.reasoningPath: It is screened as a one-day event with meal breaks, which puts it around seven hours, so somewhere near 420-450 minutes.

questions.prompt: How old, in years, was Orson Welles at the premiere of Citizen Kane in May 1941?
questions.reveal: RKO handed the first-time director final cut, a deal almost unheard of then, and one Welles never obtained again in the remaining 44 years of his career.
questions.reasoningPath: He was already famous for the 1938 War of the Worlds radio broadcast, which he made as a very young man; Kane came three years later, so mid-twenties.

questions.prompt: How old, in years, was Mary Shelley when Frankenstein was first published in 1818?
questions.reveal: It appeared anonymously with a preface written by her husband, so several reviewers assumed Percy Shelley was the author.
questions.reasoningPath: She began it during the famous 1816 Lake Geneva summer as a teenage runaway with Percy Shelley, and publication followed about 18 months later: around 20.

questions.prompt: How old, in years, was Mozart when he composed his first symphony?
questions.reveal: His sister recalled him asking her to remind him to give the horns something worthwhile to play; he was in London at the time, kept quiet while their father was ill.
questions.reasoningPath: He was touring European courts as a keyboard prodigy from about age six, and a symphony needs more craft than playing: a few years after that, so single digits.

questions.prompt: How old, in years, was Jane Austen when Pride and Prejudice was published in 1813?
questions.reveal: She had drafted it at 20 as 'First Impressions'; a publisher refused it without reading a page, and the manuscript sat for 16 years before anyone printed it.
questions.reasoningPath: She died in 1817 aged 41, and her novels all appeared in a burst in her last six years, so at publication she was in her later thirties.

questions.prompt: How old, in years, was García Márquez when One Hundred Years of Solitude appeared in 1967?
questions.reveal: He wrote for 18 months on credit, and when the manuscript was finally posted the couple could only afford half the postage, so they sent the second half first by mistake.
questions.reasoningPath: He was a working journalist for years before the novel and lived until 2014; a first great novel by a seasoned reporter usually lands around 35-45.

questions.prompt: How old, in years, was J.K. Rowling when the first Harry Potter book was published in 1997?
questions.reveal: Bloomsbury paid an advance of £2,500, and the decision to publish hinged on the chairman's eight-year-old daughter reading the first chapter and demanding the rest.
questions.reasoningPath: She had taught abroad, married, had a child and separated before finishing the book, so a decade of adult life after university: around thirty.

questions.prompt: How old, in years, was Stevie Wonder when 'Fingertips' topped the US singles chart in 1963?
questions.reveal: The record is a live recording, and the next act's bass player can be heard shouting 'What key? What key?' as the band vamps on past the planned ending.
questions.reasoningPath: He was billed as 'Little Stevie Wonder' and is the youngest solo artist ever to top that chart, but he was already touring, so early teens rather than a small child.

questions.prompt: Rudyard Kipling is still the youngest Nobel literature laureate. At what age, in years, did he win?
questions.reveal: More than a century later no younger writer has taken it; the typical literature laureate is around 65, because the prize rewards a whole body of work.
questions.reasoningPath: The prize honours a career, so laureates cluster in their sixties; a record-setting young winner would still need a decade or two of famous work: about 40.

questions.prompt: Bloomsbury's first print run of Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone was how many copies?
questions.reveal: Three hundred of them went straight to libraries, which is why an intact first edition is now among the most valuable books printed in the last fifty years.
questions.reasoningPath: An unknown author's first children's book at a small publisher gets a cautious run; the going number for such a gamble is hundreds, not tens of thousands.

questions.prompt: The Hobbit's 1937 first printing ran to how many copies?
questions.reveal: It sold out by Christmas, and the publisher immediately asked for a sequel; Tolkien took seventeen years to deliver The Lord of the Rings.
questions.reasoningPath: A respected London house printing an Oxford professor's odd children's book would risk a modest run: more than a few hundred, well short of ten thousand.

questions.prompt: Roughly how many copies of the Gutenberg Bible were printed in the 1450s?
questions.reveal: About 49 copies survive today and only 21 of those are complete, which makes a single leaf worth more than most whole antique books.
questions.reasoningPath: Handmade paper and vellum were the expensive part, and the buyers were a few hundred monasteries and rich clerics; so a run in the low hundreds.

questions.prompt: Proust's In Search of Lost Time contains roughly how many words?
questions.reveal: Guinness lists it as the longest novel ever published, and Proust died before the final three volumes were edited, so the ending was published posthumously.
questions.reasoningPath: Seven volumes, roughly 4,000 pages, at about 300 words a page gives something over a million words.

questions.prompt: Pink Floyd's The Dark Side of the Moon charted for how many weeks on the US album chart from 1973 to 1988?
questions.reveal: The sound collage that opens it, of heartbeats, clocks and cash registers, was spliced together by hand from tape loops years before samplers existed.
questions.reasoningPath: It stayed on the chart for about fifteen years; at 52 weeks a year that is roughly 780, minus a few gaps.

questions.prompt: Michael Jackson's Thriller spent how many weeks at No. 1 on the US album chart?
questions.reveal: Seven of its nine tracks were issued as singles and every one reached the top ten, which no album had managed before.
questions.reasoningPath: A huge album holds the top spot for a couple of months; the best-selling album ever should be several times that, but under a full year: roughly 30-40 weeks.

questions.prompt: 'Bohemian Rhapsody' spent how many weeks at No. 1 in Britain on its original 1975 release?
questions.reveal: Queen refused to cut the six-minute song down for radio, so a DJ friend simply played the full version fourteen times over one weekend until listeners demanded it.
questions.reasoningPath: Typical chart-toppers of the era held the top for two or three weeks; a generation-defining single over Christmas would hold it for a couple of months.

questions.prompt: Haydn, the most prolific symphonist, wrote how many numbered symphonies?
questions.reveal: Mozart managed 41 and Beethoven only 9: as symphonies grew longer and more personal, composers wrote drastically fewer of them.
questions.reasoningPath: He was a salaried court composer for about thirty years expected to supply new music constantly; a few symphonies a year over that span gives around a hundred.

questions.prompt: Largest free concert ever: how many people filled Rio's Copacabana beach for Rod Stewart in 1994?
questions.reveal: The same beach drew over 1.5 million for Madonna in 2024 and about 2 million for Lady Gaga in 2025, both still short of the record.
questions.reasoningPath: A big stadium holds 80,000; this filled a four-kilometre beach on New Year's Eve in a city of six million, so millions rather than hundreds of thousands.

questions.prompt: How many days did 'Gangnam Style' take to become YouTube's first billion-view video?
questions.reveal: Its count later overflowed YouTube's 32-bit view counter, which topped out near 2.15 billion, and engineers had to rebuild the counter to keep going.
questions.reasoningPath: It was posted in mid-July 2012 and was everywhere by that December, so about five months of exponential growth: around 150 days.

questions.prompt: The complete Bible has been translated into how many languages?
questions.reveal: Some portion of scripture exists in more than 4,000 of the roughly 7,000 languages spoken today, but a full translation takes a team over a decade.
questions.reasoningPath: There are about 7,000 living languages; a complete translation is decades of work, so only the larger ones have it: a high single-digit percentage, a few hundred to a thousand.

questions.prompt: Length of the Beatles' 'Hey Jude', in seconds?
questions.reveal: The 'na-na-na' coda alone runs over four minutes, and at release it was the longest song ever to reach No. 1 on the British chart.
questions.reasoningPath: Singles of the 1960s ran about three minutes; this one is famous for its endless singalong ending, so roughly double that: around seven minutes.

questions.prompt: The Beatles released how many UK studio albums between 1963 and 1970?
questions.reveal: Their first album was recorded in a single day, with Lennon singing 'Twist and Shout' last because it would have wrecked his voice for everything else.
questions.reasoningPath: Seven years of work at the 1960s pace of one or two albums a year, tailing off as sessions grew longer: somewhere between ten and fifteen.

So defensible answers run 11, 12 or 13, and a player who answers 13 from the official catalogue is marked down against 12.
