The reveal is fine and reusable (the Wikipedia article confirms the Beatles 'recorded ten songs during a single studio session' on 11 Feb 1963 for Please Please Me, and Twist and Shout being cut last to spare Lennon's voice is well documented) — but attach it to a question with an unambiguous answer.

questions.prompt: Sagrada Família's central Tower of Jesus Christ, topped out in 2026, stands how many metres tall?
questions.reveal: Gaudí capped it deliberately just under Montjuïc hill, 173 m, on the grounds that a human work should not rise above God's. It passed Ulm Minster's 161.5 m to become the tallest church on Earth.
questions.reasoningPath: A cathedral spire is tall but not skyscraper-tall: Cologne is about 157 m, Ulm about 161 m, and this was built to beat them. Ordinary Barcelona blocks are ~20 m, so think roughly eight of those stacked: ~170 m.

questions.prompt: Interior diameter of the Pantheon's dome in Rome, still the largest unreinforced concrete dome, in metres?
questions.reveal: It is exactly as tall as it is wide, so a sphere would fit perfectly inside. The concrete gets lighter as it climbs — pumice in the top mix — and the 8.9 m oculus has been open to the rain since the second century.
questions.reasoningPath: It holds a few hundred people under one span, so it is bigger than a house and smaller than a stadium. Think of a large church crossing or a modest circus tent, roughly 40 m across.

questions.prompt: How many degrees does the Leaning Tower of Pisa lean from vertical today?
questions.reveal: Engineers pulled it back from a dangerous 5.5 degrees in the 1990s by sucking soil out from beneath the high side. The top still overhangs the base by about 3.9 m.
questions.reasoningPath: The tower is ~56 m tall and the top hangs about 4 m out in photographs. The angle is arctan(4/56), which is a few degrees — visibly tilted but nowhere near the 15 or 20 degrees the pictures feel like.

questions.prompt: In what year AD was Hagia Sophia in Constantinople completed?
questions.reveal: It went up in five years and ten months. That first dome was too flat, cracked in earthquakes, and collapsed in 558; the replacement was rebuilt steeper and has stood ever since.
questions.reasoningPath: It was Justinian's church, and Justinian ruled the Eastern Roman Empire in the mid-500s — after Rome's fall in 476, long before Islam's arrival in 1453. So somewhere in the 500s.

questions.prompt: How many metres tall is the Taj Mahal?
questions.reveal: Its four minarets were built leaning slightly outward, so that in an earthquake they would fall away from the tomb rather than onto it. The marble dome alone accounts for 23 m.
questions.reasoningPath: In photographs a person at the base is a speck about one-fortieth of the height, and the building reads as roughly as tall as it is wide. A 20-storey block is ~60 m; the Taj is in that neighbourhood.

questions.prompt: In what year did the Sydney Opera House open?
questions.reveal: Its shells carry 1,056,006 tiles in two shades. Architect Jørn Utzon quit in 1966 after a funding row, skipped the opening, and never returned to Australia to see it finished.
questions.reasoningPath: The design is modernist concrete-shell work, so post-war; it was famous by the time colour television was normal, and construction dragged 14 years from a late-1950s competition. Early 1970s.

questions.prompt: El Castillo pyramid at Chichén Itzá: how many steps does each of its four staircases have?
questions.reveal: Four staircases plus the top platform make 365 — the pyramid is a calendar. At the equinoxes the afternoon sun throws triangular shadows down the north balustrade, like a serpent sliding to the ground.
questions.reasoningPath: The pyramid is about 24 m tall without its temple, and these steep Maya steps are roughly a 25 cm rise each. 24 m divided by 0.26 m gives about 90.

questions.prompt: How many millions of people speak Mandarin Chinese as their first language?
questions.reveal: Spanish is second with roughly 490 million and English third at about 370 million. English only takes the lead once its billion-odd second-language speakers are counted.
questions.reasoningPath: China has about 1.4 billion people. Mandarin is the standard language but Cantonese, Wu, Min and dozens of others take a real share, so somewhere around two-thirds to three-quarters of the country: roughly a billion.

questions.prompt: About how many living languages are spoken in the world today?
questions.reveal: About 23 languages account for more than half of all people alive, and roughly 40% of the rest are endangered — many with only a few hundred elderly speakers left.
questions.reasoningPath: There are about 200 countries, and most hold far more than one language — Nigeria alone has hundreds, India hundreds more. Average tens per country across 200 countries lands in the thousands, not the hundreds or the millions.

questions.prompt: Papua New Guinea has more languages than any other country. How many living languages?
questions.reveal: That is roughly one language for every 12,000 people, and more than one in ten of every language on Earth, packed into a country about the size of Sweden. Mountain valleys kept neighbours apart for millennia.
questions.reasoningPath: The world has about 7,000 languages and PNG is famously the most diverse place of all — but it cannot hold half of them. A tenth of the global total, for a country of ~10 million, is the right order: several hundred.

questions.prompt: How many characters are in China's official 2013 Table of General Standard Chinese Characters?
questions.reveal: Its first tier of 3,500 covers about 99.5% of everyday printed text. The imperial Kangxi dictionary of 1716 listed over 47,000 characters, the overwhelming majority of them already obsolete.
questions.reasoningPath: Basic literacy is usually put at 2,000–3,000 characters and a fluent reader knows maybe 5,000, while big dictionaries run to tens of thousands. An official modern-use list must sit above literacy level and well below the dictionary: single-digit thousands.

questions.prompt: In what year was the Korean alphabet Hangul promulgated by King Sejong?
questions.reveal: Its consonant shapes are diagrams of the mouth making the sound: ㅁ is the lips, ㄱ the tongue humped against the palate. The literary elite dismissed it as vulgar; Korea now gives it a national holiday.
questions.reasoningPath: It replaced Chinese characters for ordinary Korean writing, and it belongs to the Joseon dynasty's cultural high point — after Europe's medieval period, before Hideyoshi's 1590s invasions. Mid-1400s.

questions.prompt: How many official languages does the European Union have?
questions.reveal: Twenty-seven member states share them: Austria and Germany both use German, Cyprus uses Greek, Belgium's three are all borrowed from neighbours. Every EU law is translated into all of them, Irish included since 2007.
questions.reasoningPath: There are 27 member states and most brought their own language, but a handful share one with a neighbour. So a couple below 27.

questions.prompt: FIFA requires pitches at international matches to be how many metres wide?
questions.reveal: The length is fixed at 105 m for those matches, but the Laws still allow ordinary pitches anywhere from 90 to 120 m long and 45 to 90 m wide — which is why no two old grounds are quite the same shape.
questions.reasoningPath: A pitch is a bit longer than it is wide, and a goalkeeper's kick from his own line reaches roughly the halfway line of a ~100 m field. Width looks about two-thirds of that: high 60s.

questions.prompt: How high is the crossbar of a football goal above the ground, in metres?
questions.reveal: Goals had no crossbar at all until 1875 — a tape was strung between the posts, and anything above it counted. The 7.32 m width has not changed since the first Laws in 1863.
questions.reasoningPath: A goalkeeper of about 1.9 m can just touch the bar with a standing arm raised, which puts it a little above 2.4 m — roughly a tall doorway plus half a metre.

questions.prompt: How many metres separate the two sets of stumps on a cricket pitch?
questions.reveal: That distance is exactly one chain, a Tudor surveyor's unit — ten chains make a furlong and eighty make a mile. The strip itself is only 3.05 m wide, and every delivery must land on it.
questions.reasoningPath: A fast bowler's delivery covers the gap in well under a second at about 140 km/h, which is roughly 39 m per second — so around half a second's flight puts the pitch near 20 m.

questions.prompt: How high is the rim of a basketball hoop above the floor, in metres?
questions.reveal: It has been the same height since 1891, when James Naismith nailed a peach basket to the balcony rail of a gymnasium — the rail simply happened to be at that height, and the game froze it there forever.
questions.reasoningPath: A two-metre player standing under the basket has to reach well above his own raised arm to dunk, but only by a little. That is about a metre above his head: just over three metres.

questions.prompt: How many national associations are members of FIFA?
questions.reveal: That is 18 more than the United Nations has member states. Twenty-three FIFA members are not sovereign countries — England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland count separately, as do Hong Kong, Macau, Gibraltar and Tahiti.
questions.reasoningPath: The UN has 193 members and almost every country plays football. FIFA also admits territories and the four British nations separately, so start at ~193 and add a couple of dozen.

questions.prompt: In what year was the first FIFA World Cup played?
questions.reveal: Only 13 teams entered and just four made the boat trip from Europe. The finalists could not agree whose ball to use, so Argentina's was used in the first half and Uruguay's in the second — Uruguay won 4-2.
questions.reasoningPath: It came after football had spread worldwide but had to be old enough for a long pre-television history, and it was interrupted by the Second World War after only three editions. Three tournaments before 1938, four years apart, puts the first around 1930.

questions.prompt: How tall is the Mona Lisa panel, in centimetres?
questions.reveal: It is painted on a single plank of poplar just 53 cm wide, warped and cracked by five centuries of humidity and braced from behind with butterfly-shaped inserts. Visitors get roughly 30 seconds in front of it.
questions.reasoningPath: Everyone who sees it reports being surprised by how small it is. It is a half-length portrait with a life-size head, so a little under a metre of canvas: head plus torso plus a border.

questions.prompt: How many metres wide is Picasso's Guernica?
questions.reveal: Picasso finished the whole thing in about 35 days in 1937, then refused to let it enter Spain while Franco lived. It hung in New York's Museum of Modern Art until 1981, six years after the dictator's death.
questions.reasoningPath: Photographs show adult viewers standing under it reaching only halfway up, so it is about 3.5 m tall, and it is roughly twice as wide as it is tall. Call it 7 or 8 m — the width of a small house.

questions.prompt: How tall is Michelangelo's David, the statue alone without its plinth, in metres?
questions.reveal: He carved it from a block two earlier sculptors had abandoned as ruined. It then stood outdoors in Florence's main square for nearly 370 years before being moved indoors in 1873; a copy stands there now.
questions.reasoningPath: In gallery photographs the statue is roughly three times the height of the people beneath it, and it was designed to be read from far below on a cathedral roofline. Three adults stacked is a bit over five metres.

questions.prompt: How many terracotta warriors are thought to be buried in the pits at Xi'an?
questions.reveal: Most are still underground, and they were once painted in brilliant colours. The lacquer beneath the paint curls within about fifteen seconds of meeting dry air and flakes away in four minutes, so digging now waits for better methods.
questions.reasoningPath: Photographs of the main pit show ranks roughly 10 wide and 60 deep — about 6,000 figures — and there are two smaller pits beside it. So several thousand, not hundreds and not a million.

questions.prompt: How many metres long is the Bayeux Tapestry?
questions.reveal: It is only 50 cm tall, and it is not a tapestry at all but an embroidery in wool on linen. It also carries the earliest known picture of Halley's Comet, which crossed the sky in the spring of 1066.
questions.reasoningPath: It tells the whole Norman conquest in about 58 numbered scenes, and each scene needs roughly a metre of cloth to hold its figures and its Latin caption. That is a strip the length of a running track's straight.

questions.prompt: How many years did Michelangelo spend painting the Sistine Chapel ceiling?
questions.reveal: He worked standing on a scaffold of his own design with his head tilted back — not lying down, as the legend has it — and complained in a poem that his beard pointed at heaven while the brush dripped in his face.
questions.reasoningPath: The vault is about 35 m by 14 m, and a fresco painter must finish each patch of plaster the same day. With assistants grinding and plastering, a few hundred square metres of figures works out to a handful of years, not decades.

DISPROVED as worded. I read IFAB Law 1 directly at theifab.com/laws/latest/the-field-of-play: for international matches the law permits length 100–110 m and WIDTH 64–75 m, and explicitly says 'competitions may determine the length of the goal line and touchline within the above dimensions'. So FIFA does not 'require' 68 m at international matches — a knowledgeable player answering 64 or 75 would be marked down against a figure the Laws do not mandate. The 105 x 68 figure is FIFA's own competition/stadium standard; the Wikipedia football pitch article words it as 'FIFA recommends that the field of play measures exactly 105 metres long and 68 metres wide'. The reveal is also wrong: it claims 'the length is fixed at 105 m for those matches', which contradicts Law 1's 100–110 m. Its other half (90–120 m by 45–90 m for ordinary pitches) is correct per IFAB. Fix: reword the prompt as supplied and rewrite the reveal to say the Laws allow 100–110 m by 64–75 m for internationals and 90–120 m by 45–90 m elsewhere, which is why old grounds differ. Answer 68 and range 30..120 are fine (position 0.422).

verdicts.note: The graded number is right — Wikipedia's football pitch and goal articles both give the crossbar at 8 ft (2.44 m) and the posts 8 yd (7.32 m) apart, matching the IFAB Laws. But the REVEAL is factually inverted. Per the Laws of the Game history: before 1866 goals could be scored at ANY height; in 1866 a tape was added between the posts and the ball had to pass UNDER it; in 1875 a crossbar became an allowed alternative to tape; in 1883 the crossbar became compulsory. The reveal's 'a tape was strung between the posts, and anything above it counted' states the opposite of the rule — above the tape did NOT count. Keep the answer 2.44, range 1.5..4 (position 0.376), but replace the reveal with something like: 'Until 1866 a goal counted at any height at all. That year a tape was strung between the posts and the ball had to pass under it; a solid crossbar became optional in 1875 and compulsory in 1883. The 7.32 m width has not changed since the first Laws in 1863.' The 1863 eight-yard width is correct as written.
verdicts.correctedReveal: Under the FA's original laws a goal had no upper limit — a shot counted however high it flew between the posts. A tape was strung across in 1866, and a solid crossbar only became compulsory in 1883.
